searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded; grey-pinkish when young, becoming brown with maturity
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat or slightly depressed; cream, beige to brownish; smooth when young, with brownish scales; margin initially inrolled
searchText.stipe: Short, very stout, solid, cylindrical to slightly tapering toward base; whitish, often browning below; thick sheathing ring
searchText.spore-print: Spore print chocolate-brown to dark brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic in grasslands, coastal dunes, sandy and saline soils, parks, roadsides and other disturbed urban habitats, notably where winter road salt accumulates; solitary or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but generally not highly valued
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–8 cm long and ~2–5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, thick and firm, turning pinkish-red to reddish-orange when cut or bruised, sometimes slowly
searchText.odour: Variable; mild mushroomy or faintly anise-like when young, often becoming briny, iodine-like or fishy with age
searchText.taste: Mild when young, sometimes unpleasant or iodine-like in mature specimens
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ovoid to subglobose, smooth, thick-walled, dark brown, ~5.5–7.5 × 5–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, clavate to cylindrical
searchText.overview: Stout salt-tolerant Agaricus with coarse brownish scales and reddening flesh

searchText.hymenium: Gills free, close to crowded; pale pink when young, becoming reddish-brown to dark chocolate-brown at maturity
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; white to whitish, smooth or finely flaky/scaly, often dirty with soil; thick and firm
searchText.stipe: Short, stout, solid, cylindrical to slightly tapering or enlarged below; whitish, smooth to finely scaly near apex; with a thick sheathing double ring
searchText.description: Saprobic on compacted or disturbed soil, roadsides, paths, gardens, parks, verges, cracks in paving and sometimes pushing through asphalt; late spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible and firm-textured
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~2–10 cm long, ~1–4 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh white, thick, firm, usually unchanging when cut, very rarely slightly pinkish in wet/old specimens
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative on cap surface, no yellowing
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, thick-walled, ~5–7 × 4–5.5 µm; basidia mostly 2- to 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia inconspicuous or basidiole-like; pleurocystidia absent
searchText.overview: Compact pavement mushroom emerging from hard-packed urban soil

searchText.hymenium: Crowded; whitish when very young, becoming greyish-pink to pink and finally dark chocolate-brown as spores mature
searchText.cap: Initially hemispherical to convex, later broadly convex or almost flat; pale cream beneath appressed brown fibrils or scales, often darkest toward the centre; margin may retain veil fragments when young
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Free — gills do not reach the stipe
searchText.stipe: Robust, whitish, cylindrical to slightly clavate or tapering and often rooting deeply; substantial superior to median ring, with whitish to brownish veil zones or a characteristic boot-like sheath below the ring
searchText.spore-print: Spore print chocolate-brown to dark brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on humus-rich, disturbed or grassy ground (parks, gardens and roadside verges); often reported sharing soil with other Agaric species (A. bitorquis, A. bisporus, A. campestris); gregarious; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but of indifferent or poor culinary quality
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–12 cm long and ~1.5–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh whitish, firm; may remain unchanged or slowly stain pale pink to reddish when cut, particularly toward the stipe base; never characteristically yellow-staining
searchText.odour: Mild, mushroomy, sometimes becoming liquorice-like in old specimens
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, thick-walled, brown in KOH, ~6–8 × 4–5.5 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia abundant, clavate to subclavate, ~20–30 × 6–8 µm; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis
searchText.overview: Robust brown-scaled Agaricus of parks and disturbed ground

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded, whitish when very young, becoming greyish-pink to pink and finally chocolate-brown as spores mature
searchText.cap: Ovoid to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; white to cream, smooth to finely silky-fibrillose; slowly bruising yellow to ochre-yellow, particularly near the margin
searchText.stipe: Slender, white, cylindrical, usually with a distinctly bulbous base; yellowing when handled; large, thin, pendulous white ring, often with yellowish floccose scales or a cogwheel-like pattern beneath
searchText.ecology: Saprobic in coniferous, deciduous and mixed woodland; alone, scattered or gregariously, often among leaf or needle litter; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Good edible, with pleasant flavour
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–10 cm long and ~1–2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, firm, sometimes faintly yellowing when cut; bruised outer surfaces gradually yellow to ochre
searchText.chemical-reactions: Schaeffer reaction positive, orange-red on cap surface; KOH yellow
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, ~5–6.5 × 3.5–4.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, subglobose to ellipsoid or clavate
searchText.overview: White woodland Agaricus with aniseed odour, yellow bruising and a bulbous stipe base

searchText.hymenium: Crowded; whitish when very young, becoming pinkish and finally dark chocolate-brown as spores mature
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; whitish to cream or pale grey-brown, smooth to finely fibrillose, often somewhat squared or flattened at the centre; bruises rapidly bright chrome-yellow, especially along the margin
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Free — gills do not reach the stipe
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, whitish, slightly enlarged or bulbous at base; rapidly stains bright yellow when rubbed or cut, particularly at the base; with a large, persistent, flaring double ring with a thickened outer margin
searchText.spore-print: Spore print very dark brown to chocolate-brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on nutrient-rich and disturbed soils (lawns, gardens, parks, roadside verges, hedgerows); solitary to clustered or forming arcs; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous,causes gastrointestinal poisoning
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–15 cm long and ~1–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh white, sometimes weakly yellowing elsewhere but turning conspicuously bright chrome-yellow in the stipe base when cut or bruised, yellow colour may later fade or become brownish
searchText.odour: Strongly phenolic, ink-like, iodine-like or carbolic, intensified by cooking
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, brownish in KOH, ~4.5–5 × 3–4 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia clavate to subcylindrical, ~20–30 × 4–8 µm; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis
searchText.overview: Toxic white Agaricus distinguished by its extremely rapid chrome-yellow bruising and strong phenolic odour

searchText.hymenium: Gills close to crowded, whitish at first, becoming dull greyish-brown to clay-brown as spores mature
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; whitish, cream to dull yellowish, slightly tacky when fresh but soon dry; often cracking with age and retaining pale veil fragments around the margin
searchText.stipe: Rigid, cylindrical, whitish, sometimes browning toward the base; with a thin, fragile and often short-lived whitish ring
searchText.ecology: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, fields, grassy roadside verges and gardens; solitary, scattered, gregarious or occasionally in fairy rings; late spring to summer
searchText.edibility: Reported as edible after thorough cooking but bitter and of poor quality
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~5–10 cm long, ~0.3–1.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh white, firm, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative to yellowish on the cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, 11–16(–19) × 6–9(–10) µm, with a conspicuous germ pore; basidia clavate, 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia and pleurocystidia broadly utriform to clavate
searchText.overview: Pale grassland fieldcap with a frequently cracked cap and fringed veil remnants

searchText.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced; creamy-beige to pale yellow-brown when young, becoming grey-brown to rust-brown with maturity; edges often paler
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; smooth, sometimes slightly greasy or sticky when fresh; honey-yellow, ochre-yellow to pale brownish-yellow, fading when dry; young margin may retain ephemeral white veil fragments
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnexed to narrowly adnate, sometimes with a slight decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, whitish to pale ochre-yellow or cap-coloured; finely pruinose to fibrillose, solid when young and becoming hollow; ring absent, with white basal mycelium or fine rhizomorphs
searchText.spore-print: Spore print dark brown to dull cinnamon-brown
searchText.description: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, pastures, grassy parkland, roadside verges and dune grasslands; occasionally on compost, manure or woodchips; alone or gregariously; spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; insubstantial, easily confused
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2–8 cm long and ~0.2–0.6 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish, thin, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH red to pink on cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, ~9.5–15(–18) × 7–10 µm, with a conspicuous germ pore; basidia 4-spored with basal clamps; cheilocystidia lageniform to ventricose, often capitate; pleurocystidia sparse or absent
searchText.overview: Small honey-yellow grassland fieldcap with no persistent ring

searchText.hymenium: Pores very small, round to angular, white to cream when fresh, sometimes faintly yellowish or greenish when bruised; ~3–5 pores per mm
searchText.cap: Irregularly rounded, convex to flattened or centrally depressed; often strongly fused with neighbouring caps; cream, apricot, salmon-orange to pinkish-buff or ochre, dry and smooth, sometimes cracking with age
searchText.stipe: Short, stout, central to eccentric or lateral; whitish to cream or pinkish-buff, smooth, frequently fused with adjacent stipes in clustered fruit bodies
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers (spruce, boreal conifers); terrestrial on forest soil, gregarious and commonly forming large fused clusters; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible when young but generally considered mediocre; older specimens become tough and the taste may be bitter or cabbage-like
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to very large when clustered; individual stipes ~3–8 cm long and ~1–3 cm thick; fused masses may reach ~30–50 cm across
searchText.flesh: Flesh cream to whitish, thick and fairly soft when fresh, becoming firm or hard when dry; often developing pale pink, salmon or brick-red tones on drying
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH Purple on cap, pore surface and flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, weakly amyloid, ~4–5.5 × 2.5–4 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cystidia absent; hyphal system monomitic with frequent clamp connections and scattered gloeoplerous hyphae
searchText.overview: Terrestrial conifer-associated polypore forming large fused masses of apricot- to salmon-coloured caps

searchText.hymenium: Pores, small and round (≈2–5/mm), white to creamy or pale yellow; pores may become slightly angular near stipe
searchText.cap: Convex to flat or shallowly depressed, surface smooth when young, often developing areolate pattern in maturity; color white to off-white, buff with age
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent pores (pores extend down the stipe)
searchText.stipe: Central or slightly off-center, color whitish to tan; smooth to faintly velvety; may be stout or thick
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers, terrestrial, occurs in clusters, august to october
searchText.edibility: Edible (young, properly cooked), slimy or laxative effect reported
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large, stipe 3–10 cm long, 1–4 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Cut surface slowly turns yellowish, then greenish, then turns gray
searchText.chemical-reactions: Flesh turns dirty golden yellow with KOH application
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, ~4.0–5.0×2.5–3.5µm, inamyloid, often with a germ pore, no clamp connections
searchText.overview: Fleshy polypore found beneath conifers, with a white-to-buff cracked cap, decurrent white pores, and a stout stipe

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to faintly cream or citrine-tinged, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to almost flat; pale lemon-yellow, citrine, straw-yellow to nearly white; usually carrying irregular whitish to ochraceous universal-veil patches or warts; margin generally non-striate
searchText.stipe: White to pale yellowish, cylindrical and tapering upward; prominent abruptly marginate basal bulb surrounded by an adherent circumscissile volva forming a gutter-like rim; large persistent, pendulous pale ring
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods or conifers; alone, scattered, or gregariously; in forests and woodland edges; neutral to alkaline soils; summer and autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, potential confusion with toxic species and mild toxicity
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–8(–13) cm long and ~0.6–2.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, sometimes faintly citrine immediately beneath the cap surface; fairly firm and unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores globose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, approximately ~6.5–10 × 6–9 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; lamellar trama bilateral
searchText.overview: Pale lemon-yellow woodland Amanita

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, broad, with shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to almost flat; grey-brown, olive-brown to dark brown; usually covered with irregular whitish-grey to grey universal-veil patches or warts; margin generally non-striate
searchText.stipe: White to greyish, robust, cylindrical and tapering upward from a swollen base; smooth or striate above the ring and finely scaly below; ring broad, membranous, persistent and distinctly striate above; volva fragmented and inconspicuous, without a distinct gutter-like rim
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; alone, scattered or gregariously; in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests and woodland edges; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible after thorough cooking but not recommended; toxic raw and easily confused
searchText.uses-compounds: Thermolabile hemolysins present in raw fruit bodies
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~8–15 cm long and ~1.5–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, firm, usually unchanging when cut; occasionally faintly pinkish or reddish toward the stipe base
searchText.odour: Faint radish-like to slightly unpleasant, sometimes indistinct
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~8–11 × 6–8.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidia
searchText.overview: Grey-brown woodland Amanita with grey veil patches and a distinctly striate ring

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Ovoid to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat with a small central umbo; tawny-orange, reddish-brown to orange-brown, usually without veil remnants; margin prominently striate
searchText.stipe: Slender, fragile, hollow, white to pale tawny, tapering upward and often finely fibrillose; ring absent; base enclosed in a large loose, sack-like white volva that may become stained tawny-brown
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers, especially birch, oak, chestnut, pine and spruce; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests and woodland paths; particularly acidic soils; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible only after thorough cooking, but not recommended due to possible toxicity when raw and dangerous confusion
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~7–16 cm long and ~0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, soft and relatively thin; unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores globose to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, non-amyloid, ~9–12.5 × 9–12.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidia; lamellar trama bilateral
searchText.overview: Tawny-orange ringless woodland Amanita with a striate cap margin and large sack-like volva

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; bright scarlet-red; covered with loose white universal-veil warts that may wash away; margin increasingly striate at maturity
searchText.stipe: White, cylindrical to clavate, tapering upward; basal bulb surrounded by concentric rings or scales of volval remnants; large membranous, pendulous white ring, sometimes with a yellowish margin
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers (birch, pine and spruce); alone, scattered or gregariously; sandy or peaty soils; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous and psychoactive
searchText.uses-compounds:
Used as microdosing nootrop and as folk medicine
Ibotenic acid, muscimol, muscarine
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large; stipe ~8–25 cm long and ~1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, with yellow to orange-yellow tissue immediately beneath the cap skin; unchanging when cut or bruised
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–10.5 × 6–8 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored
searchText.overview: Iconic red woodland Amanita with white veil warts, pendulous ring and concentric volval rings around a bulbous base

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; yellow, golden-yellow to orange-yellow or tawny-orange, sometimes darker centrally; covered with yellowish to whitish universal-veil warts that may wash away; margin increasingly striate at maturity
searchText.stipe: White to faintly yellowish, cylindrical to clavate, tapering upward; basal bulb surrounded by concentric rings or scales of yellowish volval remnants; large membranous, pendulous pale ring
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers, especially beech, birch, spruce and pine; alone, scattered or gregariously; deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests; often acidic to siliceous soils; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous and psychoactive; causes variable neurological intoxication and gastrointestinal symptoms
searchText.uses-compounds:
Historically used in folk and ethnomycological practices
Ibotenic acid, muscimol, muscarine
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~8–20 cm long and ~1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, sometimes yellowish immediately beneath the cap skin; unchanging when cut or bruised
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–10.5 × 6–8 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; gill trama bilateral
searchText.overview: Yellow to orange-yellow fly agaric with pale veil warts, pendulous ring and concentric volval rings around a bulbous base

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, broad, with numerous shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; ochre-brown, hazel-brown to dark brown; covered with numerous pure white to cream universal-veil warts that may wash away; margin distinctly striate at maturity
searchText.stipe: White, cylindrical and tapering upward; base distinctly bulbous, with an adherent volva forming a characteristic collar or gutter-like rim and often one or more concentric rings above; membranous, pendulous white ring, usually smooth on its upper surface
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with hardwoods; alone, scattered or gregariously; deciduous, mixed forests and woodland edges; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous and psychoactive; severe neurological intoxication with agitation, confusion, hallucinations, ataxia, CNS depression and gastrointestinal symptoms
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–15 cm long and ~0.6–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, firm, unchanging when cut or bruised; does not redden
searchText.odour: Mild to indistinct, sometimes slightly radish-like or raw-potato-like when bruised
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–12 × 6–8 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidial bases
searchText.overview: Brown woodland Amanita with pure white veil warts, striate cap margin, smooth ring and characteristic gutter-like volval collar around a bulbous base

searchText.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae; developing pinkish to reddish stains when bruised or with age
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; highly variable, pale pinkish-brown, grey-brown, reddish-brown to dark brown; usually covered with irregular greyish-white, pinkish-grey to brownish universal-veil warts; margin generally non-striate
searchText.stipe: White to pale pinkish, cylindrical, often slightly enlarged or bulbous at base; progressively staining pink to wine-red when damaged; volva poorly developed and usually disappearing with age; membranous, pendulous ring distinctly striate on upper surface
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; alone, scattered or gregariously; deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests; especially frequent on acidic, nutrient-poor soils; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible only after thorough cooking; poisonous raw, easily confused
searchText.uses-compounds: Rubescenslysin, a thermolabile haemolytic/cytolytic protein toxin
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~7–15 cm long and ~1–2(–3) cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, slowly turning pale pink, wine-red to reddish when cut, bruised or damaged, especially in the stipe base and around insect tunnels
searchText.odour: Mild, indistinct, mushroomy; sometimes unpleasant in old specimens
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~8–10 × 5–7 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidial bases; lamellar trama bilateral
searchText.overview: Brown-pink woodland Amanita characteristically blushing wine-red wherever damaged

species.identification: Ampulloclitocybe clavipes (Pers.) Redhead, Lutzoni, Moncalvo & Vilgalys

searchText.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced, with frequent lamellulae; white to cream when young, becoming pale ochre to brownish with age
searchText.cap: Convex to nearly flat when young, later centrally depressed to funnel-shaped; smooth to slightly rugged centrally; grey-brown, yellow-brown to dark brown, usually darker at centre and paler toward margin
searchText.stipe: Short, robust, buff to pale brownish; characteristically club-shaped or bulbous at base, though sometimes nearly equal with age; base often spongy with white mycelium; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Ecology uncertain, reported as saprobic or possibly mycorrhizal; primarily under conifers, sometimes hardwoods; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests, mainly heathland; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, not recommended; alcohol may trigger a disulfiram-like reaction
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~2.5–8 cm long and ~0.5–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, soft to spongy, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid or elongated-ellipsoid, smooth to minutely ornamented, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6–10 × 3–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; occasional clavate pseudocystidia; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Grey-brown funnel with strongly decurrent gills and a distinctive club-shaped stipe

species.identification: Antherospora scillae (Cif.) R.Bauer, M.Lutz, Begerow, Piątek & Vánky

searchText.hymenium: hymenium is not applicable due to the nature of the organism, which is a rust fungus
searchText.cap: cap is not applicable, as rust fungi do not form traditional mushroom caps
searchText.stipe: stipe is not applicable
searchText.spore-print: spore print is not typically obtained, but the spores are often orangish or rust-colored
searchText.ecology: ecology is parasitic, typically found on the leaves, stems, and bulbs of Scilla species and other host plants
searchText.edibility: not applicable, as rust fungi are not typically considered for consumption
searchText.fruit-body: size varies, but the fungal structures visible on the host plant are typically very small
searchText.overview: Rust fungus that infects members of the Scilla genus, a group of flowering plants commonly known as squills. It forms tiny, pustule-like structures on the surfaces of the host plants, which release spores to infect new hosts. The life cycle of rust fungi is complex and involves different types of spores that serve various purposes in the fungus's reproductive process.

searchText.hymenium: Irregular, maze-like or labyrinthine pores with a whitish to cream coloration.
searchText.cap: Absent or indistinct, as this species primarily forms resupinate fruiting bodies directly on the substrate.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Resupinate, forming a thin, crust-like layer directly on the substrate.
searchText.stipe: Absent.
searchText.description: White.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, primarily found on dead or decaying hardwoods, often on fallen branches or logs in forested habitats.
searchText.edibility: Not typically considered edible.
searchText.fruit-body: The fruiting bodies can vary widely in size and shape, ranging from small patches to extensive crust-like formations.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoidal to cylindrical, smooth, 4-6 x 2-3 µm.
searchText.overview: Characterized by its resupinate growth form, forming thin, crust-like fruiting bodies directly on the substrate. Grows on alder wood where Inonotus radiatus already decomposed.

searchText.hymenium: Internal gleba is white and firm when young, turning olive-brown and powdery as it matures, filled with spores
searchText.cap: Pear-shaped to round, covered with small, fine spines or granules that wear off with age, giving the surface a smooth, pale brown to tan appearance
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Gasteroid fungi, spore mass is internal)
searchText.stipe: Pseudostipe, shorter and less defined, often off-center or absent, typically blends with the cap, leading to its pear-like shape
searchText.spore-print: Spore print olive-brown to dark brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing in dense clusters on decaying wood, especially stumps and logs of both deciduous and coniferous trees, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible when young, but only before the gleba turns dark and powdery, not highly regarded, though safe to eat when firm and white inside
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, up to 3–5 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores round, 3.5–4.5 µm, covered with fine spines or warts, produced inside gleba
searchText.overview: Small, pear-shaped puffball that grows on decaying wood, often found in dense clusters

searchText.hymenium: Gills, white when young, yellow-to-cream tinged with age, spacing moderate to somewhat distant
searchText.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age, honey-yellow to red-brown, often darker toward the center, surface smooth or slightly scaly-toward center, sticky when wet, margin may become striate or wavy
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, tapering at base, upper portion paler, whitish, lower portion yellow-brown to reddish, has a prominent ring, base with dark black rhizomorphs and connected clumps
searchText.ecology: Parasitic (causes root rot) and saprotrophic on dead wood, found at the base of living or dead trees, on stumps, especially hardwoods, in dense clusters
searchText.edibility: Edible and choice, young specimens preferred, ring and caps more palatable
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large clusters, stipe 5–17 cm long, 0.5–3 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: No widely documented dramatic color chemical reactions
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, with a prominent apiculus, 6–9 × 4–6 µm; hyaline in KOH; basidia 2- and 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia present (25–40 × 2.5–10 µm), thin-walled, pleurocystidia absent
searchText.overview: Honey-coloured clustered mushroom that grows parasitically and saprotrophically on woody bases of trees

searchText.hymenium: Gills, arising from cap margin, moderate spacing, slightly darker than cap surface.
searchText.cap: Fan- or kidney-shaped, thin and sessile; smooth surface, medium grey-brown, margin incurved when young, later lobed; base attached by a fuzzy tomentum.
searchText.stipe: Lateral, short, pale brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic and bryophilous, growing on dead wood fragments, on mossy soil among twigs and debris along forest paths
searchText.edibility: Edibility too small and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, up to ~15 mm across
searchText.microscopy: Spores narrowly elliptical to lacrymoid, smooth, hyaline, average ~7.4×3.8µm, basidia 4-spored, 21–25×6–7µm, cystidia absent, clamps present
searchText.overview: Tiny, grey-brown oysterling growing on wood debris or mossy soil among forest litter

searchText.hymenium: Gills, smooth, typically pale gray-brown, decurrent to slightly decurrent, moderately spaced
searchText.cap: Convex to shallowly umbilicate or funnel-shaped, smooth to finely tomentose, gray to brownish-gray, often scaly at the center when fresh
searchText.stipe: Thin, cylindrical, smooth or slightly pruinose, pale gray to brownish, sometimes with whitish basal mycelium
searchText.ecology: Sphagnicolous—grows in association with Sphagnum mosses, found in bogs, wet heaths, and moss-rich coniferous substrates
searchText.edibility: Inedible—too small and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe generally 3–6 cm long, thin
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, 6.8–12.4 × 3.4–5.1 µm, basidia 4-spored, ~24 × 7 µm
searchText.overview: Small, omphalinoid gray to brownish peatland mushroom

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering the outer surfaces of the branches; whitish to pale yellowish, becoming tan or faintly pinkish with age
searchText.fruit-body:
Repeatedly branched, coral- to candelabra-shaped; branch tips characteristically crown-shaped, each ending in a shallow cup surrounded by 3–6 pointed teeth
Fruit body medium; ~4–13 cm tall and ~2–10 cm wide
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
searchText.stipe: Short basal trunk, whitish to pinkish-brown, finely fuzzy, repeatedly dividing into upright branches
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on well-decayed hardwood logs and fallen trunks, especially aspen, poplar, ash; solitary to clustered; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Young specimens reported edible, but often tough, peppery or bitter
searchText.flesh: Whitish, tough and pliable, sometimes slowly browning when bruised
searchText.chemical-reactions: FeSO₄ negative to greyish or brownish on branches and base
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, minutely pitted, hyaline, amyloid, ~4–5 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia variably fusoid, cylindrical or clavate; gloeoplerous hyphae present; clamp connections abundant
searchText.overview: Crown-tipped hardwood coral with miniature cup-like branch ends

observations.location: Vienna - Am Mühlwasser, Danube-Auen National Park, Austria

searchText.hymenium: Apothecial disc surface smooth, gelatinous, violet-pink to purple, underside sometimes finely fuzzy or lighter in tone
searchText.apothecium: Begins as irregular, brain-like gelatinous lobes (anamorphic form), then becomes more cup- or disc-shaped, lobed margin
searchText.stipe: Absent / rudimentary when present
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on heavily decayed hardwood, autumn to winter, in clustered patches
searchText.description: Insignificant
searchText.fruit-body: Apothecium size up to ~5–15 cm when clustered (discs merging)
searchText.dimensions: Individual apothecia few mm to ~1–2 cm in diameter
searchText.flesh: Flesh gelatinous, fleshy, violet-pink unchanging color
searchText.microscopy: Spores fusiform/ellipsoid, hyaline, smooth, ~13–21×3.5–5 µm; biguttulate early, asci 8-spored cylinders (~115–130×8–10 µm), paraphyses filiform (~1–2 µm width)
searchText.overview: Gelatinous, violet-pink disc fungus that begins as brain-like lobes and later forms cup-shaped apothecia en masse on decaying wood

searchText.hymenium: Gills—thick, distant, often reduced or poorly formed, sometimes vein-like rather than clearly gilled, whitish to pale grey
searchText.cap: Convex to nearly round, dry, initially whitish and a bit lumpy or roughened, quickly becoming covered by a dense orangish-brown chlamydospores powder
searchText.stipe: Slender, more or less equal, surface dry, initially whitish or pale, becoming powdery orangish-brown, basal mycelium white
searchText.ecology: Parasitic on decaying mushrooms (Russula, Lactarius spp.), appears when the host has begun to blacken and decay, singly, groups in mixed, hardwood, coniferous forests, summer through autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible—too insubstantial, with foul smell
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 4–30 mm long, ~2–5 mm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: No significant staining reactions noted, flesh unchanging when cut
searchText.odour: Rotten and foul to decaying fungi substrate
searchText.microscopy: Basidiospores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline in KOH, ~5–6 × 4–5 µm, 4-sterigmate, chlamydospores globose to subglobose, ornamented, 16–20 × 14–17 µm, hyaline to faintly yellowish
searchText.overview: Parasite fungi with malformed gills that fruiting on decaying Russula mushrooms, unique due to prolific asexual spore production.

searchText.hymenium: Teeth densely crowded, cylindrical and pointed, ~1–3 mm long; whitish when young, becoming pale brown to grey-brown with age
searchText.cap: Kidney- to semicircular, broadly convex to flat; dry, finely bristly or hairy, sometimes smoother with age; reddish-brown, chestnut to nearly black, usually with a paler margin
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile teeth cover the underside of the cap
searchText.stipe: Slender, tough, lateral to strongly eccentric; reddish-brown to dark brown, densely hairy; often arising directly from a buried cone
searchText.ecology: Saprobic primarily on fallen and often partly buried pine cones, occasionally other conifer cones and litter; solitary or scattered; coniferous and mixed forests; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible; tiny, tough and leathery
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2–7 cm long and up to ~0.3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to brownish, thin, fibrous and tough, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH instantly black on cap and stipe
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, finely warted to minutely spiny at maturity, hyaline, amyloid, ~4–6 × 3.5–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia fusoid, clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Tiny dark tooth fungus growing characteristically from fallen pine cones

searchText.plasmodium-color: Often yellowish, turning brown with age
searchText.fruit-body: Stalked sporangia
searchText.ecology: Habitat: Decaying wood, leaves, and organic material
searchText.description: Lifecycle stages: Amoeba → multicellular slug → sporulating fruit body
searchText.overview: Recognizable by its utricular sporangia, the Badhamia utricularis slime mold can be found on rotting wood and leaves. Its lifecycle is captivating, shifting from amoeba-like cells, grouping to form a slug-like mass, and eventually becoming the fruiting body. As a decomposer, it helps recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems, and its distinct sporangia offer a fascinating study for mycologists and naturalists alike.

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, white to pale cream when young, becoming yellowish or slightly brownish with age
searchText.cap: Initially convex, flattening with age, surface smooth and dry, pale tan to light brown, sometimes slightly translucent-striate near the edges
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, usually with a finely fibrillose surface, cream to pale tan, slightly darker towards the base, no ring or veil
searchText.description: Saprobic, primarily on decaying conifer cones, especially those of pine and spruce, found in clusters or groups, late autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, due to small size and insubstantial flesh
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, delicate structure, stipe 1.5-5 cm long and 1-2 mm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative or faintly olive on cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical to nearly cylindric, smooth, amyloid, 3-4.5 x 1.5-2 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Small, delicate mushroom that grows directly from decaying conifer cones

searchText.hymenium: Pores, small and angular (≈5–7 / mm), initially greyish, aging to dark grey or black, forming the undersurface of the bracket
searchText.cap: Bracket- or shelf-like, sometimes effused-reflexed, upper surface velvety, pale buff, tan to greyish, often zoned, margin whitish when young
searchText.stipe: Absent
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic (weakly parasitic) on dead hardwoods, causing white-rot of fallen logs, stumps, autumn to winter (year-round)
Inedible - tough, leathery
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium
searchText.flesh: Flesh whitish to buff, leathery-corky, no color change
searchText.microscopy: Spores roughly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~4–6×2.5–3.5 µm, clamp-connections, no cystidia
searchText.overview: Bracket fungus, forms thin, overlapping shelves or flattened crusts on the dead wood of hardwood trees

observations.location: Kullamaa Püha Nikolause kirik, Läänemaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Pores, angular to slightly irregular, ≈2–5/mm, color buff to pale smoky-gray when young, later darker, surface clearly separated from tissue by a darker line
searchText.bracket: Sessile, often effused-reflexed, buff to pale ochre or smoky-buff above, surface finely tomentose, zoned, margin thin
searchText.stipe: Absent
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot in hardwoods, dead or decaying broadleaf wood (logs, stump), year-round
Inedible - tough, leathery
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium
searchText.flesh: Flesh buff to pale, tough, cork-like
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, short-cylindrical to ellipsoid, hyaline, ~5.5–7×2.5–3.5 µm, basidia club-shaped, ~20–22 µm long
searchText.overview: Wood-decaying bracket fungus, forming thin but firm shelf-like fruit bodies on dead hardwood

searchText.hymenium: Pores—small, rounded, whitish when young, aging to greenish-yellow or olive tones
searchText.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age, smooth to slightly velvety or slightly sticky when moist, color ranges from light tan to reddish-brown
searchText.stipe: Solid, robust, cylindrical to slightly clubbed, whitish to pale cream with a fine reticulate pattern, especially near the apex
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers and deciduous trees (pines, spruces, oaks, beeches) in forest or mixed settings, fruits in summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Choice edible, highly prized for flavor and texture
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large, stipe 8–20 x ~10 cm
searchText.flesh: Flesh is white and unchanging when cut, no blue staining
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH reaction: dull orange color change on the flesh, cap surface remains negative
searchText.microscopy: Spores subfusiform (ellipsoid to spindle-shaped), smooth, ~14–17×5–7µm, basidia predominantly 4-sterigmate.
searchText.overview: Large, robust, edible bolete with a brown, convex cap, white flesh that resists staining, stipe adorned with a reticulation

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.cap: 8-25 cm in diameter. Convex to broadly convex, sometimes flat in older specimens. The surface is velvety to slightly sticky, deep brown to reddish-brown.
searchText.hymenium: Tubular or poroid. Pores are initially small and red but become yellowish and larger with age, often staining blue when bruised.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly descending on the stipe.
searchText.stipe: Stout and cylindrical, often swollen or bulbous. Yellowish at the top, reddening downwards, and covered with a fine, mesh-like network (reticulate).
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, mainly associated with pine (Pinus) but can also be found with spruce (Picea) and other conifers.
searchText.edibility: Edible and considered very good.
searchText.fruit-body: 8-25 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are fusiform, 13-17 x 4-5 µm.
searchText.overview: Closely related to the more famous Boletus edulis. However, its preference for coniferous forests, especially pine stands, and its redder coloration set it apart.

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, waxy, thin layer that forms a continuous, web-like surface over the substrate, white to cream-colored when fresh to pale yellow
searchText.cap: (Forms a resupinate, crust-like layer directly on substrate)
searchText.hymenium-attachment: (The hymenium forms directly on the surface of the substrate without a cap)
searchText.stipe: Absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, decomposing dead wood and plant material, found on birch branches, fallen logs, in all seasons
searchText.edibility: Inedible, lacking substantial flesh and considered insignificant for culinary use
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body crust-like, spreading irregularly, forming patches up to 1–20 cm across, with a thickness of only 0.1–0.5 mm
searchText.chemical-reactions: Yellowish tint and occuring on birch (Betula sp) dead wood
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thin-walled, 6–10 x 2.5–4 µm, hyaline in KOH, basidia 4-spored and clavate
searchText.overview: Crust-like, white to cream-colored fungus that forms extensive patches on decaying wood

searchText.hymenium: Gills, initially pale grey-brown with white edges, later darkening to deep brown
searchText.cap: Conical to convex, later bell-shaped but not completely flat, smooth, silky when moist, hygrophanous, colors from reddish-clay-brown when wet to pale ochre when dry, darker center
searchText.stipe: Slender and hollow; white to pale, often fused at the base in clusters; stems may be wavy, tapering slightly upward
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing in dense tufts on soil, leaf litter, buried or decayed hardwoodin grassy, woodland or edge habitats, from summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Little culinary value (insubstantial, fragile)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stems 7–12 cm long, many stems clustered together
searchText.flesh: Flesh thin, white, no staining
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, with a germ pore, ~6.5–10×3.5–4 µm, basidia 4-sterigmate, with clamp connections
searchText.overview: Clustered brittlestem mushroom that forms dense tufts from a common base, often likened to many feet

searchText.hymenium: Pores, pale yellow to lemon-yellow when young, turning olive-yellow as mature, pores bruise blue when handled
searchText.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to nearly flat with age, surface is smooth and slightly sticky when moist, typically silvery-grey to pale greyish-brown
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to clavate, pale yellow, often with a reddish flush near the base, surface is typically smooth, sometimes exhibit slight reticulation near the apex
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with oak and beech, grows in calcareous soils, in mixed forests, appearing from late spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, considered a choice mushroom
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 12 cm tall
searchText.odour: Odour: Mild, pleasant with a slight nutty aroma
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, 12–16 x 5–6.5 µm, smooth, inamyloid, basidia four-spored
searchText.overview: Distinctive bolete known for its smooth, silvery-grey cap, yellow pores which bruise blue

searchText.hymenium: Pores small, rounded, lemon-yellow when young, later to olive-yellow, rapidly bruising blue when touched
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex, later broadly convex; pale buff, ivory, greyish-whitish-brown; dry, finely downy when young, cracked or uneven with age
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to adnexed, sometimes slightly depressed around the stipe
searchText.stipe: Stout, swollen to barrel-shaped when young, later elongated and rooting/tapering at base; yellow near apex, paler to brownish below; fine pale reticulation near the upper part
searchText.spore-print: Spore print: Olive-brown to olivaceous walnut-brown
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved trees: oak, beech, hornbeam, chestnut and lime; woodland, parks and calcareous or base-rich soils; summer to early autumn
searchText.edibility: Strongly inedible, extremely bitter, causes severe gastrointestinal symptoms
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Large and robust; stipe ~5–10 cm long, ~3–5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh pale yellow to whitish, rapidly turning blue when cut or bruised
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH orange on flesh; red-brown on cap
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, smooth, ~11.5–14 × 4–5.5 µm; pileipellis a trichodermium of interwoven septate, finely incrusted hyphae
searchText.overview: Large pale rooting bolete with yellow pores that bruise blue, bitter taste and reticulation

searchText.cap: 0.5-2 cm across. Initially convex, becoming more irregular and lobed, often elongated, bright yellow to orange-yellow, gelatinous in texture, sometimes forked at the tip.
searchText.hymenium: No true gills or pores, but a smooth, gelatinous surface.
searchText.stipe: Tapered, gelatinous, bright yellow, and often forked or branched.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; growing on coniferous wood, especially on fallen logs and stumps.
searchText.edibility: Inedible; tough and gelatinous consistency.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 10 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical, smooth, 9-11 x 3-3.5 µm.
searchText.overview: Conspicuous jelly fungus due to its vibrant coloration and unique branched, antler-like appearance. Despite the resemblance to true coral fungi, it belongs to the Dacrymycetes order, characterized by their distinctive Y-shaped basidia.

searchText.hymenium: Gills, white to cream-colored, crowded
searchText.cap: convex to flat with age, smooth surface, color ranging from white to yellowish or pale ochre, margin often inrolled when young
searchText.stipe: Stout, white to yellowish, sometimes slightly bulbous at the base, surface smooth, lacking a ring
searchText.ecology: Ecology saprotrophic, occasionally mycorrhizal, grasslands, meadows, roadside verges, woodlands, calcareous soils, fairy rings, may till june
searchText.edibility: Choice edible, highly prized in various European cuisines, traditionally consumed sautéed or in omelettes
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe 3–10 cm long and 1–4 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 4–7 × 2–3.5 µm, inamyloid
searchText.overview: Fruits in spring, often around St. George's Day (April 23), hence the common name St. George's Mushroom

searchText.hymenium: Internal, forming the gleba, initially white and firm, becoming yellowish-green to olive-brown as spores mature
searchText.cap: No distinct cap, the fruiting body is a large, smooth, rounded, or irregularly shaped puffball, with a leathery outer skin that cracks and flakes as it ages
searchText.stipe: Lacking, the fruiting body is sessile or attached to the ground by a small base of mycelial threads
searchText.description: Saprobic found in nutrient-rich soils, meadows, fields, and open woodlands, often in grass or alongside paths, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible only when the gleba is firm and pure white, mature specimens are inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large, typically 10–50 cm in diameter, may exceed 70 cm
searchText.odour: Odour mild and pleasant when young, unpleasant and musty when mature
searchText.taste: Taste mild when young, unpleasant when mature
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to globose, 2.5–4 µm, with or without a short pedicel, smooth, thick-walled, hyaline to yellowish in KOH
searchText.overview: Massive, iconic puffball fungus, recognized for its large size and white spherical fruiting body

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, forms the inner surface of the apothecium, bright yellow to lemon-yellow
searchText.cap: Cup- or disc-shaped, often shallow, lemon-yellow, smooth, and slightly translucent when fresh
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Hymenium forms the internal surface of the cup)
searchText.stipe: With or without a tiny, tapering pseudostem;
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, grows on decaying wood, twigs, in moist, shaded environments, found in large groups, during autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its tiny size and insubstantial flesh
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body very small, with or without a tiny, tapering pseudostem
searchText.microscopy: Spores elongated-ellipsoid, smooth, sometimes becoming 1–2-septate, often biguttulate, hyaline in KOH, 12–16 x 3.5–5 µm, asci 120–175 x 5–8 µm, 8-spored
searchText.overview: Small, vibrant yellow cup fungus that forms dense clusters on decaying wood

searchText.hymenium: Gills are initially pale but become purplish-brown to almost black as the spores mature. They are crowded and often have a slightly jagged edge.
searchText.cap: conic to convex or flat, often with a slightly upturned, ragged edge when mature. It's thin-fleshed, hygrophanous, and can be pale brown when moist, drying to a lighter color, almost straw-yellow or pale grayish.
searchText.stipe: Slender, pale at the top, becoming brownish towards the base, with a annulus which can be lost in age.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic/ Sometimes growing in groups or clusters, especially in places where wood chippings have been applied.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but not highly regarded due to its insubstantial nature.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 8 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Fragile and common mushroom found in grassy habitats. It is recognizable by its thin, hygrophanous cap that changes color as it dries and its crowded, dark gills.

searchText.hymenium: Folded, irregular gill-like ridges—intermediate between chanterelles and typical gills
searchText.cap: No distinct cap, tan to whitish, surface resembling an omphalinoid or chanterelle form
searchText.stipe: Present but slender, not prominently differentiated from cap-like structure
searchText.ecology: Ecology, bryophilous—grows among mosses on calcareous soils, summer-autumn
searchText.description:
Rare and too small to eat
Red list fungi
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, 0.7-1.5 cm, stipe 1.0 x 0.1-0.2 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, inamyloid, 4.5-6(-6.5) x 2.5-4 µm, no cystidia
searchText.overview: Rare, moss-associated agaric with folded hymenial ridges and omphalinoid-chanterelle resemblance

searchText.hymenium: Gills, frequently forked, white when young
searchText.cap: Convex to flat with a small bump, surface grayish, minutely tomentose, radially wrinkled or slightly striate, margin incurved when young and becoming wavy
searchText.stipe: Slender, often equal or slightly tapering, color similar to cap, sometimes moist, base with moss/mycelial attachment
searchText.ecology: Saprotrophic, bryophilous (Polytrichum and other mosses), under conifers, heathlands, acidic soils, summer and autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible (especially when young), not highly prized
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 2.5–12.5 cm long, 0.3–0.7 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh is white, when bruised, flesh and gills may stain reddish
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid-to-elongate, smooth, ~6–10×3–5µm, amyloid in iodine, absence of cystidia is typical, no cheilocystidia or pleurocystidia
searchText.overview: Modest gray-toned mushroom, fruiting in association with moss, distinguished by its umbonate cap

searchText.hymenium: False gills / thick forked ridges, not true lamellae; blunt, wrinkled, strongly decurrent, yellow to pale yellow
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, later shallowly funnel-shaped; margin wavy and irregular; smooth, egg-yolk yellow to golden-yellow
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent — ridges run down the stipe
searchText.stipe: Solid, smooth, fleshy, same colour as or slightly paler than cap, merging gradually into the cap
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale yellow to creamy white, sometimes faintly pinkish
searchText.ecology: Ecology ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved and coniferous trees, especially oak, chestnut, hazel and conifers; woodland soils, often acid; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edibility choice edible, highly prized for flavour and texture
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; usually ~3–10 cm tall
searchText.flesh: Flesh firm, pale yellowish-white, fibrous, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: No distinctive macroscopic reaction; spores hyaline in KOH
searchText.odour: Odour fruity, apricot-like, sometimes faint when fresh
searchText.taste: Taste mild, pleasant, not strongly distinctive raw
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~7–11 × 4–6 µm; basidia typically 4–6-spored, hymenium formed on blunt ridges rather than true gills
searchText.overview: Classic choice edible golden chanterelle with wavy yellow cap

searchText.plasmodium-phase: Watery, translucent to whitish, sometimes faintly yellowish or pinkish
searchText.fruiting-bodies: Dense colonies of erect, simple to repeatedly branched, finger- or coral-shaped columns; gelatinous and translucent at first, later white, cream or pale yellow
searchText.peridium: The spores are produced openly on the outer surface rather than enclosed within a sporangium
searchText.attachment: Macroscopic columns sessile on a confluent, mucilaginous hypothallus; each individual spore supported by a delicate microscopic pedicel
searchText.description:
Spore mass white to pale yellow
Amoeboflagellate cells → multinucleate plasmodium → coral-like sporophores bearing external stalked spores → spores germinate to release amoeboid or flagellated cells
searchText.ecology: On moist, heavily decayed logs, stumps, branches and other plant debris, often appearing in extensive clustered sheets after rain; late spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Tiny, gelatinous slime mould with no culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Individual columns approximately 1–10 mm tall and ~0.2–1 mm wide; colonies may spread across many centimetres of decaying wood
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, thin-walled, hyaline to very pale yellow, globose, ovoid or ellipsoid, approximately 6–8 × 10–13 µm; borne individually on slender pedicels about 7–20 µm long; true capillitium absent
searchText.overview: Common coral slime forming delicate white, frost-covered miniature antlers or icicles on wet rotten wood

searchText.hymenium: hymenium is poroid, cream to yellowish in color
searchText.cap: cap is semicircular or fan-shaped, with dark brown scales on a lighter background, becoming more convex with age
searchText.hymenium-attachment: hymenium attachment is not applicable as it grows directly out of the wood
searchText.stipe: lacks a stipe
searchText.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic or parasitic, found on deciduous trees, especially willows and poplars
searchText.edibility: edibility: edible when young, but older specimens can be tough and have a strong flavor
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 10-40 cm across
searchText.overview: Recognizable by its semicircular, fan-shaped cap that bears dark brown scales on a lighter background. The underside contains small pores rather than gills, where it releases its spores. This mushroom is found on dead logs or living trees, where it can act as a decomposer or a parasite. While edible, only the younger specimens are recommended for consumption as the older ones can be quite tough and have a strong flavor. The smell of a fresh specimen is often compared to watermelon rind. As always, proper identification is crucial as there are many species of Polypores, and not all of them are edible.

searchText.hymenium: Pores angular, whitish to pale grey when young, becoming dingy brownish with age; sometimes bruising faintly brown; approximately 3–5 pores per mm
searchText.cap: Plane-convex to flat, later centrally depressed with an uplifted margin; round to kidney-shaped; dry, smooth or finely radially fibrillose; dull yellow to pale tan, often radially streaked
searchText.stipe: Central, eccentric or lateral, short and tough; pale near apex, becoming dark brown to black and finely velvety from the base upward
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot on decaying hardwood sticks, fallen branches and small barkless logs; solitary or scattered; late spring to autumn
Inedible, too tough, leathery and woody

searchText.flesh: Flesh whitish to dull yellowish, thin, very tough
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH brownish-orange on cap surface and flesh
