searchText.overview: Small pale stemmed polypore on dead hardwood, with radially streaked tan cap, decurrent whitish pores, stipe that progressively blackens upward from the base

searchText.hymenium: A membranous, gill-like palisade of hyphae (~20 × 3–5 µm), lacking a true subhymenium
searchText.cap: Convex to flattened, thin and delicate, smooth, pale yellowish straw-colored, developing dark spots when dry
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Marginal (forms the underside edge of the cap)
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, smooth to slightly fibrillose, paler than cap, tapering slightly toward base; basal white mycelium present
searchText.ecology: Ecology humus saprotrophic, nutrient-rich or calcareous soils, forests, woodlands, and pastures, along forest tracks and grassy margins, early summer to autumn
searchText.description:
Rare red list mushroom!!
Covered in dew-like orange droplets
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium stipe 3–4 cm long, 7–10 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ovoid, smooth, 4–5 × 4 µm; binucleate, inamyloid; basidia 18–26 × 5–7.5 µm, 4-spored
searchText.overview: Rare critically endangered (CR) mushroom features a thin, membranous cap atop a slender stipe

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, exposed on the inner surface of the apothecium, bright blue-green to turquoise in color
searchText.cap: Small, cup-shaped to disc-like, thin and delicate, typically bright blue-green
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Forms the inner surface of the cup)
searchText.stipe: Short, slender, bluish-green, sometimes absent or very reduced
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white (microscopic spore mass on the substrate)
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, especially hardwoods, causing a characteristic blue-green stain in the wood, found throughout the year
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its small size and insignificant flesh
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe up to 1-2 mm long when present
searchText.microscopy: Spores subfusiform to nearly cylindric, smooth, 6-8 x 1-2 µ, biguttulate with a small oil droplet near each end
searchText.overview: Small, blue-green cup fungus known for staining decaying wood a blue-green color

searchText.hymenium: Gills widely spaced, and have a waxy texture. Initially, the gills are pale greyish, becoming darker with age and developing dark brown to blackish spots
searchText.cap: convex when young, later flattening, and sometimes developing a central depression, surface is smooth, slimy when wet, and shiny when dry, with a coppery color, with purplish tinges
searchText.stipe: cylindrical, often slightly tapering towards the base, and concolorous with the cap, solid at first but becomes hollow with age, with a sticky surface when moist
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines, found in sandy, acidic soils in pine forests, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but not highly regarded due to its slimy texture and somewhat bland taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit Body: 6–12 cm tall, stipe 4–12 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, elongated, fusiform, 17–22 x 6–7 µm, basidia tetrasporic, cystidia present on the gill edges, hyphal system monomitic
searchText.overview: Easily recognizable by its shiny, coppery to reddish-brown cap

searchText.hymenium: Cup-shaped, often irregular, with a smooth or finely wrinkled inner surface. Typically orange to reddish-brown in color.
searchText.cap: Cup-shaped, with a smooth or finely hairy surface. Colors vary from orange to brown.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable, as this species forms cup-shaped fruiting bodies.
searchText.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.
searchText.description: Saprobic, commonly found on catkins (amenta) of various deciduous trees, particularly alders.
searchText.edibility: Not typically considered edible.
searchText.fruit-body: Cup diameter ranges from 0.5-2 cm.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to oblong, smooth, 7-10 x 4-6 µm.
searchText.overview: Characterized by its small cup-shaped fruiting bodies, often found on alder catkins in early spring. The cups may vary in color from orange to reddish-brown, and they contribute to the decomposition of organic matter.

searchText.hymenium: Cup-shaped, often irregular, with a smooth or finely wrinkled inner surface. Typically orange to reddish-brown in color.
searchText.cap: Cup-shaped, with a smooth or finely hairy surface. Colors vary from orange to brown.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable, as this species forms cup-shaped fruiting bodies.
searchText.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.
searchText.description: Saprobic, commonly found on catkins (amenta) of various deciduous trees, particularly alders.
searchText.edibility: Not typically considered edible.
searchText.fruit-body: Cup diameter ranges from 0.5-2 cm.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to oblong, smooth, 7-10 x 4-6 µm.
searchText.overview: Characterized by its small cup-shaped fruiting bodies, often found on alder catkins in early spring. The cups may vary in color from orange to reddish-brown, and they contribute to the decomposition of organic matter.

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer club surface; short basal portion sterile
searchText.fruit-body:
Slender, cylindrical to narrowly club-shaped, usually unbranched, straight to wavy and sometimes slightly flattened or longitudinally grooved; pure white to cream, tips becoming pale yellow then brownish with age
Fruit body small to medium; individual clubs ~2–12(–15) cm tall and ~3–5(–7) mm thick
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the club
searchText.stipe: Indistinct; short, slightly narrowed, often translucent sterile basal zone
searchText.description:
Saprobic on soil in unimproved grasslands, meadows, mossy lawns, woodland edges and clearings, occasionally leaf litter; usually densely tufted; summer to late autumn
Insubstantial for food
searchText.flesh: White, very thin, soft and extremely brittle
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to pip-shaped, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–7 × 3–4 µm; basidia clavate, 4-spored, ~30–50 × 6–8 µm; cystidia absent; hyphae monomitic, thin-walled, without clamp connections
searchText.overview: Fragile white fairy clubs forming dense tufts in old grassland

searchText.hymenium: Club-shaped fruit bodies, with a smooth, even hymenium covering the entire exterior surface.
searchText.cap: Absent, as the mushroom is club-shaped and lacks a distinctive cap.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable due to the club-shaped structure of the fruit body.
searchText.stipe: Typically not differentiated from the main club-like structure, although the base may be somewhat tapered.
searchText.description: White to pale yellow.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, decaying coniferous wood debris in forested areas.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but not highly sought after for culinary use due to its slightly bitter flavor.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 10 cm tall and 1-2 cm in diameter.
searchText.overview: Characterized by its slender, erect, and often curved club-shaped fruit bodies. The surface is smooth to slightly wrinkled, and the color ranges from pale yellow to orange-yellow.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid,  7-10 x 4-6 µm, smooth, and hyaline.

searchText.hymenium: (Ascomycete fungi with perithecia embedded in the stroma)
searchText.cap: Forms sclerotia instead of a cap)
searchText.stipe: Stipe
searchText.description:
Ascospores produced in perithecia; conidia produced in honeydew stage.
Odour not applicable
searchText.ecology: Parasitic on grasses, particularly rye and other cereals; produces sclerotia that replace grains.
searchText.edibility: Toxic; causes ergotism if ingested.
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores are filiform (thread-like), 50-70 x 1-2 μm; conidia produced in the honeydew stage are ellipsoid to cylindrical.
searchText.overview: Commonly known as ergot, is a parasitic fungus that infects grasses, especially rye. The fungus replaces the grains of the host plant with hard, dark purple to black sclerotia, which contain toxic alkaloids. These sclerotia are the overwintering stage and germinate to produce fruiting bodies that release ascospores. During the growing season, the fungus also produces conidia in a sticky honeydew that spreads the infection.

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering the entire surface of the upright, amphigenous branches
searchText.cap: No distinct cap; fruit body consists of intricately branched, upright coral structures, tips blunt or pointed, surface is smooth to slightly wrinkled, dull lilac‑grey to pale or dark grey, sometimes with brownish tones
searchText.stipe: Absent or very rudimentary; branches arise from a short base
searchText.ecology: Ecology ectomycorrhizal, found on soil under mixed woodlands—deciduous trees, summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Occasionally consumed raw or preserved in oil
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, 2–8 cm tall, 2–6 cm wide
searchText.chemical-reactions: May turn green with FeSO₄ on branch surface, KOH reaction negative
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, thin-walled, non-amyloid, 7–10.5 × 5.5–9 µm; basidia 2-spored
searchText.overview: Grayish‑white coral fungus with smooth, branching fruit bodies that arise from a short base

observations.location: Harku mõisa park, Tallinn-Harku, Harjumaa, Eesti

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer branch surface; white to cream
searchText.fruit-body:
Coral-like, repeatedly branched; white to cream, sometimes faintly grey, buff or pinkish; branch tips characteristically flattened and divided into several sharp, comb-like or crown-like points
Fruit body small to medium; ~2–8 cm tall and up to ~3–8 cm wide
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
searchText.stipe: Short basal trunk, whitish to greyish, sometimes indistinct; branches often fused near base
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale yellowish
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; on soil among litter and humus, occasionally appearing from strongly decayed wood; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but poor culinary value; thin, brittle and insubstantial
searchText.flesh: Whitish, brittle to slightly tough, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~7–11 × 6–10 µm; basidia predominantly 2-spored; cystidia absent; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: White coral with distinctive flattened comb-like branch tips

species.identification: Clavulinopsis laeticolor (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) R.H. Petersen

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer club surface; yellow-orange to orange
searchText.fruit-body:
Slender, cylindrical to narrowly club-shaped, unbranched; straight to slightly curved, sometimes flattened or grooved; apex rounded, spatulate or occasionally pointed; yellow-orange to orange, paler toward base
Fruit body small; ~2–5(–6) cm tall and ~1.5–4 mm thick
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the club
searchText.stipe: Indistinct; base narrowed, whitish to pale yellow, sometimes with white basal mycelium
searchText.description:
Saprobic on soil, moss, humus and leaf litter; unimproved grasslands, meadows, heathland, woodland edges; solitary, scattered or in small clusters; summer to late autumn
Insubstantial
searchText.flesh: Pale yellow to orange, thin and pliant, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH yellow-green to green on flesh; FeSO₄ dingy greenish on hymenium
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose or pyriform, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–8 × 3.5–5.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Bright orange-yellow fairy club with smooth spores and a prominent apiculus

searchText.hymenium: Spines, densely packed, up to 10 mm long, initially white, becoming cream to yellowish as they age
searchText.cap: Overlapping, shelf-like to semicircular, with a rough, warty, or lumpy surface, color ranges from white to cream, becoming yellowish with age, margin is wavy and irregular
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (spines on the underside of the cap)
searchText.stipe: N/A (sessile, without a distinct stem)
searchText.ecology:
Parasitic and saprobic, found on living or dead hardwood trees, particularly beech and maple, causes a white rot in the heartwood of its host trees, fruits from late summer to autumn
Inedible, the fruit bodies are tough and woody
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 40 cm in diameter
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, 5–7 x 4–5 µm, smooth, inamyloid.
searchText.overview: Large, shelf-like polypore known for its overlapping, semicircular caps with a rough, warty surface

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately crowded, cream to pale beige or faintly pinkish
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later flat to shallowly depressed or funnel-shaped; smooth, hygrophanous; beige to pale buff when moist, almost white when dry; margin translucently striate
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, smooth to slightly fibrillose; cream, pale buff; base with white mycelial tomentum; ring absent
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale cream, sometimes faintly orange-cream
searchText.ecology: Saprobic among leaf litter, moss and humus in deciduous, mixed and coniferous forests, hedgerows, parkland and grasslands; solitary or in small groups; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; edibility disputed and easily confused with toxic species
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2.5–6.5 cm long and ~0.2–0.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale cream, thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6.5–9 × 3.5–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Small pale hygrophanous funnel with a distinctive aniseed scent

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, pale cream to light grayish-buff
searchText.cap: Convex when young, becoming broadly convex to flat with a slight depression in the center, surface smooth, moist to greasy, grayish-brown to smoky-gray, with a frosted or nebulous appearance
searchText.stipe: Stout, cylindrical, slightly bulbous at the base, smooth or slightly fibrillose, whitish to pale gray, with a mealy coating near the apex
searchText.spore-print: Spore print whitish in a thin print, but pale yellowish in thick prints
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing in leaf litter in deciduous and coniferous woodlands, often in dense clusters, late summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible when cooked, but causes digestive upset in some individuals
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large, stipe 5–12 cm long, 1–3 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, 5–7 × 3.5–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored, 30–40 × 5–7 µm
searchText.overview: Smoky-gray mushroom with a smooth, frosted cap and crowded pale gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially white to cream, ageing to ochre-buff or faint buff tones
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming shallowly funnel-shaped; surface smooth, whitish with a fine frosted bloom when young, developing buff spots with age
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly tapering, smooth, whitish, no ring, base often with white mycelial tomentum
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale pink-ish ochraceous or white to very pale buff
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on leaf- and needle-litter and soil in coniferous woodland, under trees, novemeber - december
searchText.edibility: Poisonous (contains muscarine-type toxins)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium
searchText.flesh: Flesh white to pale, firmish; unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, ~4–5.5×3–4µm, basidia 4-spored; hyphae with clamp connections
searchText.overview: Whitish funnel-shaped clitocybe with frosted-looking cap bloom, crowded gills, woodland litter habitat

searchText.hymenium: Gills are closely spaced, white to cream, becoming buff-colored with age.
searchText.cap: 3-6 cm in diameter. Convex, later becoming flat or slightly depressed; creamy-white to buff, often with darker center.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to emarginate or slightly decurrent.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, smooth, and white, often with a somewhat swollen base.
searchText.description: Saprobic; often found in grassy areas, parks, and gardens; occasionally in woodlands.
searchText.edibility: Toxic; contains muscarine, which can cause severe poisoning.
searchText.fruit-body: 2-4 cm in height.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, and non-amyloid.
searchText.overview: Toxic species commonly mistaken for edible agarics. It contains muscarine, a toxin causing severe poisoning when ingested.

searchText.hymenium: Gills, white when young, turning pinkish with age as spores mature, gills are decurrent and crowded
searchText.cap: Convex to flat or slightly depressed in the center, often irregularly shaped, surface is smooth, dry, and finely velvety, color ranges from white to pale grey or greyish-brown
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical or slightly tapered towards the base, white, smooth, and often curved, stipe is firm but may become hollow with age
searchText.description: Saprobic; found growing alone or in groups on leaf litter or moss in deciduous and mixed forests, often under beech, oak
searchText.edibility: Edible and considered highly prized
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body is 3–8 cm tall
searchText.odour: Odour is distinctive mealy or flour-like smell
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid to cylindrical, 9–12 × 5–6.5 μm, with characteristic longitudinal ridges. The basidia are four-spored and clavate. Pileipellis consists of cutis with thin-walled, hyaline hyphae
searchText.overview: Saprobic species typically found growing on forest floors rich in leaf litter or moss

searchText.hymenium: Gills, relatively crowded, white to cream in color, becoming slightly yellowish or brownish with age
searchText.cap: convex to flat when mature, sometimes with a small central depression, surface is smooth, often translucent-striate, colored white to cream, margin is initially incurved, becoming wavy with age
searchText.stipe: thin, and thread-like, color is white to pale yellow, surface is smooth, slightly translucent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decayed remains of old fruit bodies of Russula or Lactarius spp, damp, decaying litter in deciduous and coniferous forests, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, insubstantial to be of culinary interest
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit Body: 1–4 cm tall, stipe 1–3 cm long, 0.5–1 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth,  non-amyloid, 4–6 x 2.5–3.5 µm, basidia mostly two- to four-spored, pileipellis is composed of filamentous hyphae
searchText.overview: Tiny and fragile saprobic mushroom that grows on decayed remnants of other fungi

searchText.hymenium: Lamellar, white to cream, becoming pale brown with age.
searchText.cap: Convex when young, expanding to almost flat, smooth, ranging from reddish-brown to ochre.
searchText.stipe: Slender, fibrous, whitish to brownish at the base, and darker towards the top.
searchText.spore-print: spore print: Pale brown to tan.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; growing in deciduous and coniferous forests, particularly on decaying wood or among leaf litter.
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its small size and tough texture.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body is 2-6 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Widespread woodland mushroom recognized by its tufted growth often seen on decaying wood. The combination of its smooth cap, slightly decurrent gills, and preference for forested habitats distinguishes it from other forest fungi. Commonly encountered in Europe and North America.

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, with small, angular pores.
searchText.cap: 3-8 cm in diameter. Convex to flat, becoming slightly depressed at maturity; with a zonate pattern, orange-brown to dark brown.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, extending slightly down the stipe.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, central, and somewhat fibrous; the same color or paler than the cap, sometimes with a zonate pattern.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, typically found growing on the ground in coniferous or mixed woods, particularly on well-decayed wood or woody debris.
searchText.edibility: Not considered edible due to its tough texture.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 8 cm in diameter for the cap, stipe up to 5 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical to allantoid, 7-9 x 3-4 µm.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its perennial growth habit, zonate pattern on the cap, and its preference for well-decayed wood. The species name "perennis" suggests its perennial nature, meaning it can persist and possibly grow over more than one season.

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, spread across the surface of the substrate, brown to dark brown in color, with a waxy or velvety texture
searchText.cap: N/A (Resupinate, crust-like fungi without a true cap)
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Directly attached to substrate, covering surfaces in a crust-like layer)
searchText.stipe: N/A (Lacks a stipe, growing directly on wood)
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic and wood-decaying, commonly found on damp, decaying wood in buildings and forested environments; known as a significant cause of brown rot in timber structures, persisting year-round
Inedible and potentially hazardous due to its role in structural wood decay
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body forms crust-like patches, 1–4 mm thick, can cover extensive areas on wood surfaces
searchText.dimensions: Spread patches can vary greatly in size, up to several meters in favorable conditions
searchText.odour: Odour often described as musty or unpleasantly earthy, especially in confined, damp spaces
searchText.microscopy: Ellipsoidal, smooth, 6–8 x 4–5 µm, brownish, inamyloid, produced on a smooth hymenial layer
searchText.overview: A wood-decay fungus that produces brown, crust-like patches on damp wood

searchText.hymenium: Gills, close, cream-buff, young ones whitish
searchText.cap: Convex when young with incurved margin, at maturity broadly convex to nearly flat, surface smooth, glabrous, moist/subviscid when fresh, color dingy reddish-brown, fading when dry to buff-brown
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate or narrowly attached to appearing nearly free
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow, cartilaginous, equal, cylindrical, surface smooth or faintly fibrillose in lower part, apex paler vinaceous-brown, base fused or clustered with other stipes, base with mycelium
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, in dense clusters on decaying coniferous wood, summer-autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, stipe length about 4–10 cm; thickness ~2–3 mm
searchText.flesh: Cap flesh unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: No known color changes to reagents
searchText.microscopy: Spores 5.0–7.0 × 2.0–2.5 µm, smooth, narrowly tear-shaped or ellipsoid to nearly cylindrical, inamyloid, pleurocystidia absent, cheilocystidia up to ~40 µm long
searchText.overview: Reddish-brown clustered agaric growing on decomposing conifer wood

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially whitish to pale, becoming cinnamon-brown to rust-colored as spores mature
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, becoming broadly convex to almost flat with age, delicate, pale cream to whitish, a slight brownish tint in the center, smooth in texture
searchText.stipe: Slender, fragile, hollow, pale whitish, covered in fine fibrils, lacking a ring, and often bruising easily
searchText.description: Saprobic, commonly found on lawns, pastures, and grassy areas, after rain, late spring to early autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, due to its fragile nature and potential confusion with toxic species
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small and delicate, 7–10 cm long, 1–3 mm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH gray to lilac gray on cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, large pore, smooth, 10–15 x 6–8 µm, walls 0.5–1 µm thick, orangish brown in KOH, orangish in Melzer's, basidia 20 x 12 µm, abruptly clavate, 4-spored
searchText.overview: Small, fragile mushroom with a delicate whitish cap

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded; pale ochre when young, becoming cinnamon to rust-brown with maturity; edges distinctly paler
searchText.cap: Conical when young, later bell-shaped; smooth, dry, hygrophanous; ochre-brown, cinnamon to rust-brown, fading yellowish-beige when dry; margin faintly striate
searchText.stipe: Slender, straight, whitish to pale ochre-brown with rusty tones; finely pruinose or granular, hollow and very fragile; base sometimes slightly swollen; ring absent
searchText.description: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, pastures, parks, gardens; disturbed nutrient-rich soil; occasionally on leaf litter or woodchips; solitary or scattered; spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; insubstantial, difficult to identify
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–9 cm long and ~0.1–0.4 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Cream to pale ochre, very thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, ~9–14 × 5–8 µm, with a conspicuous germ pore; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia and caulocystidia lecythiform; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis hymeniform
searchText.overview: Delicate cinnamon-brown grassland conecap with a fragile ringless stipe

searchText.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced; white when young, becoming grey then blackish with maturity
searchText.cap: Ovoid when young, later bell-shaped to broadly convex; whitish to pale grey when young, becoming grey-brown with a darker brown centre; deeply radially grooved almost to the centre; finely granular or hairy when young
searchText.stipe: Very slender, cylindrical, hollow, smooth, white and extremely fragile; often slightly curved; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood, especially stumps, buried roots and woody debris; typically in dense troops of dozens to hundreds; spring to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body very small; stipe ~1.5–4 cm long and ~0.1–0.2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish, extremely thin and fragile, do not deliquesce into black ink
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, ~6.5–10 × 4–6 µm, with a central germ pore; basidia 4-spored, surrounded by brachybasidia; cheilocystidia cylindrical; pleurocystidia absent; pileocystidia lageniform to subcapitate; clamp connections absent
searchText.overview: Tiny grey pleated inkcap forming enormous troops on decaying wood

observations.location: Kumna mansion park, Kumna, Harju County, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially white, turning black then deliquescing as spores mature
searchText.cap: Starts bell-shaped, expanding to flat, ochre‑brown to gray‑brown, hygrophanous, covered in shiny, mica-like veil granules when young
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow, white to pale tan, smooth to finely pruinose, with potential basal veil remnants
searchText.spore-print: Spore print very dark brown to black
searchText.ecology: Ecology saprobic, clustering on decaying wood and stumps (buried or exposed), in spring through autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible when young but delicate, not recommended with alcohol (coprine)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, stipe 3–10 cm long, 2–6 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Ellipsoid to mitriform, smooth, 7–10 × 4.5–6 µm, with central germ pore, basidia 10–15 × 4–7 µm, 4-spored
searchText.overview: Common inkcap with mica‑sparkling cap, dark gills, and delicate hollow stem, becomes inky after spore release, grows in clusters on decaying wood year-round

observations.location: Vienna - Am Mühlwasser, Danube-Auen National Park, Austria

searchText.hymenium: Gills, free and very crowded; white when young, turning gray, then black and liquefying
searchText.cap: Starts egg-shaped or bell-shaped, then becomes convex or flat; smooth; gray to gray-brown; margin often splits before deliquescing
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow, smooth or slightly fibrous; whitish above, darker or grayer below; no persistent ring (veil is ephemeral)
searchText.spore-print: Spore print very dark brown to black
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, on buried or decayed wood, root systems, stumps, or mixed with soil in lawns, gardens, and disturbed sites, spring through autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible when young, poisonous with alcohol (coprine, causing a disulfiram-like reaction)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe ~8–15 cm length, 0.6–2 cm thick
searchText.description: Inky deliquescence tied to autolysis of gills
searchText.flesh: Flesh no staining when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to almond-shaped, smooth, ~7.5–11×4.5–6 μm, with a distinct apical germ pore, 4-spored basidia
searchText.overview: Classic inky mushroom whose gills dissolve to black ink. The bell-shaped grayish cap, free gills that deliquesce, hollow stipe, and black spore print.

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded; white when young, becoming faintly reddish-grey, then grey-black
searchText.cap: Ovoid when young, later conical, bell-shaped to flattened with upturned margin; grey-brown to dark grey; densely covered in ephemeral silvery-white woolly hairs when young, becoming smooth; strongly striate
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow and very fragile; white, initially covered with ephemeral white hairs, becoming smooth; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on humus-rich soil, leaf litter, decaying woody debris and woodchip mulch; solitary to densely gregarious; forests, woodland tracks and disturbed habitats; spring to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible; extremely fragile and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~4–10 cm long and ~0.3–0.6 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to greyish, extremely thin and fragile, rapidly collapsing as the gills deliquesce
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, dark, non-amyloid, ~10–14 × 6–8.5 µm, with acentral germ pore; basidia 4-spored with brachybasidia; pleurocystidia and cheilocystidia large
searchText.overview: Woolly young inkcap rapidly transforming into a black deliquescent bowl

searchText.hymenium: Gills, free and extremely crowded; start white, then turn pinkish with maturing spores, then rapidly become black and undergo deliquescence
searchText.cap: Initially cylindrical or egg-shaped, later bell-shaped to broadly conical, surface white, shaggy with fibrous scales, becoming smooth near the top
searchText.stipe: Tall, hollow, smooth; white to creamy; bears a movable ring (veil remnant) that may slip with spore drop
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on soil, lawns, roadsides, compost, grassy patches, in disturbed locations, late spring through autumn
searchText.edibility: Choice edible when young (before deliquescence), shortly after harvesting
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe length ~10–25 cm, 1–2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh white, firm, no staining
searchText.description: Deliquescence of gills into black ink
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, ~10–13×6.5–8 µm, with germ pore, pleurocystidia absent, cheilocystidia present
searchText.overview: Recognizable inky-cap mushroom with white shaggy fibrous scales cylinder and gills that turn into ink

searchText.cap: 1-2.5 cm in length. Typically small and club-shaped, bright orange or reddish-orange. The surface can be smooth to slightly granular.
searchText.hymenium: Not applicable in the traditional sense; Cordyceps species produce spores from the surface of the fruiting body.
searchText.stipe: Long, slender, and cylindrical, similar in color to the cap or slightly paler.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: Whitish to pale orange.
searchText.description: Parasitic on underground pupae and larvae of various insects, particularly caterpillars. When the fungus matures, it bursts forth from the host body.
searchText.uses-compounds: Traditionally used in Chinese medicine for various health benefits, including boosting the immune system.
searchText.fruit-body: 5-15 cm in length.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical, hyaline, 3-5 x 1-1.5 µm.
searchText.overview: Known for its striking appearance and its parasitic lifestyle on insects. It's one of the few species within the genus Cordyceps that can be cultivated, and it's often used as a substitute for the more famous Ophiocordyceps sinensis, the caterpillar fungus of Tibetan Plateau fame.

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded to fairly crowded, relatively narrow; pale beige-grey to clay-cinnamon; edges slightly paler
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to almost plane, sometimes irregular or wavy; dry-looking, finely radial-fibrillose; sand-brown to ochre-tan with a darker centre and paler whitish margin
searchText.stipe: Robust, cylindrical to smoothly clavate; cream-white below, pale ochre-brown above; longitudinally fibrillose; base enlarged but not clearly marginate-bulbous; abundant white cobwebby cortina when young
searchText.ecology: Presumably mycorrhizal; gregarious in a rich wooded meadow among aspen, birch, pine, hazel, oak and apple trees; Nedrema, Estonia; autumn
searchText.edibility: Do not consume; exact species unresolved within a difficult Cortinarius–Phlegmacium complex
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit bodies medium to large and robust
searchText.overview: Robust sand-brown Phlegmacium with crowded pale clay-coloured gills, a smoothly clavate pale stipe and conspicuous white cortina; provisionally cf. P. balteaticlavatum

searchText.hymenium: Gills, initially pale lilac, becoming brown as spores mature, moderately spaced
searchText.cap: Conical to umbonate when young, flattening with age, surface dry, silky, and smooth, color silvery-violet, often fading to pale ochre with age
searchText.stipe: clavate, with a slightly bulbous base, silvery-violet, with remnants of a white universal veil, partial veil is white and cobwebby ​
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with hardwood trees (beech and birch), deciduous and mixed forests, summer and autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended due to conflicting reports
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4–10 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, finely warty, measuring 7.5–9 × 4.5–6 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: A medium-sized webcap mushroom characterized by its silky, lilac-white cap and stipe and rusty brown spore print

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, initially light with a pinkish tinge that gradually darken to a brownish hue
searchText.cap: Convex when young, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, surface smooth/viscid, reddish-brown with a slightly paler margin, developing subtle striations
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, somewhat bulbous base, surface smooth to faintly fibrillose, reddish-brown color, retaining vestigial cortina remnants
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with both deciduous and coniferous trees (frequently found under birch, oak, or pine) in mixed or coniferous woodlands, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, toxic
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 5–12 cm long and 1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, roughened to finely verrucose, 8–12 × 5–7 µm, inamyloid, basidia are usually 4-spored
searchText.overview: Cortinate mushroom with reddish-brown cap with a smooth surface

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, bright yellow when young, becoming rusty-brown as spores mature
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often with a slight umbo, bright saffron-yellow to orange-yellow, slimy or sticky when wet, fading slightly with age
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, yellowish to orange-yellow, often with rusty-brown fibrils from the veil, slightly swollen at the base
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with conifer trees, growing alone or scattered, in mossy forest floors, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, not recommended for consumption due to potential confusion with toxic species
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, 3-7 cm long, up to 1 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface red, then dark red to black
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, slightly to moderately roughened, 6.5-9 x 4.5-6 µ, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Small to medium-sized mushroom with a saffron-yellow cap and gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced to distant, at first bluish, becoming buff tinged with violet as the spores mature
searchText.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, smooth and viscid when wet, pale yellow, slight brown tint in the center
searchText.stipe: Finely fibrillose, clavate at base, surface sticky, covered with yellowish veil remnants that stain rust-brown once spores begin to fall
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with birch, beech and spruce, found in damp mixed woodlands, autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, not recommended for consumption due to potential confusion with toxic species
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5-9 cm long and 3-6 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subspherical, coarsely verrucose, 7-9.5 x 6-7µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: A medium-sized mycorrhizal mushroom with a slimy, pale yellow cap

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately crowded; grey-buff to brown when young, rusty to dark brown with maturity; edges usually paler
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; hygrophanous; dark brown to violet-brown when moist, fading grey-brown to pale fawn when dry; densely covered with fine whitish veil scales
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often curved; grey-brown with a violet flush near apex; conspicuous white fibrillose veil remnants forming incomplete bands or zones; cortina ephemeral
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce and pine; moist coniferous and mixed forests, among mosses and Sphagnum; scattered to gregariously; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Considered inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~4–8 cm long and ~0.3–0.7 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Pale brown to ochraceous, thin, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, finely to moderately verrucose, yellow-ochre to rusty-brown, ~7–9 × 4.5–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; pileipellis filamentous with clamp connections
searchText.overview: Small hygrophanous webcap with white veil scales and distinctive Pelargonium scent

searchText.hymenium: Gills, initially pale gray to olive-brown, becoming dark brown as the spores mature
searchText.cap: Convex to plano-convex, with a slight central depression when mature, surface is dry, matte, and finely fibrillose to somewhat scaly, with a color ranging from dark olive-brown to almost blackish, margin is usually inrolled when young, later becoming wavy or irregular
searchText.stipe: 5–10 cm long and 1–2.5 cm thick, cylindrical or slightly tapering toward the base, with a dry, fibrillose surface, base of the stipe may be slightly bulbous
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal primarily with deciduous trees beech, oak, found in mixed forests on well-drained soils, from late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, has a very bitter taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 15 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, 8–10 x 5–6 µm, finely warted, with a distinct plage, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium-sized mushroom characterized by its dark olive-brown cap

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, initially pale brownish, becoming rusty-brown with age as spores mature
searchText.cap: Convex, becoming broadly convex or nearly flat with age, slimy and sticky when wet, reddish-brown to yellowish-brown, darker at the center
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, sticky, whitish to pale yellow, often covered in a slimy veil when young, slightly clavate at the base
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines and with other conifers, growing alone, scattered, or gregariously, late summer and fall
searchText.edibility: No nutritional value and considered inedible, tends to accumulate heavy metals in large quantities
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large-sized, stipe 4-10 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH blackish red on cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores amygdaliform, moderately to strongly verrucose, 11-17 x 5-7.5 µ, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium to large-sized, slimy mushroom with a characteristic sticky cap and stipe

searchText.hymenium: Gills, starting as yellowish to rusty-brown, eventually becoming darker brown with age
searchText.cap: Initially conical to bell-shaped, later expanding to become broadly umbonate, surface is dry, with a fibrous texture and a reddish-orange to brick-red color
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often with a bulbous base, surface is orange to reddish and may feature some fibrous veils forming a cortina
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pine and spruce, commonly found in mixed forests, grows solitary or in small groups on mossy forest floors during late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Deadly poisonous, contains orellanine, which can cause severe kidney damage or failure, with symptoms often delayed for days
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 15 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores are almond-shaped, warty, 9-12 x 6.5-8.5µm, the basidia are four-spored, cystidia are rare or absent
searchText.overview: Highly toxic mushroom distinguished by its conical to bell-shaped reddish-orange cap, slender stipe with a bulbous base, and rusty-brown gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; bright carmine to blood-red when young, becoming rusty red-brown with maturity
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, later plane, often with a broad umbo; hygrophanous, finely silky-fibrillose; rich blood-red, dark red to dull reddish-brown
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, blood-red to dark red; orange-yellow to reddish-yellow basal mycelium; cortina red and ephemeral; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce; mesic to damp mossy coniferous forests, often among Sphagnum and bilberry on nutrient-rich ground; scattered or gregariously; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; considered inedible
searchText.uses-compounds: Anthraquinone pigments including emodin, dermocybin, dermolutein and dermorubin
searchText.description: Dye fungus, yields red and reddish-brown shades
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–8.5 cm long and ~0.3–0.7 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Dark red to blood-red, with orange tints toward the stipe base; unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH distinctly aniline-red on cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores amygdaloid to ellipsoid, moderately verrucose, weakly dextrinoid, ~5.6–7.3 × 3.1–4.6 µm; basidia 4-spored; pileipellis hyphae lacking or with only slight encrustation; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Blood-red spruce webcap with carmine gills and rusty spores

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, color of the gills is initially light yellow to olive-yellow, eventually darkening with a reddish tinge
searchText.cap: conical to bell-shaped when young, becoming convex or nearly flat in maturity, with a small umbo, surface is smooth, dry, fibrillose, colors rom olive-brown to yellow-brown
searchText.stipe: cylindrical and sometimes tapering toward the base, color is pale yellow, surface is dry, silky-fibrillose, may develop longitudinal streaks of rust near the top
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines and spruces, on acidic, nutrient-poor soils in coniferous forests, in mossy or grassy areas, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, consumption is not recommended due to its potential toxicity
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 3–10 cm in height, stipe 4–10 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to almond-shaped, 9–12 x 6–7 µm, with a rough, warty surface, basidia four-spored, gill trama has a parallel structure
searchText.overview: Striking mushroom with an yellow-brown cap and vivid red gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, adnate to slightly decurrent, pale violet when young, becoming later rusty-brown
searchText.cap: Convex to flat with a pronounced central umbo, surface is dry and covered with fine, fibrous scales, color ranges from pale lilac to purplish-brown, fading with age
searchText.stipe: Club-shaped, thick, solid, and covered with a fibrous, pale lilac to violet veil when young
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in coniferous and mixed forests, forming symbiotic associations with pine and spruce trees, grows usually in acidic soils
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to unpleasant odor and toxicity
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 10–25 cm
searchText.odour: Odour is strong, foetid and goat-like
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to almond-shaped, 8–9 x 5–5.5 μm, with fine dots, basidia are typically four-spored, 30–35 x 6.5–7.5 μm.
searchText.overview: Can be easily identified by its strong, unpleasant, goat-like odor and lilac to violet colors when young

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are close together, violet in color.
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, occasionally nearly flat when mature; deep violet, often with a slightly campanulate or bell-shaped center.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, sometimes slightly swollen in the middle, with a violet hue throughout; often fibrillose or covered in fine, velvety scales.
searchText.description: reddish-brown.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, primarily associating with deciduous trees in mixed and coniferous forests, especially with birches and pines.
searchText.edibility: Not recommended for consumption due to potential confusion with toxic species.
searchText.fruit-body: Cap 6-10 cm in diameter, stipe up to 15 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Renowned for its striking violet hue stands out among other fungi. The vibrant coloration is present both on the cap and stipe.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid, 9-11 x 5-6.5 µm, with a rough surface.

searchText.ascomata: Non-stromatic or weakly stromatic perithecia, superficial on host surface, bright reddish-orange when fresh, turning dark red or reddish-brown with age
searchText.body: Teleomorph appearing as clusters of tiny perithecia immersed or superficial on the decaying stromata of a host fungus (not on wood directly)
searchText.ecology: Fungicolous (mycoparasitic), growing on the dead stromata of fungi in the genus Annulohypoxylon
searchText.microscopy:
Inedible, microscopic
Ascospores ellipsoid, verrucose, 8.5-9.5(–10) × 3.8-4.2 µm, 1-septate, hyaline becoming pale yellow-brown at maturity, asci unitunicate cylindrical, ~70–75 × 4–5 µm, 8-spored
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body microscopic, perithecial clusters < 1 mm in height
searchText.overview: Obscure, highly specialised red-perithecial ascomycete that parasitises the stromata of Annulohypoxylon fungi

searchText.hymenium: Smooth to slightly wrinkled, pale yellow to orange-yellow, with the hymenium running down the stem, surface appear almost vein-like
searchText.cap: Funnel-shaped to tubular, thin and fragile, often with wavy edges. The cap surface is typically yellowish to orange or brownish
searchText.hymenium-attachment: The hymenium is decurrent and runs down the stipe
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow, and often somewhat twisted, with a color that matches the cap or is slightly paler
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pine and spruce, mossy and damp areas of coniferous forests, in groups or small clusters
searchText.edibility: Edible and highly regarded, with a fruity aroma and a mild, slightly peppery taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 6–10 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical to slightly ovoid, 8–12 x 6–8 µm, smooth surface, basidia four-spored, hyphae in the flesh are interwoven
searchText.overview: Distinctive mushroom known for its thin, funnel-shaped cap and its association with damp, mossy areas in coniferous forests

searchText.hymenium: Gills, radiating from the point of attachment, close, whitish when young, later dull brown
searchText.cap: Semicircular or fan-shaped, cap surface with fine brown scales, pallid cream/yellowish under the fibrils, slightly rubbery texture when moist due to a gelatinized zone under pileipellis
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (no cap-stem structure; gills attach at the lateral or basal point of the cap)
searchText.stipe: Absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on dead hardwood (oak and aspen), sometimes bark of living trees, solitary to gregarious, in moist conditions, autumn to early winter
searchText.edibility: Edibility unknown, unsubstantial for culinary use
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small-to-medium
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface dull-reddish, on gills red
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subamygdaliform, smooth, 6–9 × 4.5–6.0 µm, basidia 4-sterigmate, 18–25 × 4–6 µm, cheilocystidia present (30-60 × 3-5 µm)
searchText.overview: Small, wood-decay oysterling with a rubbery, scaly cap

observations.location: Kloostrimetsa soo õpperada, Tallinn, Harjumaa, Eesti

searchText.hymenium: Internal, smooth, forms the inner surface of the peridium, pale to dark brown when mature
searchText.cap: Cup-shaped peridium that is initially covered by a thin, yellowish to brown membrane; once the membrane breaks, inner surface reveals white to grey, lens-shaped peridioles resembling eggs inside nest
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Hymenium forms the inner surface of the peridium)
searchText.stipe: None
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white (peridioles contain microscopic spores)
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, decomposing organic matter, found on dead wood, twigs, woody debris, and plant stems; grows in clusters in damp, shaded environments, summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, with no culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, peridium (nest) 4–10 mm tall and 3–8 mm in diameter
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, colorless, 6–8 x 3–4 µm, produced within the peridioles (1–2 mm wide)
searchText.overview: Tiny, bird's nest-shaped fungus with small, white to gray peridioles that resemble eggs inside a nest

searchText.cap: 0.5-1.5 cm in diameter. Initially convex, becoming flatter or slightly depressed, tan to ochre-brown, smooth to slightly wrinkled, edges typically turned down and inrolled.
searchText.hymenium: Smooth surface, no true gills or pores, pale brown to ochre.
searchText.stipe: Same color as cap, but paler and often more translucent, slightly tapered, and with a smooth surface.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: Pale ochre to light brown.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; found on soil among mosses, leaf litter, and decaying organic matter in mixed and coniferous forests.
searchText.edibility: Not recommended for consumption due to its small size and unknown edibility.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 3 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, 16-20 x 6-8 µm.
searchText.overview: Small club-like fungus, notable for its simple, undivided appearance and preference for growing among moss.

searchText.hymenium: Gills, decurrent, waxy in texture; whitish to pale, sometimes tinged cream
searchText.cap: Convex to flat or slightly depressed with age; smooth, dry to somewhat greasy when damp; white to ivory, sometimes with brownish tints centrally
searchText.stipe: smooth, cylindrical or tapering at base; white to ivory, sometimes discolored near base
searchText.description: Occurs in old, unimproved grassland, in woodland on mossy substrates elsewhere, neither strictly saprotrophic nor mycorrhizal, but form associations with mosses or act as biotrophic endophytes
searchText.edibility: Edible and regarded as good (though not highly prized)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body variable size, stipe up to ~7 cm long
searchText.dimensions: Cap ~1–5 cm up to ~7.5 cm in larger specimens
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH reaction on cap surface is yellowish.
searchText.odour: Very mild smell of coconut cookies
searchText.microscopy: Spores: Ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid; about 7.0–8.5 × 4.5–5.0 µm
searchText.overview: Pale, waxy-gilled mushroom often found in mossy, unimproved grasslands

searchText.hymenium: Gleba lining inner surfaces of peridium, peridioles are attached by funiculi cords and dispersed by splash mechanism
searchText.peridium: Small cup- or urn-shaped nest, inner surface with distinct vertical striations, outer surface hairy or tomentose
searchText.peridioles: Disc-shaped, ~1–1.5 mm wide, occasionally up to 2 mm, sometimes encased in thin tunica membrane
searchText.funiculus: A structural hyphal cord with ballooned purse, coiled cord, basal and middle portions.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on woody debris, mulch, forest litter, woodchips, tends to cluster, summer to early winter
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body size ~7–10 mm tall, ~6–8 mm wide
searchText.microscopy: Spores ~15–20×8–12 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, with a notch, basidia clavate and sessile, 4-spored
searchText.overview: Fungus with miniature cup fruit bodies that resemble tiny nests filled with lens-shaped peridioles

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately crowded, whitish becoming pale yellowish
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often flattening with age, covered with a granular surface, light yellow to yellowish-brown, margin scalloped
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, with a distinct, powdery to fibrous surface, pale yellow to brownish, adorned with a small, fragile ring near the top
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing in grasslands, heathlands, and woodland edges, in moss under conifers, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but not recommended due to confusion with toxic species
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, stipe 3-7 cm long, 3-8 mm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface rusty red
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 4-7 x 3-4 µm, weakly amyloid, basidia 4-spored, cystidia absent
searchText.overview: Small to medium-sized mushroom with a granular, yellowish-brown cap and a distinctive powdery stipe

searchText.hymenium: N/A in the usual sense (gelatinous basidiocarp without typical gills or pores)
searchText.cap: Absent in typical format — fruit bodies are small, cushion-shaped or blob-like, gelatinous orange-yellow turning brown/red with age
searchText.stipe: Absent or extremely rudimentary
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood of both hardwoods and conifers, fruiting whenever damp
searchText.edibility: Too small and gelatinous to be of culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit bodyv Very small, can appear larger when merged
searchText.flesh: Flesh gelatinous, translucent to orange-yellow, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores sausage-shaped or elongated (14–17×~5–6µm); 3-septate at maturity, basidia Y-shaped and chains of arthrospores present
searchText.overview: Tiny orange-gelatinous cushions or blobs on decaying wood, often merging into irregular masses

searchText.hymenium: Pores large, elongated, winding and labyrinthine, sometimes gill-like; thick blunt walls ~1–3 mm wide; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming ochre-buff; not bruising
searchText.cap: Semicircular to fan- or shelf-shaped, broadly attached; surface uneven, sometimes concentrically zoned, smooth to finely velvety; whitish, greyish-buff, ochre-brown to dark brown with age; margin thick, rounded and often paler
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Maze-like pore surface covers the underside of the bracket
searchText.stipe: Absent; fruit body sessile, broadly attached to wood
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, causing brown rot on dead hardwood (Quercus); fallen branches, trunks, stumps and standing dead wood; solitary or in overlapping groups; perennial, visible year-round
Inedible; extremely tough, corky and woody
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale ochre-brown, thick, corky to woody, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH dark grey to black on cap, hymenium and flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–7 × 2–4 µm; basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Thick oak bracket with distinctive labyrinthine pores and a black KOH reaction

searchText.fruit-body:
Thin, flat to slightly raised carbonaceous stromata forming crust-like patches on bark of dead branches, stromata are blackish, with a whitish entostromal layer underneath
Dimensions: Stromatal patches can cover branch surfaces; perithecia ostioles about 5–7 µm wide by 75–95 µm long in stalk length
searchText.perithecia: Perithecia immersed to erumpent, arranged singly, often with black sulcate ostioles visible on surface of stromata
searchText.stipe: N/A
searchText.description:
Spores dispersed from perithecia
Asci: Long-stalked, 8-spored.
Ascospores: Allantoid, pale olivaceous, ~ 5–8 × ~1 µm
searchText.ecology: Parasite, pathogen, saprobe on birch (monophagous on Betula spp.) branches, especially dead or dying bark
searchText.edibility: Inedible, microscopic
searchText.dimensions: Crust width: Extent variable depending on branch area
searchText.microscopy: Microscopic features:
searchText.overview: Appears as thin, blackish crusts on dead birch branches. The fruiting bodies (perithecia) are embedded in stromata, with visible, often sulcate, black ostioles.

searchText.hymenium: Pores, round to angular, small (4–5 per mm), bright yellow to pale cream when fresh, becoming duller with age

searchText.hymenium-attachment: Poroid, directly attached to the substrate without a stipe or cap margin
searchText.stipe: Lacking, as it is a crust fungus
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, growing on dead conifer wood, including fallen logs, branches, and stumps, in moist environments, spring to autumn
Inedible due to tough texture and insubstantial flesh.

searchText.chemical-reactions: Yellowish on the surface and hymenium

searchText.overview: Bright yellow resupinate fungus with a soft, spongy texture when fresh

searchText.hymenium: Smooth to slightly wrinkled fertile surface lining the upper side of the apothecium; reddish-chestnut-dark-brown
searchText.apothecium: Irregularly cup-, ear- or saddle-shaped, often lobed and folded; margin wavy or contorted; outer surface paler, finely tomentose to smooth

searchText.stipe: Short, thick, ribbed or folded, often partially buried, whitish to pale brown
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying conifer wood, buried timber, wood debris, after snowy winter, spring to early summer

searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large
searchText.flesh: Fragile, fleshy to brittle, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, smooth, hyaline, ~30–38 × 12–15 µm with oil droplets and apiculi; asci cylindrical, 8-spored; paraphyses slender, septate, slightly enlarged apically
searchText.overview: Spring-fruiting brown cup fungus with irregular folded saddle-like apothecia

searchText.hymenium: Pale to medium grey fertile discs within minute dark apothecia, emerging through the epidermis of overwintered fallen leaves
searchText.body: Tiny cup- to disc-shaped apothecia, initially immersed, later erumpent; asexual stage forming small greyish acervuli within dark brown, circular to irregular leaf spots, often surrounded by yellowing tissue

Spore mass hyaline to whitish
Parasitic on living leaves of Ribes species; causes anthracnose, leaf spotting and premature defoliation; overwinters saprobically on fallen leaves; airborne ascospores in spring, rain-splashed conidia during summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible; microscopic plant pathogen
searchText.fruit-body: Microscopic; infected leaf spots usually ~1–2 mm across, sometimes merging into larger necrotic patches
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, hyaline, aseptate, ~16–22 × 7–9.5 µm; asci clavate, 4–8-spored, ~65–105 × 18–21 µm, with iodine-blue apical ring; paraphyses filiform, slightly enlarged apically; macroconidia falcate, aseptate, ~17.5–24 × 5.5–7 µm; microconidia cylindrical, ~4–6.5 × 2–3 µm
searchText.overview: Currant and gooseberry anthracnose fungus producing brown leaf spots and minute overwintering apothecia

searchText.hymenium: Smooth or minutely hairy, typically pale brown to tan in color.
searchText.cap: Cup-shaped to irregularly shaped, with a fuzzy or tomentose surface. Colors vary from tan to brown.

searchText.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.

searchText.overview: Characterized by its cup-shaped fruiting bodies with a fuzzy or tomentose surface. It is commonly found on decaying wood in forested areas, where it contributes to the decomposition process.

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced, rather thick; whitish to pale grey when young, sometimes faintly bluish, becoming dirty salmon-pink with maturity
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often shallowly umbilicate; finely velvety to minutely squamulose; dark steel-blue, blue-black to purplish-brown, sometimes becoming browner with age
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical to slightly flattened or longitudinally grooved; steel-blue to blue-black with longitudinal fibres, often paler toward apex; white tomentum at base; ring absent
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale pink to salmon-pink
searchText.ecology: Ecology saprotrophic(?); unimproved nutrient-poor grasslands, moist meadows, heathland and deciduous woodland; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, potentially poisonous
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.2–0.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Grey-blue to pale bluish, thin, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores heterodiametrical, angular with 5–9 facets, ~8.5–12.5 × 6–8.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia cylindrical to slender-clavate; pileipellis transitional between cutis and trichoderm; clamp connections absent
searchText.overview: Dark steel-blue pinkgill with a finely velvety cap

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately distant; pure white when young, becoming pale pink with maturity; edges concolorous

searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate with a slight decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, white to yellowish-ochre; pruinose near apex, smooth and polished below; hollow and fragile; ring absent
searchText.description: Saprobic mainly in semi-natural grasslands, meadows and grassy woodland edges, also parkland and deciduous woodland; scattered or in small groups, occasionally arcs; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2–4 cm long and ~0.1–0.2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, thin and brittle, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores heterodiametrical, distinctly 5–7-angled, ~9.5–14 × 7–9.5 µm; basidia 4-spored with clamps; cheilocystidia scattered, cylindrical, fusiform to lageniform, ~35–50 × 7–11.5 µm; pileipellis transitional between cutis and trichoderm
searchText.overview: Tiny white pinkgill gradually turning yellow-ochre with age

searchText.description: gills adhering to the stem almost or freely from it, quite frequent, in young mushrooms are white, brownish or grayish, turning pink with age
searchText.cap: cap is sharply conical at a young age, opening to flat-convex, with a tubercle in the center, hygrophanous, brown in color, darker in the central part than closer to the edge, smooth, silky, fibrous
searchText.hymenium: hymenium is lamellar
searchText.stipe: stipe is bare
searchText.ecology: ecology is saprotroph
searchText.edibility: edibility: poisonous
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 2-9 cm, leg 0.2-1 cm thick

searchText.perithecia-ostioles: Perithecia immersed to slightly erumpent, with small black ostioles breaking through the stromal surface.

Asci: 8-spored asci
Ascospores: Allantoid (curved) spores, hyaline, ~ 3 × 15-18 µm

searchText.overview: Wood-inhabiting ascomycete that forms black stromatal crusts on dead hardwood bark

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, located on the outer surface, forming a gelatinous mass, dark brown to black in color

searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, directly attached to substrate, often forming overlapping lobes

searchText.microscopy: Spores allantoid, smooth, 14-19 x 4.5-5.5 µm, inamyloid.
searchText.overview: Common jelly fungus with a black, gelatinous, lobed appearance

searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, up to 2–5 cm across and 1–3 cm tall

searchText.overview: Gelatinous, irregularly lobed fungus with a shiny surface, growing on decaying conifer wood

searchText.overview: Parasitic fungus that causes pink to reddish swellings on the shoots and flowers of Vaccinium species

This fungus causes noticeable abnormalities in the host plant, including swelling, discoloration, and malformations of leaves and stems. Affected tissues may turn reddish, pink, or whitish, depending on the severity of the infection.

pores on hymenium, small and round, white to grayish

searchText.overview: Polypore mushroom known for its hard, woody texture and its historical use as tinder for starting fires. The fruiting bodies are perennial and can persist for many years, growing slowly and developing new layers of tubes. The fungus has also been used traditionally for making amadou, a material prepared from the flesh of the fruiting bodies and used for various purposes, including as a firestarter and as a material for hats and other items.

searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, sometimes weakly parasitic, causing brown cubical rot on dead or living conifers and hardwoods; perennial, year-round
Woody and inedible

Saprotrophic (and wood-decay) fungus, causes white rot on dead hardwoods, occurs on branches, stumps, logs, often in shaded, moist environments.

Spores globose to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, non-amyloid

Saprobic on the deadwood of spruces and pines, causing a brown rot, growing alone or gregariously, annual, spring through fall

Saprobic, typically found on decaying wood or in mossy forest floors, in mixed or coniferous forests, from late summer to autumn

searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 3–6 cm long, 0.3–0.8 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH reddish-orange on cap surface, flesh unchanging in ammonia
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, roughened to verrucose, 7–9 × 4–5 µm, rusty orange in KOH, dextrinoid, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia clavate to lageniform
searchText.overview: Small, orange-brown saprobic rustgill mushroom, recognized by its growth on conifer wood chips, cinnamon gills, bitter taste, and rusty orange spore print

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded to moderately spaced, pale yellow to golden-yellow, becoming rust-brown with spore maturation
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, surface smooth, orange-brown to reddish-brown, fading to a paler shade with age, margin initially inrolled, later straight
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, orange to reddish-brown, darker towards the base, surface smooth or faintly fibrillose
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, logs, or stumps of deciduous and coniferous trees, solitary or in small clusters, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, potentially toxic
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, stipe 3–8 cm long, 0.3–0.8 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, roughened, dextrinoid, 7–9 x 4–5 µm, rusty orange-brown in KOH, basidia clavate, 4-spored
searchText.overview: Orange-brown mushroom with a bitter taste

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are broad, close to moderately spaced, and pale pinkish to creamy-brown, becoming darker with age.
searchText.cap: initially convex, later flat or slightly upturned; smooth, moist but not sticky, tan to brownish or occasionally reddish-brown.
searchText.stipe: 3-10 cm tall, 0.1-0.5 cm thick; smooth to slightly hairy; pale to brownish, often darker at the base.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: 4-15 cm tall.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale cream.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; found in leaf litter, rotting wood, and grassy areas, particularly under oaks and other hardwoods.
searchText.edibility: Edible but not of high culinary value.
searchText.microscopy: Spores 6-9 x 2.5-4 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, and hyaline.
searchText.overview: Small and slender mushroom commonly found in deciduous forests, especially under oaks. It is recognized by its tan to brownish cap, adnate gills, and a preference for hardwood-rich environments.

searchText.hymenium: Pores, large, angular to irregular, yellowish when young, becoming olive to brownish with age
searchText.cap: Convex to flat or slightly depressed with age, velvety when young, later smooth, dull yellow to olive-brown or tawny, margin initially inrolled, becoming wavy
searchText.stipe: Short, thick, cylindrical or slightly tapering, often curved, pale yellow to brownish, smooth or slightly fibrillose, no ring or veil
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with alder (Alnus spp.), found in moist, swampy areas, riparian zones, or near wet woodlands, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but not highly valued, consume only when young
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium-sized, cap 5–15 cm in diameter, stipe 3–7 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: Flesh slowly stains blue when cut, especially in the stipe base
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, yellowish-brown in KOH, 10–13 × 4–5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium-sized bolete distinguished by its large, angular pores, association with alder trees

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming clay- to cinnamon-brown with maturity; edges whitish
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to flat, sometimes obtusely umbonate; smooth, viscid when moist; whitish-buff, pale tan, usually darker centrally and paler toward margin
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, white to pale cream; pruinose or floccose-granular near apex, fibrillose below; base sometimes enlarged with white mycelial threads; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; forests, woodland edges, dunes and grassy places beneath trees; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous; causes gastrointestinal upset, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea
searchText.description: Gills often exuding clear droplets in moist weather that dry as rusty-brown spots
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–13 cm long and ~0.5–2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, thick and firm, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores amygdaloid, verrucose, yellow-brown, weakly dextrinoid, ~9–12 × 5–6.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, clavate- to spathulate-stipitate; pleurocystidia absent; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Pale sticky poisonpie with weeping gills and radish-like odour

searchText.hymenium: Gills close to crowded; cream to pale clay-brown when young, becoming brown; edges often paler
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; smooth, distinctly sticky when moist; pinkish-brown centrally, contrasting with a pale buff to nearly whitish margin; young margin often with whitish veil remnants
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to notched, sometimes with a slight decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, whitish to pale buff, gradually browning from base; silky-fibrillose; partial veil ephemeral to persistent, leaving fibrils
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, especially with pine; scattered to gregariously; forests, woodland edges, sandy and often acidic soils; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Might be poisonous and result in severe gastrointestinal upset; in Mexico this species is eaten and widely marketed
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–9 cm long and up to ~1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish, moderately firm, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, very finely verrucose to nearly smooth, ~8.5–11 × 5–7 µm, non-dextrinoid; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant; pileipellis an ixocutis
searchText.overview: Two-toned sticky poisonpie with veil remnants and radish-like odour

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, adnate to sinuate, cream to pale clay-brown when young, turning darker with age, and often with a white, jagged edge
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, often with a slight umbo, becoming slightly depressed with age, surface is smooth and sticky when wet, with colors ranging from pale beige to ochre-brown
searchText.stipe: Stout, cylindrical, often tapering slightly towards the base, with a bulbous bas, white to pale beige and covered with silky fibrils
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with oaks, beeches, and birches, found in deciduous and mixed woodlands, in well-drained soils, sometimes in large groups
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its bitter taste and toxicity
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 5–15 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical to almond-shaped, 10–14 x 6–8 µm, finely roughened surface, basidia four-spored
searchText.overview: Robust mushroom notable for its convex to flat cap, featuring a sticky, smooth beige-ochre-brown surface

searchText.cap: no distinct cap, but rather a lobed, cup-shaped structure, grayish-brown to dark brown, smooth or slightly wrinkled
searchText.hymenium: hymenium is smooth
searchText.stipe: stipe is hollow, cylindrical, furrowed, whitish to pale grayish-brown
searchText.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic
searchText.edibility: edibility: not recommended, as some Helvella species contain the toxin gyromitrin
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 3-10 cm tall
searchText.overview: Commonly known as the "Vinegar Cup," Helvella acetabulum is easily recognized by its distinct cup-shaped, lobed structure and furrowed stipe. It usually grows on the ground in mixed forests, particularly under hardwoods.

observations.location: Vienna - Am Mühlwasser, Danube-Auen National Park, Austria

searchText.hymenium: Smooth to wrinkled or irregularly folded, covering the exposed upper surface of the saddle-shaped apothecium; ivory-white to cream or pale buff
searchText.apothecium: Irregularly saddle-, mitre- to lobed-shaped, usually with 2–4 strongly folded or curled lobes; whitish, ivory to pale cream; margin wavy
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Ffertile surface exposed over the upper lobes
searchText.stipe: Robust, white to cream, hollow and strongly longitudinally ribbed, fluted and chambered; ribs often branch and reconnect
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, mainly with hardwoods such as beech and oak, occasionally with conifers; woodland, path edges and disturbed forest soil; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous (hydrazine toxins); historically eaten after cooking
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–10 cm long and ~0.8–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish; unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, usually with one large central oil droplet, ~17–21 × 10–13 µm; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~220–300 × 12–18 µm, inamyloid;
searchText.overview: Ivory saddle fungus with a deeply fluted hollow stipe

searchText.cap: 2-6 cm across. Saddle-shaped, often with irregular lobes. The surface is smooth, dark gray to almost black, and appears somewhat wrinkled or veined.
searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering the undersurface of the cap's lobes.
searchText.stipe: Tall and distinctive, with deep, irregular pits and ridges. It is hollow, with a similarly dark color as the cap but can be somewhat paler.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale cream.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, found on the ground in mixed woods, particularly under hardwood trees.
searchText.edibility: Not recommended for consumption.
searchText.fruit-body: 5-15 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, 17-20 x 10-13 µm.
searchText.overview: Notably recognized for its unique saddle-shaped cap and deeply ridged stipe. Its dark coloration and the presence in wooded areas, often after rains, make it stand out.

searchText.plasmodium-color-stage: In active phase, plasmodium is white or pale, later may show orange or salmon tints toward maturity
searchText.fruiting-bodies: Sporocarps borne on slender stalks, typically egg-shaped or conical; the sporangia are often clustered and brightly colored in development
searchText.peridium: Thin peridium, often shining, ranging from orange-yellow to more olive or brown with age; peridium may persist as a calyculus when spores dehisce
searchText.description:
Stalk is part of the sporocarp
Spore mass olive to olive-yellow spore mass inside sporangium
Amoeboflagellate cells → multinucleate → sporulation producing stalked sporangia with internal spores → spores released and germinating back to amoeboflagellates
Spores: Globose to subglobose, ~10–13 µm in diameter, reticulate or warty
Stalk: Tissue may contain pseudocclusions in some populations
searchText.ecology: Habitat: On decaying wood (logs, branches) in conifer and mixed forests, present in clusters on rotten wood surfaces in humid conditions
searchText.fruit-body: Sporangia dimensions: Sporangia up to ~0.6–0.8 mm in diameter, stalked up to ~3 mm tall (or less) in many populations
searchText.microscopy: Spores & supportive structures:
searchText.spore-print: Capillitia: net-like network of threads that often take on the spore color
searchText.overview: Visually striking slime mold that produces clustered, bright orange to olive sporangia on decaying wood—resembling salmon eggs.

searchText.hymenium: Pores angular, yellow at first, becoming dull olive-yellow with age, bruising blue
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; dry, smooth to finely velvety when young; bright ruby-red, cherry-red to pinkish-red, often fading and cracking with age
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe
searchText.stipe: Slender, yellow at apex, pinkish-red to red below, often with red dots or points, not reticulate
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved trees, especially oaks; in woodland edges, parks, gardens, lawns, meadows and disturbed roadsides; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but poor quality, often maggot-infested and sometimes described as soapy
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long, ~0.4–1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh: whitish to yellowish, slowly and slightly blueing when cut
