searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH: Dull orange on cap surface and flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores subfusoid, smooth, ~10–13 × 4–5 µm; golden in KOH; hymenial cystidia lageniform; pileipellis a palisadoderm of septate, encrusted elements
searchText.overview: Small ruby-red garden or oak-associated bolete with yellow pores that bruise blue

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, hymenial surface exposed in mature specimens.
searchText.cap: Hemispherical, initially covered in a layer of white mycelium, later revealing orange-brown to dark brown surface.
searchText.stipe: Absent or rudimentary.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale yellow.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, often found on well-decayed wood or forest floor rich in organic material.
searchText.edibility: Unknown, not recommended for consumption.
searchText.fruit-body: Typically 1-3 cm in diameter.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical and hyaline.
searchText.overview: Ascomycete fungus recognizable by its hemispherical fruit bodies and the smooth hymenial surface that is exposed as the fruit body matures.

searchText.hymenium: Consists of spines or teeth, varying from pale yellow to orange.
searchText.cap: 3-10 cm across, typically irregular or lobed, bright orange when young, fading with age.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Spines are decurrent along the stipe.
searchText.stipe: 2-6 cm long, 0.5-1.5 cm thick; typically lighter than the cap, often covered in orange mycelium at the base.
searchText.fruit-body: 5-16 cm tall.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found under conifers.
searchText.edibility: Inedible; tough and woody texture.
searchText.microscopy: Spores 4.5-6 x 3-4.5 µm, elliptical, with warts.
searchText.overview: Hydnellum aurantiacum is a visually striking, inedible mushroom known for its bright orange cap and spines or "teeth" on the underside. It is most commonly found in coniferous forests where it forms a mycorrhizal relationship with the trees.

searchText.hymenium: Spines, whitish when young, becoming brown with age, 3–6 mm long, hanging down from the underside of the cap
searchText.cap: Irregularly shaped, and convex with a depressed center, surface is rough and covered with a white to pinkish crust that exudes blood-like droplets when young, color of the cap darkens to a brownish/tan as it matures
searchText.stipe: Off-center, cylindrical, and covered with a rough, fibrous surface that is similar in color to the cap
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with coniferous trees (pines and spruces), on the ground, among moss and litter, solitary or in small groups from late summer to early autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its bitter taste and tough, fibrous texture
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up 5 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores roughly spherical, 5–6 x 4–5 µm, covered with small spines, hyphae are monomitic, with clamp connections
searchText.overview: Striking fungus recognized by its irregularly shaped pinkish cap that often exudes blood-like droplets when young

searchText.hymenium: Gills broad, moderately spaced; pale yellow to lemon-yellow, becoming yellow-orange with maturity
searchText.cap: Sharply conical to conical-campanulate, later broadly conical with pointed umbo; smooth, viscid when moist; lemon-yellow, golden-yellow; margin translucent-striate and often splitting with age
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, sometimes twisted or longitudinally grooved; yellow to orange with a whitish base; smooth to finely fibrillose; ring absent
searchText.description: Symbiotic with higher plants and mosses; associated with unimproved nutrient-poor grasslands, meadows; neutral to calcareous soils; solitary or scattered; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–8(–13) cm long and ~0.3–1.2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Yellowish, thin and fragile, does not blacken
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~9–12 × 5–7 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; hymenial cystidia absent; lamellar trama parallel; pileipellis an ixocutis
searchText.overview: Persistent yellow-orange conical waxcap that does not blacken

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are spaced moderately apart, white to pale cream, becoming more yellowish with age.
searchText.cap: Initially conical or bell-shaped, expanding to become broadly convex or almost flat; bright scarlet to red-orange, sometimes fading with age.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapering towards the base; similarly colored to the cap or slightly paler, moist but not slimy.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: 3-8 cm tall.
searchText.description: Saprobic, found in grasslands, meadows, and other grassy areas, often after rains.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but not particularly sought after due to its small size and rarity.
searchText.microscopy: Spores 7-10 x 4-5 µm, ellipsoid, hyaline, smooth.
searchText.odour: Not particularly distinctive, sometimes faintly sweet or fragrant.
searchText.overview: Striking mushroom due to its vibrant red-orange coloration. This mushroom often appears in grassy areas, especially after rains, catching the eye with its radiant hue.

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately close, initially pale yellow to orange-yellow, becoming orange and finally grey-black
searchText.cap: Sharply conical to bell-shaped, sometimes broadly conical with age; smooth, greasy to slightly viscid when moist, silky when dry; yellow, orange to scarlet-red
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, sometimes flattened or longitudinally grooved; yellow to orange-yellow, paler toward base; fragile, ring absent
searchText.ecology: Ecology uncertain; in unimproved nutrient-poor grasslands, meadows, lawns, churchyards, roadside verges and mossy turf; alone or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended, may be poisonous
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–10 cm long and ~0.3–1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Yellow to orange, thin and fragile, rapidly becoming grey-black to jet black when cut or bruised
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–11.5 × 5–7.5 µm; basidia 2- or 4-spored; hymenial cystidia absent; lamellar trama parallel; pileipellis an ixocutis
searchText.overview: Bright conical waxcap rapidly blackening throughout

observations.location: Väike-Rõsna küla, Setomaa vald, Värska, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, pale orange to reddish-orange, sometimes with a yellowish edge
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, often with a small central depression, surface dry, finely scurfy or granular, bright scarlet to orange-red, fading to orange or yellowish with age
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, dry, smooth or faintly fibrous, scarlet to reddish-orange, often paler towards the base, hollow
searchText.description: Likely saprobic, in mossy grasslands, heaths, woodland edges, nutrient-poor or acidic soils, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, but insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 3–6 cm long, 2–4 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid or constricted and subpyriform, smooth, 5–9 x 3–4.5 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 35–45 µm, 4-sterigmate
searchText.overview: Small, brightly colored waxcap with a dry, scarlet to orange cap

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, decurrent, white to pale gray, sometimes with a slight waxy appearance
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming flat with age, smooth, viscid or slimy when wet, gray to grayish-brown, margin incurved when young
searchText.stipe: Slender to thick, cylindrical, white to grayish, sometimes with a faint, slimy coating when young, becoming dry with age
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, found in association with conifers (spruces and pines), in coniferous and mixed forests, autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, with a mild taste and pleasant fragrance, though not widely consumed
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4-8 cm long, 0.5-1.5 cm thick
searchText.odour: Odour strong, pleasant, almond-like or marzipan-like scent
searchText.microscopy: Ellipsoid, smooth, 7-10 x 4-5 µ, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate, 45-60 µ long
searchText.overview: Medium-sized, grayish mushroom with a slimy cap and almond-like odor

searchText.hymenium: Gills broad, waxy and moderately distant; white to cream, sometimes developing faint ochraceous tones with age
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later to nearly flat; strongly glutinous; honey-brown, chestnut to ochraceous-brown, usually darker centrally and paler toward margin
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, strongly glutinous below; whitish and dry near apex, with ochraceous-brown to olive-brown bands or patches lower down; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods, especially oak, also beech and hazel; deciduous forests and groves, on calcareous soil; scattered to gregariously; autumn to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but modest; thick gluten often removed before cooking
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~5–12 cm long and ~0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, firm when young, becoming slightly spongy with age; unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: NH₄OH greenish-blue on cap and stipe gluten; KOH dark blue-green on cap, reddish-orange toward stipe base
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8.1–10.8(–11.3) × 5.3–6.7 µm; basidia 4-spored, occasionally 2-spored; cystidia absent
searchText.overview: Brown glutinous oak waxcap with banded slimy stipe and blue-green alkali reaction

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, pale yellow to egg-yellow, sometimes olive-yellow or ochraceous; becoming ochre-brown with age
searchText.apothecium: Cup- to shallow disc-shaped, later nearly flat; fleshy-waxy, pale yellow to yellow-orange; often slightly reddening when damaged
searchText.stipe: Very short to rudimentary, pale yellow to whitish; sometimes nearly sessile
searchText.description:
Saprobic on decaying broadleaf litter, especially fallen leaves of oak, beech, maple, hornbeam and birch; also petioles and other small plant debris; scattered to densely gregarious; late summer to late autumn
Paraphyses cylindrical with strongly refractive yellowish guttules
searchText.edibility: Inedible; tiny and without culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny; usually only a few millimetres tall
searchText.flesh: Pale yellow to whitish, thin and waxy; sometimes reddening slightly when damaged
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores asymmetric fusiform to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, usually ~15–23 × 3–5.5 µm, aseptate when young and occasionally septate when overmature, with several oil droplets; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~90–135 × 9–11 µm, apical pore amyloid
searchText.overview: Tiny yellow-olive leaf-litter cup with slender fusiform spores

searchText.hymenium: Smooth fertile disc, whitish to cream or pale yellow-ochre; flat to slightly concave, becoming flatter with maturity
searchText.apothecium: Minute, cup- to disc-shaped, soft and waxy; outer surface whitish, smooth to minutely downy
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Exposed on upper surface of the apothecium
searchText.stipe: Slender, cream to pale yellowish
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on fallen acorns, acorn cupules and other decaying nut shells, especially Quercus; also reported from Fagus, Corylus and Carpinus fruits; usually in small groups; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible; extremely small
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny; stipe ~0.5–10 mm long
searchText.flesh: Whitish to cream, thin, soft and waxy, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores fusiform-ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~13–21 × 3–5 µm, aseptate when young and sometimes 1-septate at maturity; asci cylindrical-clavate, 8-spored, ~80–140 × 7–10 µm, apical pore hemiamyloid; paraphyses filiform
searchText.overview: Tiny pale stalked cups growing on fallen acorns and nut shells

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, exposed on the inner surface of the apothecium, pale yellow to cream in color
searchText.cap: Cup-shaped to saucer-shaped, pale yellow to ochre, thin and fragile
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Forms the interior surface of the cup)
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, translucent white to pale yellow
searchText.description: Saprobic, grows on decaying pine cones (Pinus sp.), in coniferous forests, in damp forest floors, late spring to early autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, too small and insignificant
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 5–15 mm long, 0.5–1 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to elliptical, smooth, 10–15 x 3–5 µm, hyaline, inamyloid, basidia 8-spored
searchText.overview: Small cup fungus with delicate yellowish fruit bodies, specifically found growing on decaying pine cones in coniferous forests

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially pale orangish-yellow, pale grey when mature, later darker purple/brown
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming slightly flattened with age, honey-yellow to orange-brown, often paler at the margin, with a smooth and slightly sticky surface
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, yellowish to orange-brown, darker towards the base, fibrous, with faint remnants of a cortina or veil
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, found growing in clusters on decaying coniferous wood, especially stumps and logs, autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible with mild taste, but can be confused with the poisonous Hypholoma fasciculare, so caution is advised
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5–10 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 6–8 x 3.5–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium-sized saprobic mushroom with a yellowish to orange-brown cap and smoky gray gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded, adnate; sulphur-yellow when young, becoming olive-green, then dark purplish-brown to blackish
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; sulphur-greenish-yellow, darker orange-brown in centre; smooth, dry, sometimes with small veil fragments at margin
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often curved; yellow to tawny, browner toward base; partial veil evanescent, sometimes leaving a faint fibrillose ring zone
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on dead wood, stumps, fallen trunks, buried roots and logs of hardwoods and conifers, often in dense clustered tufts, mainly summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous, severe gastrointestinal poisoning
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, stipe ~3–12 cm long, ~0.4–1.0 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh thin, sulphur-yellow, firm, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH: No distinctive macroscopic field reaction documented; spores yellowish in KOH microscopically
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thin-walled, with germ pore, ~5–8 × 3–4.5 µm; pleurochrysocystidia fusoid-ventricose to mucronate; pileipellis a cutis or ixocutis with encrusted elements
searchText.overview: Bright sulphur-yellow clustered wood-decayer with olive-green gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially yellowish or pale gray but turning dark gray to purple-brown as the spores mature
searchText.cap: convex when young, flattening with age, and often with a broad, umbonate, brick-red to orange-red, sometimes fading toward the margin
searchText.stipe: cylindrical, fibrous, yellowish to reddish-brown, lighter near the top and darker toward the base, with veil remnants of faint ring or fibrous zone
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, grows in dense clusters on decaying hardwood logs, stumps, and buried wood, in deciduous forests, autumn, also in spring
searchText.edibility: Edible (nutty-flavour), potential confusion with toxic species
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5–10 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid, 6–7 x 4–5 µm, with prominent germ pore, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia are flask-shaped or clavate
searchText.overview: Medium-sized saprobic mushroom with brick red cap that grows in dense clusters on decaying deciduous hardwood

searchText.hymenium: Smooth in the early (white) stage, later becomes covered by golden-yellow or reddish-brown spore masses, final sexual stages produce perithecia giving it a crusted texture
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white (early asexual stages), yellow when spore coating is abundant, sexual sporulation less visible for spore print
searchText.ecology: Parasitic on bolete mushrooms (Boletaceae), begins infecting the pore surface and spreads over cap and stem, summer through autumn, more noticeable in wet seasons
searchText.edibility: Toxic
searchText.microscopy: Spores:
searchText.description:
Asexual: Ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline; ~ 8-12 × 3.5-5 µm.
Aleuriospores: Round, warty/spiny, yellow; ~ 9-20 µm diameter.
Ascospores (sexual): Fusiform to lanceolate, often bi-septate or bicellular, ~ 20-30 × 4-6 µm.
Initially appears as a white cottony or floccose coat, turning golden yellow then reddish-brown and crusty.
It produces multiple spore types in its lifecycle (two asexual, one sexual), progressively changing texture and coloration.
searchText.overview: Widespread parasitic mold that overgrows bolete mushrooms

searchText.hymenium: Perithecia immersed to partly exposed in the subiculum, dark amber to reddish-brown, appearing as minute pimples over the infected surface
searchText.body: Dense coating covering and deforming the host hymenium; initially white to lemon-yellow, becoming buff, ochre, orange-brown and finally brick-red to reddish-brown
searchText.description:
Spore mass hyaline; mature infected surface ochre to brick-red
Parasitized host becomes firm, deformed and partially mummified
searchText.ecology: Fungicolous parasite mainly on Lactarius species, especially orange-milkcaps; covers undeveloped gills; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edibility depends on the correctly identified host mushroom
searchText.fruit-body: Fruiting layer thin, spreading across substantial portions or nearly all of the host hymenium
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH subiculum negative; perithecia becoming yellowish
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores fusiform to lanceolate/naviculate, finely verrucose, aseptate, ~15–27 × 3.5–5.5 µm, with conspicuous acute apiculi at both ends; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~90–150 × 4–8 µm; anamorph forms subglobose aseptate conidia ~5–6.5 × 4.5–6 µm
searchText.overview: Brick-red gill parasite deforming and mummifying Lactarius fruit bodies

searchText.hymenium: Not applicable
searchText.cap: Not applicable
searchText.stipe: Not applicable
searchText.ecology: Parasitic on the fruit bodies of mushrooms, particularly species of Russula and Lactarius.
searchText.edibility: Not typically consumed. While not known to be toxic, the altered texture and appearance due to the parasitic mold make it unappetizing.
searchText.fruit-body: Varies depending on the size of the host mushroom, but is completely transformed in appearance by the mold.
searchText.dimensions: Cap size varies depending on the host.
searchText.overview: Parasitic fungus that infects and transforms the fruiting bodies of its host mushrooms, particularly those in the Russula and Lactarius genera. When infected, the host mushroom is entirely covered by a powdery layer of the mold that is distinctly yellow to greenish-yellow in color. This dramatic color change, combined with the altered texture, makes infected mushrooms easy to identify in the wild.

searchText.hymenium: N/A
searchText.cap: N/A
searchText.stipe: N/A
searchText.spore-print: Spore print dark brown to black
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, primarily found on dead or dying wood of hazel species (sometimes found on other hardwood species), contributes to wood decay and is commonly found on fallen branches and dead trunks in forests and woodland areas
searchText.edibility: Inedible.
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, 8–12 x 3.5–5 µm, smooth, and feature a distinct germ slit that runs the length of the spore, perithecia are embedded within a dark brown to black stromatic tissue, which forms irregular crusts on the surface of the host wood
searchText.overview: Common ascomycete fungus primarily found on the dead or dying wood of hazel tree. The fungus produces dark brown to black, cushion-like stromata that form irregular crusts on the surface of the wood. These stromata house the perithecia, from which the dark, smooth spores are released

searchText.hymenium: Pores, small and round, yellowish when young, turning olive to brown with age
searchText.cap: Convex to flat with maturity, smooth, slightly sticky when wet, chestnut-brown to dark brown, often with a velvety sheen when dry.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe
searchText.stipe: Slender to slightly bulbous, cylindrical, smooth or faintly wrinkled, pale brown to reddish-brown, lacking a ring or veil
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, associated with pines, spruces, and birches, grows in soil, mossy areas, leaf litter, summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible and highly regarded, firm texture and pleasant nutty flavor
searchText.fruit-body: Medium to large, cap 5–15 cm in diameter, stipe 4–12 cm long, 1–3 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: Flesh quickly blue when cut or bruised
searchText.microscopy: Spores boletoid-fusiform, 11–15 x 4–6 µm, smooth, ochraceous in KOH, basidia 2- or 4-sterigmate
searchText.overview: Popular edible bolete, known for its chestnut-brown cap, pale stipe, and blue-staining pores

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded, broad; whitish to cream when young, pale buff to yellowish with age
searchText.cap: Convex when young with a prominent central umbo, then flat to deeply funnel-shaped; smooth to finely felted; cream, buff, pale ochre to tan; margin strongly inrolled when young, then wavy
searchText.stipe:
Tall, robust, solid to spongy with age, cylindrical to distinctly enlarged toward base; whitish to pale buff, finely fibrillose; white basal mycelium; ring absent
Good edible when young; stipe too fibrous and tough
searchText.description: Saprobic in leaf and needle litter, humus and grassy woodland soils; woodland edges, parks and grasslands; often in large troops, arcs or impressive fairy rings; late summer to late autumn
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large; stipe ~6–20 cm long and ~1.3–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, thick, firm and slightly elastic, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: Guaiac slowly dark blue-green on flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid or sublacrymoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6–9.5 × 5–7 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Large pale funnel with a central umbo, tall stout stipe and strongly decurrent gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills narrow, close to crowded; white to cream, becoming pale buff with age
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly depressed to deeply funnel-shaped, retaining a small central umbo; smooth; cream, pinkish-buff to pale ochre-brown; margin initially inrolled, later wavy
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, tough and fibrous, cream to pale buff; slightly enlarged at base with conspicuous white cottony mycelium; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic among leaf and needle litter and humus; scattered, gregarious; forests, woodland edges and heathland; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, modest
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.5–1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish, thin, soft, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH sometimes briefly pale green on fresh cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores lacrymoid to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–8 × 3–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Pale woodland funnel with deeply decurrent gills and white basal mycelium

observations.location: Väike-Rõsna küla, Setomaa vald, Värska, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, and start off pale or cream-colored, eventually becoming grayish-brown with maturity
searchText.cap: The cap is conical to convex, sometimes becoming broadly umbonate with age, surface is fibrillose to scaly, color brownish, with a more reddish-brown center, margins are striate when moist
searchText.stipe: 4–7 cm long, 0.5–1 cm thick, cylindrical, slightly enlarged at the base, surface is fibrillose, typically the same color as the cap or paler, sometimes with faint brownish fibrils, no ring
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with deciduous trees (beech, oak) and conifers, in mixed and coniferous woodlands, on the forest floor, in well-drained soils, in autumn
searchText.edibility: Toxic, contains muscarine, poisonous if ingested (sweating, salivation, abdominal pain, vomiting diarrhea)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit Body: Medium-sized, stipe 4–7 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, amygdaliform, 7–10 x 4.5–6 µm, cystidia fusiform, have thick-walled structures, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Toxic mycorrhizal mushroom found in woodlands, primarily associated with both deciduous and coniferous trees

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are crowded, adnexed to almost free; initially pale then becoming brownish as the spores mature.
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped, often with a small umbo; smooth or with tiny fibrous scales; white or pale lilac in variety lilacina.
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, and often swollen at the base; fibrous, white or slightly lilac in variety lilacina, with a bulbous base.
searchText.description: Brown.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broad-leaved trees, especially in grassy areas and parks.
searchText.odour: Mild, sometimes with a slightly mealy scent.
searchText.edibility: Toxic; contains muscarine which can cause serious poisoning.
searchText.fruit-body: Cap diameter of 1.5-4 cm; stipe length of 4-6 cm.
searchText.overview: Small, delicate mushroom recognized by its pale colors and distinctive conical cap. The variety lilacina exhibits lilac hues on its cap and stipe.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are almond-shaped, 7-9 x 4-5 µm, smooth, and brown in mass.

observations.location: Tallinn Botanical Garden, Kloostrimetsa, Harju County

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially pale then turning snuff-brown with age; edges whitish and often exhibiting a delicate cortina in youth
searchText.cap: convex to broadly convex with a persistent central bump; surface silky, somewhat sticky when fresh, then dry; often lilac in center fading toward margins
searchText.stipe: subequal or slightly swollen at base; surface silky, whitish above, lilac below, becoming hollow; basal mycelium white
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers, singly/in small groups in forested or woodland habitats, summer–autumn
searchText.edibility: Toxic (muscarine)
searchText.fruit-body: Small, stipe 2–4 cm long, 2–4 mm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh whitish, fragile, no staining
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, elliptic to subamygdaliform, ~10–12×4–5 µm; basidia ~20–23×5–7 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate, cheilocystidia/pleurocystidia 40–65 × 10–15 µm lageniform
searchText.overview: Inocybe lilacina is a small, slender, lilac-tinged mycorrhizal fibrecap

searchText.cap: no distinct cap
searchText.hymenium: hymenium is smooth
searchText.stipe: lacks a stripe
searchText.description: sterile form
searchText.ecology: ecology is parasitic
searchText.edibility: edibility: choice, medicinal
searchText.overview: The sterile conk is irregularly formed and resembles burnt charcoal. It is not the fruiting body of the fungus, but a sclerotium or mass of mycelium, mostly black because of a great amount of melanin.

observations.location: Vienna - Am Mühlwasser, Danube-Auen National Park, Austria

searchText.hymenium: Gills, adnexed to adnate, crowded, initially whitish, becoming pinkish-brown to reddish-brown with age.
searchText.cap: 2-7 cm in diameter, convex to bell-shaped, often with an umbo; smooth to fibrillose; color ranges from white to cream, often bruising reddish or pinkish.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, sometimes with a bulbous base; white to cream, bruising reddish; often fibrillose.
searchText.ecology: Ecology is mycorrhizal, forming symbiotic relationships with broadleaf trees such as beech and oak.
searchText.edibility: Toxic; contains muscarine and can cause serious poisoning.
searchText.fruit-body: Typically 5-10 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to oblong, 8-11 x 5-6 μm; cystidia present on gills, often thick-walled and encrusted.
searchText.overview: Toxic mushroom recognizable by its whitish to cream-colored cap that often bruises reddish or pinkish.

searchText.hymenium: Pores, creamy, bruising brown, in maturity dark brown and hard, 3–4 per mm, tubes 2–4 mm deep.
searchText.cap: Semicircular to fan-shaped, dark brown to reddish-brown, velvety when young, becoming smooth and darker with age, margin paler and wavy
searchText.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, directly attached to wood
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on dead coniferous wood, particularly spruce and fir, causing white rot, annual, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to tough structure, reported edible at a young age
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH black on cap surface and flesh
searchText.odour: Odour pleasant, reminiscent of anise or vanilla when fresh
searchText.microscopy: Spores allantoid, smooth, 5–7 x 1–2 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, cystidia not found
searchText.overview: Medium to large polypore with a dark brown, velvety cap

searchText.hymenium: Typically located on the irregular, crust-like surface of the fruiting body, dark gray to black, turning powdery or ash-like with age
searchText.cap: Lacks a true cap, forms as an encrusting, flattened mass that adheres closely to the substrate, often with a rough, cracked, or uneven texture, initially pale gray to dark gray, becoming black with age
searchText.stipe: N/A
searchText.ecology: Parasitic and saprobic, primarily on hardwoods, causes white rot decay in living trees, on dead wood or decayed sections of living trees, throughout the growing season
searchText.edibility: Inedible, known to be toxic
searchText.fruit-body: Fruiting body crust-like, spreading, often covering areas up to 10–30 cm in diameter
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative, does not react visibly with common reagents
searchText.odour: Odour indistinct or slightly unpleasant when fresh
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 16–30 x 5–9 µm, black in mass, hyaline to slightly tinted individually
searchText.overview: Crust-like, black, and brittle fungus that causes a destructive white rot

searchText.hymenium: Gills thick, broad and moderately distant; pinkish-flesh to salmon or pale reddish-brown, becoming paler as spores mature
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to flat or centrally depressed; smooth to finely fibrillose; orange-brown, reddish-brown to tan when moist, fading to almost whitish when dry
searchText.stipe: Slender, tough and fibrous, cylindrical or tapering toward base; coloured similarly to cap, becoming paler when dry; finely hairy toward base with white basal mycelium; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests, woodland edges and heathland; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but modest; caps usable, stems tough and fibrous
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–10 cm long and ~1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Thin, pale orange-brown to buff, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores globose to subglobose, strongly echinulate, ~7–10 µm, with spines ~1–2 µm tall; hyaline, inamyloid; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia filamentous to subclavate; pileipellis a cutis
searchText.overview: Highly variable orange-brown woodland deceiver with thick pinkish gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, cream to pale yellow, often turning darker with age or when bruised
searchText.cap: Initially convex, becoming more flattened with a central depression as it matures, surface is smooth to slightly sticky, typically greyish-brown to ochre with concentric zones
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, smooth, and generally the same color as the cap, though slightly paler towards the base, hollow when mature
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, often found in association with coniferous trees
searchText.description: Before pickling, it requires a long soaking (up to 2-3 days with repeated water changes) to remove the stinging milky juice,belongs to mushrooms of 4th category.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 4–10 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores are broadly ellipsoid, with warts connected by fine ridges forming a partial reticulum, 6,1–8,4 × 4,1 µm
searchText.overview: Known for its association with moist, forested environments, often near bodies of water

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; whitish to cream when young, becoming pinkish-buff to pale ochre
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly flat to shallowly depressed; smooth, dry to slightly glossy; vivid orange, orange-red to orange-brown; unzoned, margin initially inrolled
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, smooth, orange-brown to yellow-orange, usually paler near apex; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
searchText.spore-print: Spore print ivory to pale cream
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce and pine, occasionally birch and other hardwoods; coniferous and mixed forests, often on acidic soils; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edibility disputed; generally not recommended
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2.5–7 cm long and ~0.5–1.2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale orange, brittle; abundant white latex unchanging, mild
searchText.chemical-reactions: Guaiac grey-green; FeSO₄ grey-green on flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, ~7–9.5 × 6–7.5 µm, ornamented with low amyloid warts and connecting ridges; numerous fusoid cystidia
searchText.overview: Small vivid orange milkcap with immutable white latex

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded, narrow; whitish to cream when young, becoming cream-ochre to yellowish
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later flat to centrally depressed; dry, matte, finely pruinose to velvety; pale ochre, grey-brown to smoky brown, often irregularly paler toward margin; unzoned
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapering toward base; initially white to whitish, later cream-grey; smooth to finely pruinose; becoming hollow with age
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale cream to ochre, sometimes pinkish-buff
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods, especially oak and chestnut, also beech; deciduous forests, parks and woodland edges, on calcareous soil; scattered to gregariously; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edibility disputed, taste becoming acrid
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to cream, brittle, turning salmon-pink to pink-orange within minutes when cut; abundant white latex also stains gills and flesh pink but remains white when isolated
searchText.chemical-reactions: Guaiac rapidly blue-green; KOH negative on flesh and latex; FeSO₄ weak to nearly negative
searchText.taste: Mild initially, then slightly bitter to acrid
searchText.microscopy: Spores globose to subglobose, ~7–9 × 6–8.5 µm, ornamented with amyloid warts and ridges; basidia 4-spored; cheilomacrocystidia abundant, fusiform with elongated necks; pileipellis a trichoderm
searchText.overview: Pale unzoned milkcap with white stipe and characteristic salmon-pinking flesh

searchText.hymenium: Gills, white to pale cream, crowded, adnate to slightly decurrent
searchText.cap: Convex when young, becoming flat or slightly depressed with age, surface is white to pale pinkish, often with concentric zones, sticky when wet
searchText.stipe: Stout, cylindrical, and tapers slightly at the base, white to pale cream, slightly rough surface
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with poplars, willows, and birches, grows in moist, grassy wooded meadow areas, often in large groups
searchText.edibility: Not favored due to its acrid taste, can be consumed after parboiling and soaking to remove bitterness
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 8–20 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores are broadly elliptical to subglobose, 8–10 x 6–8 µm, reticulate surface, basidia four-spored
searchText.overview: Robust mushroom characterized by pinkish cap and its crowded cream gills

searchText.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, crowded, initially pale orange, darkening with age
hymenium is lamellar
searchText.cap: cap is convex, becoming depressed with age, orange with darker orange concentric zones, often with a slightly wrinkled surface
searchText.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, hollow, orange with darker orange spots or streaks, exudes a carrot-colored latex when cut or broken
searchText.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, typically found in coniferous and mixed forests, often associated with pine trees
searchText.description: known for its delicious taste
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 5-15 cm tall
searchText.overview: Prized for its culinary qualities. It is characterized by its orange cap with darker zonations, the carrot-colored latex it exudes, and the change in gill color as it matures. The flavor is mild to slightly nutty, and the texture is tender. It's popular in various cuisines and can be cooked in various ways, including sautéing and grilling.

searchText.hymenium: Gills, closely spaced, decurrent, pale orange to carrot-orange when young
searchText.cap: convex to flat with a slight central depression, becoming funnel-shaped with age, surface is smooth and sticky when wet, orange to reddish-orange, often with concentric darker zones
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often hollow with age, 4–8 cm long and 1–2 cm thick, colored similarly to the cap—orange to reddish-orange
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, growing in association with spruce (Picea spp.). Found in coniferous forests, from late summer to autumn, prefers acidic soils
searchText.edibility: Edible, but not as highly regarded as its relative, Lactarius deliciosus
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body is 5–15 cm tall
searchText.odour: Fruity or slightly resinous, sometimes faint
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid with ridged, reticulated ornamentation, 7.5–9 × 6–7 µm. Basidia are four-spored, 40–50 × 8–10 µm
searchText.overview: One of the characteristic features of is the orange latex it exudes when cut, which quickly stains green upon exposure to air

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are adnate to slightly decurrent, close to moderately spaced, and cream-colored to pale ochre, they exude a white to slightly yellowish latex when damaged
searchText.cap: Convex when young, becoming more flattened or slightly depressed with age, surface is smooth, sticky when wet, sometimes zoned, color varies from pale yellowish to ochre
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical or slightly tapered towards the base, similar in color to the cap or paler, surface is smooth and dry
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with deciduous trees (oak and aspen), prefers calcareous soils
searchText.edibility: Inedible, not considered toxic, has an acrid taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 6–10 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, 7–8 µm x 5–6.5 µm, reticulate surface, basidia four-spored, cystidia abundant on the gill edges, swollen at the apex
searchText.overview: Medium-sized milkcap recognized for its sticky, yellowish cap and its fruity odor

searchText.hymenium: Gills, close to moderately spaced, pale cream to ochre-pink when young, darkening with age
searchText.cap: Convex to funnel-shaped, often with a central depression, smooth, dry, and somewhat velvety, color from pinkish-buff to brownish, sometimes with grayish or reddish hues
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often narrowing toward the base, typically the same color as the cap or paler, hollow and fragile with age
searchText.spore-print: Spore print is pale cream to light ochre.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in damp, mossy habitats, particularly in coniferous forests, often associated with pines and spruces, on acidic soils
searchText.edibility: Inedible and possibly toxic
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body is 5–10 cm
searchText.odour: Odour is strong and distinctive, resembling fenugreek, curry, which intensifies when the mushroom is dried
searchText.microscopy: Spores are broadly elliptic with moderately prominent warts and partial reticulation, 6.5–9 x 5.5–7 µm, pleurocystidia are spindle-shaped to narrowly fusiform
searchText.overview: Easily recognized by its strong fenugreek-like odor, which intensifies when dried

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are crowded, slightly decurrent, pale cream becoming ochre with age.
searchText.cap: Initially convex, later flattening and developing a central depression, smooth, dark brown to blackish, sometimes with a slightly paler margin.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often slightly swollen at the base, smooth, paler than the cap but still dark, with a zoned appearance.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: 8-15 cm tall.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: Cream to pale ochre.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, found predominantly under conifers, especially spruces.
searchText.description: Contains the mutagen necatorin. Choice mushroom in slavic culture for pickling (salted)
searchText.microscopy: Spores 7-9 x 6-8 µm, broadly elliptic, ornamented with warts and ridges.
searchText.overview: Stands out due to its dark, almost blackish cap. When damaged, it exudes a white latex that turns slowly to yellow and then greenish, and is notably bitter to taste.

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded, narrow, and cream to pale pinkish-buff in color, staining brownish with age or when bruised
searchText.cap: convex when young, becoming flattened to slightly depressed with age, with an inrolled margin, surface is pubescent, cream to pale pinkish in color
searchText.stipe: cylindrical, hollow with age, concolorous with the cap or slightly paler, surface is dry and downy, with a faint pinkish hue
searchText.spore-print: Spore print cream to pale yellow
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with birch, in damp areas, in mixed forests, in the vicinity of bogs and wet meadows, in groups or scattered, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible as salted pickles, of low culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body stipe 3–6 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, 7–9 x 6–8 µm, finely ornamented surface with low warts connected by thin ridges, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Distinctive species of milkcap mushroom found in damp areas, primarily under birch trees

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced to distant; pale yellow to ochre-yellow when young, becoming orange-ochre with age
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later centrally depressed to funnel-shaped; smooth, slightly viscid when moist; grey, grey-brown to grey-ochre, sometimes with olive or lilac tints; weakly zoned
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly tapering toward base; pale grey-brown to buff, usually paler than cap; smooth, becoming hollow with age; ring absent
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale ochre to yellowish-ochre
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal almost exclusively with hazel; deciduous and mixed woodland, coppices, hedgerows and woodland edges; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, acrid latex
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2.5–6.5 cm long and ~0.8–2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale grey, brittle; abundant white latex, drying yellow-olive to grey-green on damaged gills
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH turns latex yellow-orange to golden yellow; FeSO₄, NH₄OH and phenol negative
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, ~6.5–8 × 5–7 µm, ornamented with amyloid warts and broad connecting ridges forming an incomplete zebra-like network; basidia 4-spored; pleurocystidia fusiform to ventricose
searchText.overview: Grey hazel milkcap with distant yellow gills and fiercely burning white latex

searchText.cap: 5-15 cm across. Convex, later becoming flattened or slightly depressed, with a wavy or curled margin. Its surface is rough and zoned with varying shades of reddish-brown.
searchText.hymenium: Close to slightly distant gills that are adnate to slightly decurrent. Initially cream-colored, turning buff or pale ochre with age.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, same color as the cap or a bit lighter, sometimes with darker spots or streaks, and is often hollow in mature specimens.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: Cream to pale ochre.
searchText.ecology: Ecology: Mycorrhizal, associating predominantly with conifers but also found with birch in some regions.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but some may find it slightly acrid or peppery to taste.
searchText.fruit-body: 5-10 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid, 6-8 µm x 5-6 µm, with a slightly roughened surface.
searchText.overview: Notable for its zoned reddish-brown cap and its association with conifers. When damaged, it exudes a white latex that doesn't change color upon exposure to air.

searchText.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, crowded, cream-colored turning more brownish with age
hymenium is lamellar
searchText.cap: cap is convex to flat, often depressed in the center with age, light brown to olive-brown, sometimes with zones of different colors, often slightly sticky when wet
searchText.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, smooth, pale, with darker colorations or spots in some instances
searchText.spore-print: spore print is pale ochre to cream
searchText.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, commonly associated with birch trees
searchText.edibility: edibility: edible but not highly prized due to its slightly acrid taste. Best when cooked thoroughly.
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 5-12 cm tall
searchText.overview: Stands out for the milky latex it exudes when the gills or flesh are damaged, which is a characteristic trait of the genus Lactarius. This latex can sometimes have a slightly acrid taste. The mushroom primarily forms a symbiotic relationship with birch trees, helping the trees absorb nutrients while the mushroom gains carbohydrates from the tree.

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills fairly crowded; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming pale buff with age
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later flat to shallowly depressed; smooth, viscid to slimy when fresh; pale violet-grey, lilac-grey to buff-brown, darkening with age; unzoned or faintly zoned
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, pale cream to whitish, smooth, sometimes slightly viscid when young; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale cream to pale yellowish
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with birch and willow; damp woodland, bog margins and mossy acidic soils; solitary to gregariously; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; bitter, regarded as potentially poisonous
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.6–2.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to buff, firm and brittle; white latex and exposed flesh slowly stain lilac
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, ~7.5–11 × 6.5–8.5 µm, ornamented with amyloid broad ridges ~0.5–1 µm high forming an incomplete reticulum; pleuro- and cheilomacrocystidia fusiform to subventricose; pileipellis an ixocutis
searchText.overview: Slimy lilac-grey milkcap with white latex staining intensely violet-purple

searchText.hymenium:
pores on hymenium, small and round, bright yellow to orange
hymenium is tubular (composed of tubes instead of gills)
searchText.cap: cap is shelf-like, semicircular to fan-shaped, bright yellow to orange, often in overlapping clusters
searchText.stipe: stipe is not typically present, as this fungus grows directly from the wood in a shelf-like manner
searchText.spore-print: spore print is white to pale yellow
searchText.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic and sometimes parasitic, typically found on deciduous trees, especially oak, but sometimes also on conifers
searchText.edibility: tasty when young and tender, but becomes tough and inedible with age
searchText.fruit-body: individual shelves can be 5-40 cm across
searchText.overview: Known for its bright yellow to orange colors and its chicken-like taste and texture when young. It is a popular edible mushroom, but caution is advised as some individuals may have an allergic reaction to it. It's best eaten when the fruiting bodies are young and tender. Older specimens can become tough and unpalatable. It's also advised to thoroughly cook this mushroom before consumption.

searchText.hymenium: Pores, the pore surface is white to pale cream when young, becoming slightly darker with age, small and rounded, bruising brownish
searchText.cap: Convex when young, flattening out with age, color ranges from reddish-brown to orange-brown, often with a slightly dry, velvety texture
searchText.stipe: Distinctly white or pale cream throughout its length, with white or pale scales that darken slightly with age, base can have a slight bluish tinge when cut
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, primarily associated with Populus sp, late summer to autumn, typically in mixed or deciduous woodlands
searchText.edibility: Edible, considered a good edible mushroom
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 10–35 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores fusiform to somewhat ellipsoid, 14–18 x 4–6 µm, smooth, basidia 4-spored, hyphal system is monomitic
searchText.overview: Mycorrhizal bolete found primarily in association with aspen trees

searchText.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, initially white then becoming greyish with age.
searchText.cap: 5-10 cm across, convex becoming broadly convex with age. White to pale grey, smooth to slightly scaly.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, 7-15 cm tall, 1-3 cm thick. Whitish with white to grey scales that become more prominent with age.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, primarily associating with birch in damp, mossy, woodland areas.
searchText.edibility: Edible but not of high culinary value.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 15-25 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are oblong to ellipsoid, smooth, 13-17 x 4-5 µm.
searchText.overview: Aptly named for its pale appearance. It is particularly found in mossy or boggy areas alongside birch trees.

searchText.hymenium: Pores small, round to irregular; whitish to cream when young, becoming greyish to brownish with age; bruising slowly brownish
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex; dry to slightly moist, finely velvety when young and smoother with age; various shades of brown, or grey or reddish tones
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnexed to slightly depressed around the stipe
searchText.stipe: Robust, cylindrical to slightly clavate, whitish to buff; densely covered with blackish scabers, coarser toward the base; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with birch; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests, woodland edges, parks and grassy places; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible after thorough cooking; young firm specimens preferred
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~7–20 cm long and ~1–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, usually unchanging or slowly becoming faintly pinkish to greyish when cut; no rapid blue staining
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH reddish-brown on cap and flesh; FeSO₄ bluish-slate on flesh; NH₄OH negative
searchText.microscopy: Spores narrowly ellipsoid to subfusiform, smooth, ~14–20 × 4.5–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; caulocystidia clavate to fusoid-ventricose; no clamp connections
searchText.overview: Classic brown birch bolete with a pale stipe densely covered in dark scabers

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: White to cream-colored pores that become grayish or brownish with age; may bruise dark brown.
searchText.cap: initially convex, becoming nearly flat with age; orange-red to orange-brown, dry, and slightly scaly.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Attached directly to the stipe or slightly descending.
searchText.stipe: 10-25 cm long, 2-4 cm thick; white, covered with small black scab-like scales.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: 18-45 cm tall.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, commonly found under birch trees.
searchText.edibility: Edible but should be cooked well; some people may experience gastrointestinal distress.
searchText.microscopy: Spores 14-18 x 4-5 µm, fusiform (spindle-shaped).
searchText.overview: Notable for its orange to orange-brown cap and the small black scales on its white stipe. It forms a symbiotic relationship with birch trees, although it may sometimes be found near other types of trees. The mushroom is edible but should be cooked thoroughly to avoid potential gastrointestinal issues.

searchText.hymenium: Pores small, round, cream to whitish when young, later greyish-cream to yellowish-olive; tubes adnate to nearly free
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex; dry, finely woolly-fibrillose; muted fox-red, reddish-brown to cocoa-brown, darker in the centre
searchText.stipe: Stout, whitish to pale, slightly swollen toward base; covered with scabers that darken from whitish to reddish-brown, then dark brown or chocolate
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers, especially Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris), in dry pine woods, coniferous and mixed forests, often on sandy or acidic soils; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Good, tasty and edible after cooking
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~8–14 cm long, ~1–3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh white to pale; cap flesh mostly unchanging, stipe flesh slowly pinkish to wine-coloured, sometimes blue-green near the base, later greyish or steel-blue in patches
searchText.chemical-reactions: No distinctive KOH macroscopic field reaction
searchText.microscopy: Spores fusiform to subfusiform, smooth, ~11–16.5 × 3–4.7 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia ventricose to fusiform
searchText.overview: Fox-red pine-associated with scaber-stalk and muted cap colour

searchText.hymenium: Smooth to slightly glossy, olive-brown, chestnut-brown, becoming darker as it dries
searchText.apothecium: Deeply cup- or saucer-shaped when young, later spreading, irregularly lobed, undulating or split; outer surface reddish-brown to olivaceous-brown and finely furfuraceous, especially near the margin
searchText.stipe: Absent or represented by a very short, inconspicuous basal attachment
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on bare, compact, sandy or clay-rich soil in coniferous, deciduous and mixed woodland; often along paths, banks, ditches and disturbed ground; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible and without culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; approximately 1.5–3.7 cm tall
searchText.flesh: Flesh thin, brittle, pale reddish-brown
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid, hyaline to faintly yellow-brown, usually biguttulate, ~17–20 × 8–11 µm, asci cylindrical, operculate, amyloid, 8-spored, approximately 300–350 × 12–15 µm; paraphyses cylindrical, septate and slightly enlarged at the apex
searchText.overview: Dark chestnut-brown woodland cup fungus with brittle reddish-brown flesh

searchText.hymenium: Gills radiating from point of attachment, close to nearly crowded, gill edges coarsely serrated or saw-toothed, often irregular and torn
searchText.cap: Semi-circular to kidney-shaped, surface tomentose or velvety (especially toward center), darker brown at center fading toward margin, margin rolled under or lobed
searchText.stipe: Absent, fruiting bodies sessile or lateral on wood substrate
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying hardwood or conifer wood, grows clustered, overlapping shelves on logs or stumps, summer through autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, extremely bitter and acrid, not poisonous
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body size small to medium
searchText.chemical-reactions: Fresh cap surface usually KOH negative, dried flesh strong amyloid reaction with Melzer’s reagent
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, 3–4 × 2–3 µm, sparsely, finely spiny, strongly amyloid, basidia 18–20 × 3–4 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate, pleurocystidia 22–30 × 4–6 µm, fusiform or cylindric
searchText.overview: Bitter, wood-decaying shelf fungus with a brownish cap and saw-toothed pale gills

searchText.hymenium: Pores large, angular to hexagonal, whitish to pale cream becoming light brown with age
searchText.cap: Convex to depressed center, surface dry, scaly to fibrillose, color from dark brown in youth to pale tan, margin with fine hairs/cilia
searchText.stipe: Central, matching or slightly paler than cap, dry and scaly, tough in texture
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic on deciduous hardwoods (fallen logs, stumps, branches), spring to autumn
Inedible, too small, tough, and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 2–6 cm × ~1.5–4.5 mm
searchText.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, ~5.0–8.5×1.5–2.5µm, hyaline in KOH, basidia 2- to 4-sterigmate, no cystidia, pileipellis radial cutis of brown, clamped hyphae 4–7 µm wide, dimitic
searchText.overview: Small polypore bears a scaly, brown cap and decurrent large pores surface

searchText.hymenium: Gills (true lamellae, broad and tough), white or cream when young, later a pale buff
searchText.cap: Bracket- or shelf-shaped (sometimes semicircular or fan-shaped), attached laterally to wood, surface zoned in concentric rings of whitish, greyish-buff, brown tones, velvety/tomentose
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (the gills are part of the underside of the bracket)
searchText.stipe: Absent — fruit body is sessile on wood
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic causing white-rot on dead or dying hardwood, especially birch, beech and other broadleaves, all year round
Inedible - tough and corky,
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium
searchText.dimensions: Cap width up to ~10 cm or more, 2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh white, corky, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH on surface or flesh negative to weak yellow
searchText.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to allantoid, smooth, hyaline, ~5–6×1.5–2.5 µm, hyphal system monomitic/trimitic with clamp connections
searchText.overview: Polypore on hardwoods, easily recognised by its bracket form and under-surface of true gills

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded; white to cream, becoming slightly buff with age; numerous shorter lamellulae
searchText.cap: Ovoid to convex when young, later broadly bell-shaped to flat; whitish background covered with concentrically arranged reddish-brown scales; centre darker and usually smooth
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, whitish, often becoming pinkish-brown toward base; smooth to finely fibrillose; fragile white ring usually ephemeral and easily lost
searchText.ecology: Saprobic in woodland, parks, gardens, lawns, paths and disturbed ground; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous, toxic
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.2–0.4 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish, thin, fragile, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative on pale cap areas, negative to yellowish on brown scales
searchText.microscopy: Spores bullet-shaped to wedge-shaped, smooth, hyaline, dextrinoid, ~5–8 × 2.5–4(–5) µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia clavate to subclavate; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis hymeniform; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Small brown-scaled dapperling with a fleeting ring and strong rubbery odour

searchText.hymenium: Pores are white, small, and dense, becoming yellowish with age.
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, soft and spongy in texture, yellowish-white to pale orange.
searchText.stipe: Absent or rudimentary; the mushroom is often sessile.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying coniferous wood, particularly on spruce.
searchText.edibility: Generally considered inedible due to its soft and insubstantial texture.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 5-10 cm across.
searchText.overview: Wood-rotting fungus that forms soft, spongy fruit bodies on dead coniferous wood. The pale color and soft, rubbery texture are distinguishing features. This mushroom plays a vital role in nutrient recycling within forest ecosystems but is not of culinary interest due to its texture.

searchText.hymenium: Gills, free from the stipe, crowded, initially white, turning pinkish with age, and eventually brown
searchText.cap: Initially bell-shaped or convex, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, smooth and white, sometimes with a faint buff center, surface may become slightly cracked or scaly with age
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, smooth, white, hollow, and somewhat fragile with a bulbous base, persistent, movable, thin ring near the upper part
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, typically found growing in grasslands, meadows, lawns, and gardens, often in rich soil or compost
searchText.edibility: Edible, though caution is advised due to its resemblance to toxic white Amanita species, especially A. virosa and A. ocreata
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit Body: 5–12 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid, 8-11 x 5-6.5 µm, basidia are four-spored, cheilocystidia are present on the gill edges, typically clavate or flask-shaped
searchText.overview: White, medium-sized mushroom found primarily in grassy areas such as lawns, gardens, and meadows

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, cream to pale yellow, staining reddish-brown or rust with age or damage
searchText.cap: Convex to flat with a slightly depressed center, yellowish-brown to rusty-brown, often with reddish or orange tints, smooth and dry
searchText.stipe: Stout, swollen in the middle, dry, bald, white, with prominent and copious white basal mycelium
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, decomposing the litter of hardwoods, growing gregariously, summer and autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, may cause gastrointestinal upset
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe 3–6 cm long, 2–4 cm thick
searchText.odour: Odour strong and foul, reminiscent of coal tar
searchText.chemical-reactions: Cap surface grayish to dull red with KOH
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subamygdaliform (spines under 0.5 µm), 6–8 x 4–4.5 µm, amyloid, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia 35–75 x 2–3 µm
searchText.overview: Large, robust mushroom with a distinctive rusty-brown cap and yellowish gills

species.identification: Lichenomphalia umbellifera (L.) Redhead, Lutzoni, Moncalvo & Vilgalys

searchText.hymenium: Gills, pale yellowish to whitish, decurrent (running down the stem), distant, thick-waxy; may fork or form cross-links
searchText.cap: Convex to flat with a distinctly depressed center, dull yellowish to brownish-tan; thin, moist (lubricous), margin becomes wavy or pleated
searchText.stipe: slender, moist, smooth or with a fuzzy base, pale yellowish-brown to reddish at the apex
searchText.ecology: Ecology: Lichenized basidiomycete (basidiolichen) forming mutualism with green algae (Coccomyxa); grows on moist soil, moss, and rotting conifer wood, spring through fall
searchText.edibility: Nonpoisonous but too small
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe 1–3 cm long, 1–3 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–7 × 3–4 µm
searchText.overview: Tiny, lichen-forming agaric—also known as the green‑pea mushroom lichen—with a moist yellow‑tan cap, pale decurrent gills, and slender stipe

searchText.plasmodium-phase: The active, feeding phase consists of a gelatinous, amorphous mass that is translucent white to pale pink, moving slowly across decaying wood and consuming microorganisms
searchText.fruiting-bodies: Initially spherical to cushion-shaped, bright pink or salmon, turning gray, reddish-brown, or black as they mature, surface smooth to slightly roughened, eventually breaking open to release spores
searchText.description: Spore mass powdery and pinkish-gray to dark gray when mature.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying wood, bark, stumps in forests and woodlands, clusters or scattered groups, summer and autumn in moist, shaded areas
searchText.edibility: Inedible.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruiting body 2–15 mm in diameter, with the surface often slightly wrinkled or cracked as it ages
searchText.microscopy: Subglobose to slightly elongated, covered in fine warts, 6–9 µm, spore mass dispersed in a capillitium network
searchText.overview: Brightly colored slime mold in its early stages

searchText.cap: 2-5 cm across. Initially round to pear-shaped, with a rough surface covered in small white spines. As it matures, spines may shed, revealing a brownish skin beneath. The apex ruptures to release spores.
searchText.hymenium: N/A
searchText.stipe: Present in some mature specimens, elongated, and can be quite long relative to the size of the fruiting body. It's hollow and might have a reticulate surface towards the top.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, found on the ground in grassy areas, heaths, and woodlands.
searchText.edibility: Edible when young and the gleba is still white, but becomes inedible as it matures and turns to spore dust.
searchText.fruit-body: 5-15 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are round, 3.5-4.5 µm in diameter, with a finely warted surface.
searchText.overview: Pestle-like shape with a prominent stipe. This puffball stands out from others due to its long, distinct stipe and the rough, spiky texture on the young fruit body's surface.

searchText.hymenium: Initially solid, becoming powdery with maturity due to the transformation of the internal tissue into spores.
searchText.fruit-body:
Globose to slightly pear-shaped puffball, smooth to finely granulated or spiny at a young age; spines, if present, often fall off with age, leaving a net-like pattern.
Fruit body: Up to 2-4 cm in diameter.
searchText.color: Dark brown to olive-brown when mature.
searchText.ecology: Grasslands, meadows, and forest clearings; often found growing in groups.
searchText.edibility: Edible when young and the internal flesh is white and firm, but not considered a top choice.
searchText.overview: Distinguished by its small size and dark, umber to olive-brown coloration at maturity. Young specimens can be consumed when the inner flesh is still white and hasn't transformed into spores. With age, pressing on the mature puffball will release a brown "smoke" of spores.

searchText.hymenium: Gills are close and white, but may take on a grayish hue as the mushroom ages. Darkening when pressed.
searchText.cap: 5-12 cm in diameter. Initially convex, maturing to nearly flat, with a slightly inrolled margin. Smooth, and typically gray-brown to brown.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, white, and typically smooth or slightly fibrous, with no ring.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; typically growing in dense clusters on disturbed ground, often near rotting wood or wood chips.
searchText.edibility: Edible and said to be mild in flavor, but as always caution is advised.
searchText.fruit-body: Generally 5-15 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, and hyaline.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its habit of growing in clusters and its fairly large, brownish caps. It's found widely in North America and Europe.

observations.location: Jaapani aed, Kadriorg, Tallinn, Harju County

searchText.hymenium: Gills are white to pale cream.
searchText.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to nearly flat with maturity, hygrophanous, pale tan to light brown, drying paler.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, slender, pale at the top and becoming darker brown towards the base.
searchText.spore-print: spore print: White to pale cream.
searchText.ecology: ecology: Saprobic, growing on fallen twigs and woody debris, primarily of broadleaf trees.
searchText.edibility: edibility: Inedible due to its small size and tough texture, but not known to be toxic.
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body: 2-4 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Can frequently be spotted on decaying wood, specifically fallen twigs and branches of broadleaf trees. This small mushroom is characterized by its thin, wiry stem and tiny, pale cap. Despite its unassuming size, the resilience of this fungus is remarkable; after drying out, it can rehydrate and appear fresh again with the next rain. Found in various parts of the world.

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Gills very distant, few and narrow, often reduced to irregular vein-like folds, sometimes forked or interconnected; white to pale cream
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later flattened or shallowly depressed; extremely thin, dry, smooth to finely pruinose, becoming radially wrinkled; white to ivory; margin slightly wavy
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to shortly decurrent, sometimes forming a partial collar
searchText.stipe: Extremely slender, thread-like, tough and wiry; whitish near apex, dark reddish-brown toward base; finely pruinose to minutely hairy; ring absent
searchText.description: Saprobic on decaying hardwood leaves, petioles; deciduous and mixed forests, usually scattered to gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible; extremely small and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny; stipe ~0.5–3 cm long and ~0.1–0.5 mm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale cream, membranous, extremely thin and pliant; unchanging when cut; drying out and reviving with moisture
searchText.microscopy: Spores elongated-ellipsoid to lacrymoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8.5–12.5 × 3–5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; cheilocystidia fusiform to lageniform, often with elongated necks; pleurocystidia scattered; pileipellis hymeniform; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Tiny white leaf parachute with reduced vein-like gills and a hair-thin brown stipe

searchText.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, white to cream, widely spaced
hymenium is lamellar
searchText.cap: cap is convex, becoming flat with a slight central depression and often a small umbo, smooth, pale tan to buff
searchText.stipe: stipe is thin, tough, and wiry, same color as the cap or slightly paler
searchText.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic, typically found in grassy areas such as lawns, pastures, and meadows
searchText.edibility: edibility: choice, known for its excellent taste and texture, especially when dried
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 2-8 cm tall
searchText.overview: Small agaric that is often found in troops or fairy rings in grassy areas. The flesh is thin but tough. It can be eaten fresh, but its flavor greatly intensifies when dried, making it an excellent mushroom for flavoring dishes.

searchText.hymenium: Not formed as a cap-and-gill structure; spores produced in rust sori on infected willow leaves
searchText.body: Microscopic rust fungus forming yellow-orange uredinia, later dark brown to black telia on leaves of Salix species
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable; spore-producing sori erupt through or develop within host leaf tissue
searchText.stipe: N/A
searchText.ecology: Ecology obligate biotrophic parasite on willows (Salix spp.); uredinia reinfect willow leaves during the growing season, telia develop later in summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, microscopic plant pathogen
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body microscopic; visible only as small rust pustules or dark telial patches on leaves
searchText.dimensions: Sori usually minute, appearing as yellow-orange to brown-black spots or patches on willow leaves
searchText.flesh: No true flesh; infected leaf tissue may yellow, spot, brown or distort
searchText.microscopy: Urediniospores one-celled, yellowish, finely echinulate to spiny; teliospores formed in dark telia on willow leaves
searchText.overview: Willow rust producing yellow-orange summer sori and later dark telia on Salix leaves

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, white to cream sometimes slightly tinged pinkish
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex and slightly umbonate, smooth, dry, white to cream or pallid, slightly darker center, margin smooth or slightly wavy
searchText.stipe: Slender, tall, cylindrical, bulbous base, pale cream to tan, smooth, with a fibrous texture, without a ring
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white, cream or yellowish
searchText.description: Saprobic, growing in nutrient-rich soil or grassy areas, often found in meadows, gardens, and woodland clearings, spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Said to be edible but little information exists and potential misidentification possible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 8–14 cm long, 0.8–1.2 cm thick
searchText.odour: Odour mildly fragrant, sometimes slightly sweet
searchText.taste: Taste slight, smell strongly of meal
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptic,minutely warted, amyloid, 8–9 x 4.5–5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium-sized, saprobic mushroom with a slender, fibrous stipe and a pale cap

searchText.hymenium: Smooth to slightly uneven, vivid orange to orange-red or vermilion
searchText.apothecium: Sessile, initially cup-shaped, later shallowly saucer- to disc-shaped; exterior paler orange to reddish-brown, finely pubescent; margin dotted with short inconspicuous brown hairs
searchText.stipe: Absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on damp bare, mossy or sandy soil; forests, woodland tracks, roadsides and disturbed ground; scattered to gregarious; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Tiny and no culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body very small; apothecia ~1–2 mm tall
searchText.flesh: Orange-red, thin, waxy and brittle, unchanging when cut
searchText.description: Paraphyses filiform with enlarged orange-pigmented apices; marginal hairs brown, blunt, septate, up to ~200 µm long
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid, hyaline, biguttulate, ~16–20 × 9–11 µm excluding ornamentation; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~215–300 × 11–15 µm, inamyloid;
searchText.overview: Tiny vivid orange-red soil cup with short brown marginal hairs

observations.location: Saku mõisa park, Saku, Harju, Eesti

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, forms the inner surface of the apothecium, gray to gray-brown, sometimes darkening with age or when moist
searchText.cap: Disc- or cup-shaped, thin, often slightly depressed in the center, gray to grayish-brown, with a smooth or slightly roughened surface
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Forms the inner surface of the cup)
searchText.stipe: absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, plant debris, and sometimes on bark or fallen leaves, in damp, shaded areas, year-round
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its small size and insubstantial flesh
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny
searchText.microscopy: Spores fusiform, 7-12 x 2.5-3 µm, with an oil drop at each end, asci cylindrical, 40-65 x 4-5.5µm, 8 spores per ascus
searchText.overview: Tiny, inconspicuous grayish cup fungus appearing in dense clusters on decayed wood and plant debris

searchText.hymenium: hymenium is ribbed, forming a honeycomb-like pattern

searchText.stipe: stipe is hollow, cylindrical, whitish to pale grayish-brown, smooth or slightly granular
searchText.spore-print: spore print is cream to yellowish
searchText.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal
