searchText.overview: Highly prized for its culinary value. It has a distinctive honeycomb-like cap with dark pits and ridges. The mushroom typically appears in the spring, often in burned areas or in coniferous forests.

searchText.hymenium: Fertile surface smooth, lining deep pits and honeycomb-like depressions; ridges sterile, pale cream to yellow-ochre, darkening slightly with age
searchText.cap: Ovoid to broadly conical, hollow, attached to stipe at the lower margin; surface strongly pitted and ridged, yellowish, ochre, tan to pale brown
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Apothecial, fused to the stipe along the lower cap margin
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical to clavate, hollow, whitish to cream, finely granular or furfuraceous, sometimes broadened at the base
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
searchText.ecology: Facultatively mycorrhizal (hardwoods, conifers, grass plants), in woodlands, meadows, orchards, disturbed ground and calcareous soils
searchText.edibility: Choice edible after thorough cooking, toxic raw/insufficiently cooked
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe ~2–9 × 2–5 cm
searchText.flesh: Thin, brittle, whitish to pale cream, hollow, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~17–22 × 9–11 µm, asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~220–350 × 16–20 µm, paraphyses filiform to slightly enlarged apically
searchText.overview: Classic honeycomb-like yellow-brown morel

searchText.plasmodium: Pale yellow to whitish, slimy and mucilaginous when active, spreading across grass, leaves, or decaying organic matter
searchText.sporangia: Formed as a crust-like aethalium, irregularly shaped, often cushion-like, white to cream or pale yellow when fresh, turning grayish-brown or ochre as it matures. The surface is covered by a calcareous, powdery layer (peridium)
searchText.description:
Spore mass powdery, grayish-brown to dark brown
Saprotrophic, on decaying plant material, typically in meadows, gardens, or forest edges, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Aethalium size variable, typically 2–10 cm across and up to 1 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: Peridium dissolves in KOH, revealing spores, plasmodium may react faintly yellow in ammonia
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, warted, 6–9 µm, loose capillitium network
searchText.overview: Striking slime mold with a mucilaginous yellow plasmodium and distinctive crust-like aethalium

searchText.sporangia: Terminal, globose, non-apophysate; white to yellowish when immature, becoming grey-brown to dark grey at maturity; borne on tall, erect sporangiophores with prominent columellae
searchText.colony: Rapidly growing, cottony to fluffy, initially white, later grey
searchText.description: Spore mass Grey-brown to dark grey or nearly black at maturity
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on soil, dung, compost, decaying plant matter, stored grain, fruit and other moist organic substrates; widespread and often appearing under cool, humid conditions
searchText.edibility: Inedible microscopic mould
searchText.fruit-body: Microscopic mould colony, often growing several centimetres high
searchText.microscopy: Hyphae broad, coenocytic or sparsely septate; sporangiophores tall, simple or occasionally branched, lacking basal rhizoids; sporangia globose with a prominent columella and residual collarette; sporangiospores smooth, globose to slightly elongated, approximately 4–8 µm; heterothallic, producing dark, thick-walled, ornamented zygospores when compatible mating types meet
searchText.overview: Common fast-growing pin mould forming tall white cottony colonies that darken as spherical grey-black sporangia mature

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; white to cream when young, becoming faintly pinkish with age; edges sometimes gelatinous
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; smooth, strongly viscid when moist, with a separable gelatinous pellicle; pale yellowish-grey; margin distinctly translucent-striate
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly decurrent, often with a short decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Very slender, cylindrical, hollow and fragile; lemon-greenish-yellow; smooth, viscid, covered with a separable gelatinous layer; ring absent
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to very pale cream
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on conifer needle litter, moss, decaying twigs, woody debris; mainly spruce and pine forests, also mixed woodland, damp grassland and heathland; scattered to gregariously; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; tiny, fragile and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–8 cm long and ~0.1–0.3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh whitish, pale yellowish, very thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to cylindrical, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~8–11 × 4–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia irregularly clavate with numerous finger-like projections; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis an ixocutis
searchText.overview: Tiny slimy woodland bonnet with a bright yellow-green stipe and peelable gelatinous cap skin

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; white to pale grey when young, often becoming pinkish-grey with age; short lamellulae frequent, cross-veins often developing between mature gills
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat with a persistent low umbo; smooth to slightly rugose, translucent-striate toward margin; grey-brown, darker centrally and paler toward margin
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to emarginate, sometimes with a short decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow, tough and elastic; whitish near apex, grey-brown to dark brown below; base with coarse white fibrils, rooting into decayed wood; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on well-decayed hardwood logs, stumps, fallen branches and buried wood; solitary to densely clustered; late spring to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~4.5–11(–18) cm long and ~0.15–0.6 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale grey, thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to pip-shaped, smooth, amyloid, ~9–12 × 6–8 µm; basidia 2- or 4-spored; pleurocystidia absent; clamp connections present in 4-spored forms
searchText.overview: Large grey-brown wood bonnet with pinking gills and a tough rooting stipe

searchText.hymenium: Gills, adnate to slightly decurrent, moderately spaced, whitish to pale gray, darkening slightly with age
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped, becoming broadly conical with age, smooth, moist, grayish-brown to pale brown, darker at the center, translucent when moist
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, fragile, whitish to gray, exuding a white, milky latex when damaged, particularly near the base
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, found in coniferous and mixed forests, growing on decaying leaf litter, wood, and soil, often in groups or scattered, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, not considered poisonous but too small and insubstantial to be of culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 4–8 cm long, 0.2–0.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 7–9 x 4–5 µm, inamyloid
searchText.overview: Small, fragile mushroom with a conical, grayish-brown cap, white latex exuding from the stipe when damaged

searchText.hymenium: Gills whitish to pale grey or pinkish, sometimes developing reddish-brown stains; edges usually concolorous but occasionally darker
searchText.cap: Conical to bell-shaped, later broadly convex; hygrophanous, finely pruinose when young and translucent-striate when moist; reddish-brown, fading to pale pinkish-grey
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to adnexed, sometimes decurrent with a small tooth
searchText.stipe: Slender, hollow and fragile; reddish-brown, darker below, with white basal fibrils
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, usually growing in tufts or clusters on well-decayed hardwood logs, stumps and fallen branches; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Insubstantial and of poor culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~4–8 cm long and ~0.1–0.3 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh very thin, pale to vinaceous
searchText.description: Exudes dark blood-red liquid when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to pip-shaped, smooth, amyloid, ~8–11 × 5–7 µm; basidia clavate, predominantly 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia fusiform with elongated narrow apices; pleurocystidia similar when present; clamp connections abundant
searchText.overview: Reddish-brown wood-growing bonnet forming clustered tufts and releasing blood-red liquid when flesh is cut

searchText.hymenium: Gills, well-spaced, initially sordid reddish to grayish, with even, dark-red-brown edges
searchText.cap: Conical to broadly convex or bell-shaped, starting moist with whitish-grayish bloom that soon disappears, revealing a smooth, reddish-brown cap
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Hymenium attachment adnate to slightly decurrent
searchText.stipe: Fragile, same color as cap, smooth to polished above, base with coarse stiff white hairs, exudes dark reddish-purple sap when broken
searchText.ecology: Ecology saprotrophic, growing in groups on leaf-litter, moss beds, acidic soils in conifer and deciduous forests, spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Unknown; too insubstantial for culinary use
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 2–6 cm × 1–1.5 mm
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, weakly amyloid, 8–10 × 4–5 µm; basidia 4-spored, abundant pleuro- and cheilocystidia filled with red pigment
searchText.overview: Small mushroom that exudes reddish-purple sap when injured

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, narrow, color whitish to pale gray initially, gill edges distinctly green-tinged
searchText.cap: Starts conical to campanulate, flattening with age, surface pruinose when young, then glabrescent, hygrophanous and radiately striate when moist, colors olivaceous-grayish-greenish-brown, margins paler
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Narrowly adnate to adnate, occasionally with a short decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Hollow, fragile; smooth to pruinose above, glabrous below, coloration yellowish-brown, darkening toward base, apex pale, base covered in whitish fibrils
searchText.ecology: Saprotrophic, growing on decaying wood of coniferous trees, summer to autumn
searchText.description: Too small and unknown
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium, stipe 20–70 × 1–3 mm
searchText.flesh: No notable color change when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly subellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, amyloid; ~ 9–11.8 × 6–7.5 µm, Basidia 25–32 × 8–10 µm, slender-clavate, 4-spored, sterigmata 5–8 µm, cheilocystidia 23–70 × 7–18 (–29) µm
searchText.overview: Delicate, somewhat slender bonnet mushroom notable for its olive-tinged gill edges

searchText.hymenium: Gills whitish, close to almost distant, narrowly attached to the stipe
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex or bell-shaped, often with a small central depression or bump; dry, smooth to slightly wrinkled; reddish-brown when young, fading to buff or pale tan
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to adnexed, sometimes almost free
searchText.stipe: Very slender, tough, wiry, shiny and mostly smooth; pale near apex, reddish-dark-brown-blackish toward base
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on fallen conifer needles, twigs, bark, leaf litter, grass stems and woody debris; scattered to gregarious, summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, dried and used for strong garlic flavouring
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe up to ~6 cm long, ~0.5–3 mm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh very thin, pale, insubstantial, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to pip-shaped, inamyloid, ~6–10(–11) × 3–5 µm; pleurocystidia absent; cheilocystidia clavate to cylindrical or irregular, lobed, with knob-rod-like projections
searchText.overview: Tiny white-pale-brownish garlic-scented marasmioid mushroom

Lichenicolous (parasitic on lichens), especially crustose and foliose lichens (Aspicilia, Parmeliaceae hosts), grows on the thalli of host lichens in damp forest habitats

searchText.cap: Reflexed to nearly resupinate, often imbricate or arranged in rows; small tough brownish brackets with ochraceous to pale cinnamon, faintly zoned, finely tomentose upper surface
searchText.stipe: N/A
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic and brown heart-rot causing polypore, mainly on dead conifer wood, fallen trunks, stumps, logs and processed timber, common in boreal conifer forests
Inedible — tough, corky and crust-like
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, often forming fused rows or overlapping patches

searchText.chemical-reactions: No distinctive KOH field reaction documented

searchText.overview: Serried porecrust forming tough white-pored, brownish, row-like resupinate to reflexed fruit bodies on decaying conifer wood

Inedible (microscopic)

searchText.overview: Small, brown mushroom that is frequently found in lawns and other grassy areas. It's recognized by its smooth, brown cap and gills that are brownish in color. This species is considered inedible due to the presence of small amounts of the hallucinogenic compound psilocin, and it can cause gastric upset if consumed. As always, it's essential to properly identify any wild mushrooms before considering them for consumption, as many species can look similar but have vastly different edibility profiles.

searchText.body: Fast-growing, dense, white, floccose to cottony mould forming the characteristic bloomy rind of soft cheeses; colonies remain predominantly white
searchText.description:
Spore mass white to very pale cream
Domesticated saprobic fungus specialised for cheese surfaces, especially Camembert, Brie and other bloomy-rind cheeses; grows well in cool, protein- and lipid-rich environments
Deliberately cultivated to form the rind and contribute characteristic flavour, aroma and texture
searchText.fruit-body: Microscopic filamentous mould forming visible white colonies that may cover the entire cheese surface
searchText.dimensions: Colony size variable with substrate and culture conditions; typically forms a continuous felt-like rind rather than discrete fruit bodies
searchText.odour: Mushroom-like, creamy, fatty to mildly ammoniacal during advanced cheese ripening
searchText.taste: Mild, mushroomy, creamy and characteristic when growing as an intended cheese-ripening culture

searchText.description:
Spore mass sage-green to blue-green or grey-green
Saprobic; domesticated strains are deliberately cultivated inside blue-veined cheeses (Gorgonzola, Bleu de Gex, Rochebaron, Bleu d'Auvergne)
Selected cultures historically called P. glaucum have been used in some blue cheeses

searchText.taste: Characteristically mild and piquant when present as a food-grade culture in ripened blue cheese
searchText.microscopy: Branched conidiophores up to ~200–400 µm long, bearing brush-like groups of phialides; conidia globose, smooth, ~2.5 µm, in long chains
searchText.overview: Classic sage- to blue-green Penicillium mould with brush-like conidiophores

searchText.body: Rapidly growing, dense, velvety to fasciculate mould; mycelium whitish but colonies become blue-green, grey-green to dark olive-green from abundant conidia, often with a paler margin and occasional clear exudate droplets
searchText.description:
Spore mass: Blue-green, grey-green to dark green
Saprobic; domesticated strains are deliberately cultivated inside blue-veined cheeses such as Roquefort, Stilton and Danablu
searchText.edibility: Edible when used as an intentionally selected food-grade culture in properly produced blue cheese
searchText.fruit-body: Microscopic filamentous mould forming visible colonies and characteristic blue-green veins or cavities throughout ripening cheese
searchText.dimensions: Colony rapid-growing; laboratory colonies commonly reach ~4–7 cm across within about 1–2 weeks, depending strongly on strain and growth medium
searchText.odour: Strong, mouldy and characteristic; during cheese ripening contributes to the distinctive pungent blue-cheese aroma
searchText.taste: Characteristically sharp and piquant when present as a food-grade culture in ripened blue cheese
searchText.microscopy: Conidiophore stipes rough-walled, ~100–200 µm; terminal penicilli predominantly terverticillate, sometimes quaterverticillate and rarely biverticillate; phialides flask-shaped; conidia spherical, smooth, dark green, ⌀ ~3–4.5 µm, in loose chains
searchText.overview: Classic blue-cheese mould forming dense blue-green colonies deliberately cultivated to create the characteristic blue veins, aroma and flavour of Roquefort-type cheeses

searchText.hymenium: Smooth; pale ochre-yellow to clay-brown
searchText.fruit-body:
Coral-like, repeatedly dichotomously branched, compact to moderately open; branches ochre-yellow when young, becoming dull honey-brown to clay-coloured; tips initially buff-yellow to cream, usually pointed
Fruit body small to medium; ~2.5–7 cm tall and ~1.5–4 cm wide
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
searchText.stipe: Short, distinct, whitish to pale yellow; base surrounded by conspicuous white to cream tomentum and whitish-yellow rhizomorphs
searchText.spore-print: Spore print ochre-yellow to pale brown
searchText.ecology: Probably saprobic on conifer needle litter, humus and occasionally woody debris; mainly coniferous forests; scattered, gregarious or in rows; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edibility uncertain; small and tough
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale yellow, tough and leathery, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: 15% KOH briefly bright yellow on rhizomorphs
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to oblong-ellipsoid, yellowish, ornamented with numerous cyanophilous warts, ~6–10 × 3.3–5 µm; spines up to ~1–1.5 µm; basidia clavate, 4-spored with basal clamps
searchText.overview: Small ochre-yellow woodland coral with pale rhizomorphs and non-greening branches

species.identification: Phaeolepiota aurea (Bull.) R. Maire ex Konrad & Maubl.

commonNames.name: 🇷🇺🍲 Edible after cooking but not recommended

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded; pale yellowwhen young, becoming yellow-brown with maturity
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat with a low umbo; dry, densely granular to finely scaly; golden-yellow; margin often fringed with veil remnants
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate, often with a short decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Robust, clavate toward base; golden-ochre, densely granular below the ring, smoother and paler above; large membranous flaring ring, later pendulous and skirt-like
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale yellow-brown to orange-buff
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on rich humus, leaf litter, compost and disturbed nutrient-rich soil; often associated with nettles; gregarious or clustered; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible after cooking but not recommended
searchText.description: May accumulate high concentrations of cadmium and other heavy metals
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body large; stipe ~10–20(–25) cm long and ~2–5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Pale yellow to whitish, thick and firm; stipe flesh slowly darkening when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth to minutely ornamented, pale yellow-brown, ~10–14 × 5–6 µm, without a germ pore; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia absent; pleurocystidia absent or rare; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Massive golden granular agaric with a conspicuous skirt-like ring

searchText.hymenium: Pores, initially yellow, maturing to brown or olive-brown, pores angular, 1–3 per mm
searchText.cap: Typically fan-shaped or semicircular, surface velvety to woolly, ranging from yellow-brown to dark brown, often zoned with concentric bands of different colors
searchText.stipe: Short, thick, and off-center, or sometimes absent; when present, the stipe is brown to dark brown and covered with a velvety texture similar to the cap
searchText.ecology: Parasitic and saprobic, primarily found on the roots, lower trunks, and stumps of conifers, causes a brown cubical rot, late summer to autumn

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering the exposed surfaces of the gelatinous lobes
searchText.fruit-body:
Densely clustered, leaf- to seaweed-like, composed of thin undulating and folded lobes arising from a common base; ochre-brown, amber-brown to reddish-brown
Fruit body medium; ~1–5 cm tall, often several lobes fused together
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the lobes
searchText.stipe: Absent; lobes arise from a common basal attachment
searchText.ecology: Fungicolous parasite of Stereum hirsutum; grows on dead hardwood colonized by the host fungus; parasite attacks Stereum hyphae within the wood; mainly autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but gelatinous
searchText.flesh: Brownish, soft, rubbery and gelatinous when fresh; shrinking to a thin dark horny crust when dry
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative; FeSO₄ negative on surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline to faintly brownish, ~6.5–10.5 × 5–9 µm; basidia tremelloid, 4-celled, ovoid to subglobose, ~13–18 × 12–16 µm;
searchText.overview: Brown leafy jelly parasitising Stereum hirsutum on hardwood

searchText.hymenium: Small, spiky tooth-like structures on the underside.
searchText.cap: Somewhat irregular, flat to slightly convex or depressed at the center; surface is smooth, gray to bluish-black or black.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, as the spines run down onto the stem.
searchText.stipe: Central or slightly off-center, cylindrical, sometimes with a swollen base, colored similarly to the cap.
searchText.spore-print: Spore print: White to pale cream.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, commonly found under conifers, especially pine trees.
searchText.edibility: Inedible, tough and woody in texture.
searchText.fruit-body: Cap measures 3-7 cm in diameter, while the stipe is 3-6 cm long.
searchText.overview: Recognized for its gray to almost black, smooth cap and the characteristic toothed underside.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, from 3.5-4.5 x 2.5-3 µm.

searchText.hymenium: Spines, the spines are short, conical, and dense, usually white to pale grey, darkening with age to brown or grey
searchText.cap: irregularly circular, often fused with adjacent fruit bodies, surface is densely tomentose, particularly when young, color ranges from brown to dark grey or black, with zoned patterns
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, with the spines extending slightly down the stipe
searchText.stipe: cylindrical, sometimes tapered towards the base, surface is fibrous and grey to black, blending with the cap
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, in coniferous forests in association with spruces and pines, on the ground, on mossy or acidic soils, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to its tough texture and bitter taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: 2–8 cm wide, 5–10 cm tall, 2–5 cm long, 0.5–1 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose, 4–5.5 x 3.5–4.5 µm, smooth and hyaline, basidia four-spored, hyphae brownish, lacks clamp connections
searchText.overview: Mycorrhizal fungus recognized by its woolly, zoned cap, decurrent spines, and tough texture

searchText.hymenium: Gills crowded, narrow; cream to pale yellow when young, becoming ochre-brown with maturity, sometimes with olive tones; edges often whitish
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat, with a low umbo; sticky to viscid when moist; cream-yellow, straw-yellow to pale ochre with olive-greenish tints; margin fringed with veil remnants
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, cream to pale yellowish, becoming brownish toward base; finely pruinose near apex, covered with whitish to yellow-brown fibrils or small scales below; partial veil leaving a fragile ring or indistinct ring zone
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying hardwood, especially buried roots, stumps and woody debris; in grass, parks, gardens and woodland paths; solitary, scattered or clustered; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended; little culinary value
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–10 cm long and ~0.5–1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Whitish to pale yellowish, thin, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to oblong or slightly bean-shaped, smooth, yellow-brown, ~5.5–8 × 3.5–4.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; cheilocystidia cylindrical to lageniform; pileipellis an ixocutis
searchText.overview: Pale yellow sticky scalycap with darker appressed scales, often growing from buried hardwood

searchText.hymenium: Gills are adnate to subdecurrent, close, and yellowish, turning brownish with age.
searchText.cap: Up to 10 cm in diameter.Convex to flat, with a somewhat slimy, scaly surface; yellow-brown to dark brown.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, yellowish at the top and brownish toward the base, sometimes with a ring.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood or on wood chips and sometimes on the ground.
searchText.edibility: Inedible; not recommended for consumption.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 12 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Microscopic Features: Spores are elliptical, smooth, and measure approximately 6-8 x 4-5 µm.
searchText.overview: Known for its distinctive brown spore print and a cap that varies from yellow-brown to dark brown, Pholiota spumosa is primarily saprobic, thriving on decaying wood.

searchText.hymenium: Gills, close to crowded, whitish to yellowish when young, becoming greenish-yellow then cinnamon-brown
searchText.cap: convex to broadly convex, surface dry, yellow-ochre underneath buff to tawny, overlaid with upturned, coarse, brownish, recurved scales
searchText.stipe: cylindrical, dry, yellowish and covered in tawny scales below the ring zone; bears a persistent woolly or fibrous ring formed from the partial veil
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, opportunistically parasitic, clusters on living (weakened) or decaying wood, at tree bases, summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Not recommended, sever cases of poisoning (with alcohol)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 4–12 cm long, ~1.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh is white to pale yellow, no staining
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, ~6–8×4–5 µm, distinct apical pore, pleurocystidia clavate to subfusiform, ~45×14 µm, cheilocystidia subfusiform to fusoid-ventricose, ~43×15 µm
searchText.overview: Wood-decaying, scaly, medium-sized cluster mushroom with a dry, coarse-scaled cap and stem

searchText.plasmodium-phase: The active feeding phase is a slimy, shapeless mass, typically yellow, orange in color, crawling over decaying plant material and feeding on microorganisms
searchText.fruiting-bodies: Forms scattered to grouped sporangia, spherical to slightly flattened, supported by short, delicate stalks, surface is powdery, rusty-brown, with a metallic sheen as they mature
searchText.description: Spore mass powdery, rusty-brown in mature fruiting bodies
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying leaves, wood, bark on soil, in moist, shaded areas of forests or gardens, spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Individual sporangia are 0.3–1 mm in diameter, clusters may cover several centimeters of substrate
searchText.chemical-reactions: Peridium dissolves in KOH, plasmodium may stain substrates with orange pigment
searchText.microscopy: Spores spherical, warted or spiny, 8–11 µm, dense, branching capillitium network
searchText.overview: Distinctive slime mold, characterized by its rusty-brown or orange plasmodium and metallic-hued sporangia

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially white to cream, becoming more pale-yellow or buff with age
searchText.cap: Fan- to oyster-shaped, sometimes broadly convex or nearly flat in crowded clusters, margin lobed or wavy, surface smooth, velvety when fresh, colour white/grey/tan
searchText.stipe: Often short, lateral or eccentric, sometimes almost absent, white to pale, solid, may be offset or thin
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on dead or dying wood of hardwoods (logs, stumps, trunks), shelf-like clusters, year-round
searchText.edibility: Choice edible, widely cultivated and culinary valued
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large
searchText.flesh: Flesh white, firm, unchanging in colour when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, ~8–12 × 3–4 µm, basidia 4-sterigmate, clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Prominent wood-decaying agaric that forms broad, shelf-or fan-shaped caps clustered on dead hardwood logs or tree stumps

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are white to pale yellowish, running down the stipe
searchText.cap: Oyster-shaped or fan-shaped, ranging from pale grayish when young to brownish with age
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, extending down the length of the stipe
searchText.stipe: Typically off-center or even lateral, often short or sometimes even absent
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid, smooth, and hyaline, typically measuring 7-9 x 3-4 µm
searchText.odour: Pleasant, typically mushroomy, sometimes with subtle anise-like or seafood undertones
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; grows on dead and decaying wood, especially hardwoods
searchText.edibility: Edible and choice; has a mild, pleasant taste and is often used in culinary dishes
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Cap can reach up to 5-15 cm in diameter
searchText.dimensions: Cap: Up to 5-15 cm in diameter and 2-5 cm deep
searchText.overview: Closely related to the common oyster mushroom but tends to fruit during warmer summer months. Its pale coloration and smoother cap texture help differentiate it from its cousin. Like other oyster mushrooms, it grows in shelf-like clusters on wood.

searchText.hymenium: Lamellae (gills) are deeply wrinkled or folded, giving them a distinctive 'crisped' appearance.
searchText.description: Convex to flat, often with a depressed center, and smooth to slightly wrinkled surface. Cap color ranges from pale to dark brown.
searchText.stipe: Central or slightly off-center, cylindrical, and often with a tapering base. Stipe surface is smooth and colored similar to the cap.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, initiating wood decay. Typically found on decaying wood, particularly in forests.
searchText.edibility: Considered inedible due to its tough and leathery texture.
searchText.fruit-body: Cap diameter ranges from 3-10 cm, while the stipe can be 4-12 cm tall and 0.5-1 cm thick.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to spindle-shaped, smooth, 5-7 x 3-4 µm.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its crisped or wrinkled gills, which give the mushroom a unique appearance. It primarily grows on decaying wood, contributing to the decomposition process in forest ecosystems.

searchText.hymenium: Gills free, crowded, white at first, becoming pink to salmon-pink as spores mature
searchText.cap: Bell-shaped to convex, later broadly convex or nearly flat; brown, darker in centre, smooth to silky, sometimes radially streaked or fibrillose
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Free, not attached to the stipe
searchText.stipe: Central, cylindrical, whitish to pale, with brown vertical fibrils; slightly enlarged at base; no ring
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale pink to salmon-pink
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood, stumps, fallen branches, buried wood, sawdust and wood chips, on hardwood, spring to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but mediocre, not highly prized
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe ~5–12 cm long, ~0.5–2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, soft, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: Flesh without KOH reaction, spores hyaline to faintly ochraceous in KOH
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, ~6–8 × 4.5–6 µm, cheilocystidia abundant, pleurocystidia thick-walled, fusiform to utriform, with 2–5 apical hooks, clamp connections absent
searchText.overview: Wood-decaying pink-spored agaric with free gills, brown deer-coloured cap and fibrillose pale stipe

species.identification: Podosphaera mors-uvae (Schwein.) U. Braun & S. Takam.

searchText.hymenium: No exposed macroscopic hymenium; sexual spores develop within asci enclosed in globose chasmothecia, while the conspicuous white powdery coating consists mainly of superficial mycelium, conidiophores and chains of conidia
searchText.body: White, flour-like superficial colonies on leaves, young shoots and fruits, initially patchy but often becoming confluent; ageing colonies turn greyish, brown to dark brown, with minute dark chasmothecia developing later in the season
searchText.description: Spore mass white, powdery conidial mass; mature chasmothecia dark brown to black
searchText.ecology: Obligate biotrophic parasite of Ribes species; infects leaves, young shoots and berries; conidia spread infections through the growing season while chasmothecia may overwinter and release ascospores in spring
searchText.fruit-body: Microscopic
searchText.microscopy: Hyphae ~4–7 µm wide; conidiophores erect, cylindrical, ~92–165 × 9–11 µm; conidia produced in chains, broadly ellipsoid-ovoid to doliiform, ~22–31 × 14–22 µm, containing conspicuous fibrosin bodies; chasmothecia globose, ~92–104 µm, with few mycelioid appendages; each chasmothecium contains a single 8-spored ascus ~80–96 × 60–72 µm; ascospores ellipsoid-ovoid to subcylindrical, ~20–26 × 10–14 µm
searchText.overview: Powdery mildew of gooseberries and currants

searchText.hymenium: Poroid
searchText.cap: Semi-circular to fan-shaped, surface smooth to slightly rough, white to greyish or pale brown.
searchText.stipe: N/A (Typically sessile)
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; grows on dead conifer wood, particularly pine and spruce.
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit Body is ip to 10 cm wide and 3 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, 3.5-5 x 1.5-2 μm.
searchText.overview: Known for its large, semi-circular to fan-shaped fruit bodies that can grow up to 20 cm wide and 5 cm thick. The cap surface is velvety and typically white to pale cream, sometimes turning brownish with age. It has a poroid hymenium with white pores and a white spore print.

searchText.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced; pale grey when young, becoming purplish-grey to dark grey-brown or nearly black with maturity; edges often whitish
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; smooth, slightly sticky when fresh, soon dry; golden-yellow, ochre-yellow to brownish-yellow; young margin may retain white veil fragments
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate, sometimes with a slight decurrent tooth
searchText.stipe: Short, cylindrical, white to cream, sometimes yellowish below; smooth to finely fibrillose; base slightly tapered with white mycelial threads; membranous white ring persistent to fragile, characteristically grooved above and darkened by deposited spores
searchText.spore-print: Spore print dark purple-brown to blackish
searchText.description: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, pastures, parks, gardens; especially nutrient-rich soils; alone, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Poisonous
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–6 cm long and ~0.4–1 cm thick
searchText.flesh: White, soft, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores amygdaliform to ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, ~7–10 × 4–5.5 µm, with a small germ pore; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia clavate to broadly cylindrical; clamp connections
searchText.overview: Golden-yellow grassland stropharioid with a grooved ring and dark purple-brown spores

searchText.hymenium: Rhe­emata of rust pustules on host leaves (uredinia, telia) with sori breaking through the epidermis; internal hyphae intercellular, forming haustoria in host tissues
searchText.morphology: No cap; symptoms appear as yellowish to brown spots or pustules (rust sori) on leaves; pustules may be brownish and powdery
searchText.ecology: Obligate plant pathogen; heteroecious (requires alternate hosts), macrocyclic (has all typical rust life cycle stages: pycniospores, aeciospores, urediniospores, teliospores, basidiospores), primary hosts are cereals (wheat, rye) and some grasses
searchText.edibility: Edibility inapplicable
searchText.dimensions: Sorus size: pustules generally small—visible on leaves
searchText.description:
Germination of urediniospores requires free moisture
Aeciospores: 21-26 × 17-22 µm, broadly ellipsoid to spherical, hyaline.
Urediniospores: 24-32 × 20-25 µm, yellow to cinnamon-brown, often finely echinulate (spiny) walls.
Teliospores: Two-celled, long clavate when mature, 40-58 × 17-25 µm, brown.
searchText.microscopy: Spores: Different spore types:
searchText.overview: Rust fungus infecting cereals and grasses (especially wheat, rye), causing brownish pustules on leaves and serious disease

observations.location: Kloostrimetsa soo õpperada, Tallinn, Harjumaa, Eesti

searchText.hymenium: Branched coral-like structures, cream to yellowish when young, becoming tan or brownish with age.
searchText.cap: Not applicable, as this species has coral-like fruit bodies rather than distinct caps.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Coral-like branches emerge directly from the base or substrate.
searchText.stipe: Not distinctly separate due to its coral-like form, base is typically whitish to cream.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, found primarily on decaying wood and forest litter.
searchText.edibility: Not recommended for consumption
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body: Up to 15 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Striking coral fungus with intricately branched, upright fruiting bodies resembling marine corals. Its branches are cream to yellowish when young and become tan or brownish with age. Found in mixed forests, this species grows on decaying wood and forest litter, playing a vital role in nutrient cycling.

observations.location: Suurupi LKA, Suurupi skv, Harjumaa, Estonia

searchText.hymenium: Smooth
searchText.cap: N/A (Coral-like branches instead of a cap)
searchText.stipe: Short, often branched at the base, whitish to pale yellow.
searchText.ecology: Saprobic; grows on decaying wood and forest litter.
searchText.edibility: Inedible; can cause gastrointestinal upset.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit Body is up to 10 cm tall and 5 cm wide
searchText.microscopy: Spores are broadly ellipsoid to roughly spherical, with finely warted surfaces, 7-10 x 3-4.5 μm.
searchText.overview: Characterized by its coral-like, upright, and often branched fruiting bodies. The branches are typically straight and rigid.

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer branch surfaces; white to cream, becoming pale yellowish or ochre with age
searchText.fruit-body:
Coral-like, repeatedly and irregularly branched from a common base; branches slender, crowded to somewhat spreading; tips forked, pointed to blunt
Fruit body small to medium; ~3–10 cm tall
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
searchText.stipe: Short, rudimentary basal trunk, white to cream, often dividing rapidly into numerous branches
searchText.ecology: Presumed saprobic on soil among moss and grass, especially unimproved grasslands, pastures, dunes, banks and woodland clearings; occasionally in litter or on very decayed wood; solitary to clustered; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edibility uncertain; insubstantial and of little culinary value
searchText.flesh: White to cream, thin, fragile to somewhat pliant, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to ellipsoid, finely echinulate to verrucose, hyaline, ~3.5–5.5 × 3–4.5 µm, slightly dextrinoid; basidia 2–4-spored; cystidia absent; hyphae with clamp connections
searchText.overview: White coral with densely branched forked tips and finely spiny spores

searchText.hymenium: Enclosed within a chambered, labyrinthine gleba; basidia line the internal cavities
searchText.fruit-body: Subglobose, ellipsoid to irregularly potato-shaped, hypogeous to partly emerging; whitish when young, becoming honey-yellow, ochre to olive-brown; surface fibrillose to rugose
searchText.peridium: Thick, tough and leathery, initially whitish, becoming yellow-brown to ochraceous; drying very hard
searchText.stipe: Absent; attached to substrate by numerous branching rhizomorphs
searchText.description: Spore mass creamy-white to yellowish; gleba becoming olive-yellow to olive-brown at maturity
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines; sandy, acidic pine forests and plantations, often beside tracks; solitary or in small groups; late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Poor culinary value
searchText.dimensions: Fruit body small to medium, ∅ ~1.5–5(–6) cm
searchText.flesh: Gleba white and soft when young, firmer and powdery with maturity; no characteristic reddening
searchText.chemical-reactions: FeSO₄ slightly olive on surface; KOH negative
searchText.odour: Mild when young, becoming unpleasant to garlicky with age
searchText.microscopy: Spores narrowly ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline becoming pale olive-brown, ~5.5–9 × 2.5–3.5 µm, often biguttulate; basidia lageniform, usually 4–6-spored; clamp connections absent
searchText.overview: Yellow-brown pine false truffle with dense rhizomorphs and olive chambered gleba

searchText.hymenium: Developing inside elongated apothecial ascomata embedded within black stromata
searchText.body: Initially yellow-green leaf spots, developing into slightly raised, glossy tar-black stromata; irregularly circular, often surrounded by a narrow yellow to brownish margin
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Ascomata embedded beneath the surface of the stroma
searchText.stipe: Absent
searchText.description:
Spore mass hyaline to whitish
Biotrophic parasite on living maple leaves, especially sycamore and Norway maple; stromata mature on fallen overwintered leaves, releasing ascospores in spring to infect newly emerging foliage
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body microscopic
searchText.flesh: Black stromatic tissue embedded within infected leaf tissue
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores very slender, cylindrical to filiform, smooth, hyaline, aseptate, ~60–80 × 1.5–2.5 µm, with a small apical gelatinous appendage; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~105–130 × 9–12 µm; paraphyses hyaline, septate, often curved or branched apically; conidia cylindrical, ~6–10 × 1 µm
searchText.overview: Classic black tar spots on maple leaves

searchText.hymenium: Gills, white to pale cream, turning brownish with age.
searchText.cap: Convex to somewhat flattened with age, pale brown or beige, often with darker central regions.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, usually paler than the cap, fibrous, often enlarging toward the base.
searchText.dimensions: Cap: Ranging from 2-7 cm in diameter.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Typically 3-10 cm tall.
searchText.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale cream.
searchText.ecology: Saprotrophic, found on rotting wood, especially coniferous wood.
searchText.edibility: Not recommended for consumption, as its edibility status remains uncertain.
searchText.microscopy: Spores 5-8 x 3-4.5 µm, elliptical, smooth.
searchText.overview: Is often found in coniferous forests. Its placement in the genus Ripartites is due to its wood-decaying lifestyle, which differentiates it from many other gilled mushrooms.

species.identification: Rubroboletus satanas (Lenz) Kuan Zhao & Zhu L.Yang

searchText.hymenium: Pores, small, round, initially yellow, turning orange-blood-red, blue when bruised
searchText.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age, surface smooth and velvety, pale grey to light beige, margin curved inward in young specimens
searchText.stipe: Robust, bulbous to clavate, yellow at the top, transitioning to red or reddish-orange with a dense, fine red reticulation
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broad-leaved trees such as oak, beech, and birch in calcareous soils, late spring to early autumn
searchText.edibility: Highly toxic when raw, causing severe gastrointestinal distress, toxicity is not eliminated by cooking
searchText.fruit-body: Large, cap 10–25 cm in diameter, stipe 5–12 cm long, 3–7 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: Flesh stains blue when cut, KOH on cap surface produces a dark red reaction
searchText.odour: Unpleasant, reminiscent of decaying food or carrion

searchText.overview: Characterized by its yellow or ochre cap and white gills and stem. Like other members of the Russula genus, it has a brittle texture. This species forms a mycorrhizal relationship with various trees, and it is often found in coniferous and deciduous forests. It's known for its mild, nutty flavor and is considered a good edible mushroom. As always, proper identification is crucial as there are many species in the Russula genus, some of which may be inedible or have a peppery or bitter taste.

searchText.overview: Mushroom known for its large size, robust stature, and uniformly white appearance. Like other members of the Russula genus, it has a brittle texture due to the presence of spherical cells called sphaerocysts. It can often be found in association with various trees as it forms mutualistic mycorrhizal relationships. While it is considered edible, its flavor is mild and not particularly remarkable, and some individuals find it slightly bitter. It's always important to be cautious when identifying Russula species, as some can be very similar in appearance but have different edibility profiles.

searchText.overview: Russula fragilis exhibits a relatively high level of spore ornamentation, featuring warts that are isolated or only infrequently connected by lines. The gills of this species contain predominantly 4-spored basidia, contributing to its overall spore density. Additionally, it possesses intracellular pigments, which result in its vivid cap colors. This species is noted for its sensitivity to environmental conditions, particularly soil pH, favoring more acidic substrates. It is subject to parasitization by the fungus Hypomyces lactifluorum, which transforms it into the "Lobster Mushroom." Studies have shown that Russula fragilis has a high degree of mycorrhizal specificity, most commonly forming associations with members of the Pinaceae family.
