searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, subfusiform to broadly ellipsoid, 11-15 x 4.5-6.5 µm, brownish in KOH
searchText.overview: Robust bolete with olive-brown cap, bright yellow pores that bruise to blue-black, yellow stipe with red reticulation

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, pale yellow ochre when young, turning brown as spores mature, slight blueing reaction
searchText.cap: Convex when young, becoming broadly convex or flat with age, surface smooth and sticky when wet, typically brownish with a slightly darker center, and with a striate margin
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, with a scabrous to reticulate surface in the upper portion, pale to brownish, sometimes with a slightly bulbous base
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with pine trees (Pinus spp.) in coniferous and mixed woodlands, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible and not the best choice
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 7–15 cm long and 1.5–3 cm thick.
searchText.microscopy: Ellipsoid, smooth, typically measuring 8–11 × 4–5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-spored.
searchText.overview: Medium bolete with a sticky, brownish to reddish-brown cap and a reticulate, robust stipe

searchText.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, with yellow to olive pores.
searchText.cap: 5-12 cm in diameter. Convex to flat, slimy when wet, and shiny when dry. The cap is typically yellow to olive-brown.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, sometimes swollen at the base, yellow with a reddish-brown scabers towards the base.
searchText.description: Brown.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, predominantly found in association with Aleppo pine trees, particularly in sandy soils.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but the slimy cap skin should be removed before consumption.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 10 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, 8-10 x 3-4 µm.
searchText.overview: Known for its sticky cap and reddish-brown scabers on the lower stipe and its association with pines in sandy soils are key identification features.

searchText.hymenium: Pores small, round to slightly angular; pale yellow to lemon-yellow, becoming ochre-yellow with age; young pores characteristically exude milky-white droplets that dry brownish
searchText.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex; smooth, strongly viscid and sticky when moist; cinnamon-brown, orange-brown to yellow-brown, often paler toward margin
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, solid, pale yellow to straw-coloured; covered with fine yellowish to brown glandular granules; ring absent; basal mycelium white
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines, especially two-needled pines such as Scots pine; alone, scattered or gregariously; coniferous forests, parks and grassy places beneath pines; summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible after thorough cooking; mediocre quality, cap skin often removed
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~4–10 cm long and ~1–2 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Pale whitish-yellow, soft, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH olive-grey on cap, pink to reddish-lilac on flesh; FeSO₄ bluish-grey on cap and olive-grey on flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores boletoid-fusiform to elongated-ellipsoid, smooth, ~7–10 × 2.5–3.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; clamp connections absent
searchText.overview: Ringless sticky pine bolete with milky droplets and granular stipe

searchText.hymenium: Pores that are initially yellow, aging to a deeper orange or reddish hue; can bruise brownish.
searchText.cap: convex to nearly flat in maturity; sticky when wet, smooth; yellow to orange-yellow, often with reddish-brown tones in the center.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Attached directly to the stipe, sometimes slightly descending.
searchText.stipe: 4-10 cm long, 1-2.5 cm thick; yellow at the top, reddening towards the base; may have a ring-like, reticulation on the upper part.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: 9-22 cm tall.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with larch trees.
searchText.edibility: Edible and considered good by many, though some recommend peeling the sticky skin off the cap before cooking.
searchText.microscopy: Spores 8-12 x 3-4 µm, smooth, elongated-ellipsoid.
searchText.overview: Recognizable by its bright yellow to orange cap and association with larch trees. This mycorrhizal fungus establishes a beneficial relationship with its tree partner, aiding in nutrient exchange.

searchText.hymenium: Pores, large, angular, yellow, turning brown with age, exude a milky liquid when fresh
searchText.cap: convex to flattened as it matures, with a very slimy or viscid surface when wet, color is brown to chestnut, darkening with age
searchText.stipe: cylindrical, yellowish with a slimy, brown ring that may disappear in older specimens, base is often covered in white mycelium
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with pine trees, found in coniferous forests, on sandy soil, late summer to autumn, often in large numbers
searchText.edibility: Edible and widely collected, slimy cuticle of the cap removed before cooking
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 7–12 cm tall, stipe 5–10 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, spindle-shaped to ellipsoid, 7.5–10.5 x 3–4.5 µm, basidia tetrasporic, hyphal structure lacks clamp connections
searchText.overview: Distinctive mycorrhizal mushroom characterized by its large brown slimy cap

searchText.description: tubes under the cap instead of gills, yellow to olive, becoming brownish with age
searchText.cap: cap is convex, becoming broadly convex to nearly flat in age, smooth to finely velvet, reddish-brown with a variegated pattern
searchText.hymenium-attachment: hymenium attachment is adnate to decurrent
searchText.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, yellowish at the top, reddish-brown towards the base, may have a ring
searchText.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, often found in association with pine trees
searchText.edibility: edibility: edible, but should be peeled before consumption due to a potentially indigestible cuticle on the cap
searchText.fruit-body: fruit body to 6-12 cm tall
searchText.overview: Mushroom recognized by its distinctive cap with a variegated pattern of reddish-brown and yellow hues. Like other members of the Suillus genus, it has tubes instead of gills under the cap, which help to identify it as a bolete. It forms mutualistic relationships with pine trees, helping the tree to absorb nutrients while the mushroom benefits from the tree's photosynthesis products. Although it is edible, the cap's skin should be removed before cooking, as it can cause indigestion in some people.

searchText.hymenium: Naked whitish pale grey ascus layer developing on swollen fruits
searchText.body: Forms elongated, hollow, bladder- or tongue-shaped galls replacing normal fruits of bird cherry, initially pale green, later yellowish-reddish-brown
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Exposed ascus layer on the surface of infected plant tissue
searchText.stipe: N/A
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
searchText.ecology: iotrophic plant parasite on Prunus padus and related bird cherries, causing tongue-like fruit galls, spring to early summer
searchText.edibility: Inedible, infected fruits distorted, hollow and stone-less
searchText.fruit-body: Microscopic fungus, host deformations up to ~1–3 cm long
searchText.flesh: Gall tissue soft, spongy, pale green to yellowish, becoming brownish with age
searchText.microscopy: Asci cylindrical to clavate, ~50–60 × 25–52 µm, ascospores globose to subglobose, ~4–5 µm, budding within asci, no true ascomata
searchText.overview: Parasitic ascomycete causing elongated hollow galls on bird cherry fruits

searchText.hymenium: Gills, decurrent, thick and widely spaced, color ranges from pale yellow to brownish as the mushroom matures
searchText.cap: Initially convex, becoming flat to slightly funnel-shaped with age, often wavy at the edges, surface is dry and velvety, brown to dark brown, sometimes with a slight olive tinge
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, with gills running down the stipe
searchText.stipe: Short, thick, and cylindrical, velvety to the touch, and covered with dark brown to nearly black tomentum
searchText.spore-print: Spore print is brown to rusty-brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying coniferous wood, often on stumps, fallen logs, or woody debris, coniferous and mixed forests
searchText.edibility: Inedible, consumption is not recommended due to potential gastrointestinal upset
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 8–20 cm
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to almond-shaped, 6–9 x 4–5.5 µm, gill edges fertile, with basidia two- or four-spored
searchText.overview: Striking mushroom easily recognized by its dark brown velvety stipe and large, funnel-shaped cap

searchText.hymenium: Gills, thick, irregularly spaced, pale yellow to tan, darkening to ochre-brown as the fungus ages
searchText.cap: Fan-shaped to semicircular, velvety to smooth, pale yellowish-brown to dark brown, often wavy and irregular at the margin, surface becomes dry and cracked with age
searchText.stipe: Often absent, when present, short and off-center, blending into the cap, pale brown to ochre
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, typically growing on decaying wood, especially on coniferous logs, stumps, and wood piles, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, known to cause digestive discomfort if consumed
searchText.description: Characterises first enzymes in atromentin biosynthesis
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe up to 1–2 cm long
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 6–8 x 3–5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Large, fan-shaped mushroom with velvety, brownish cap and irregular gills

searchText.hymenium: Smooth to longitudinally wrinkled or striate, brown to purplish-brown, covering the lower/inner surface of the fan- or funnel-like fruit body
searchText.cap: Thin, leathery, rosette- to funnel-shaped, often centrally split or lobed; brown to purplish-brown with paler, frilled, fringed or carnation-like margins
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Not gilled; hymenium spread over the wrinkled underside/inner surface
searchText.stipe: Present, central to slightly eccentric, short, tough, brownish, merging into the funnel-shaped cap
searchText.ecology:
Ectomycorrhizal, growing on sandy soil, mossy ground or needle litter in coniferous and deciduous woodland; solitary or in small groups; summer to late autumn
Inedible, thin, tough and leathery
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium
searchText.flesh: Thin, brown, coriaceous/leathery, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores angular to irregularly lobed, warted or tuberculate, brownish to umber-purple, ~6–10 × 5–8 µm; basidia usually 2–4-sterigmate; hyphae with clamp connections
searchText.overview: Small carnation-like earthfan with a thin brown funnel-shaped rosette

searchText.hymenium: Wrinkled to irregularly ridged, covering surfaces of coral-like branches, initially pale pinkish, becoming dark brown with age
searchText.cap: Lacks a true cap, fruiting body is fan-shaped, with densely clustered, flattened branches that are rosette-shaped, surface often appears velvety or fibrous
searchText.stipe: Lacking or poorly defined; sometimes with a short, fused base connecting multiple branches
searchText.spore-print: Spore print brown to dark brown
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with conifers, on the ground, in moss or leaf litter, dense clusters, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, emitting an unpleasant odor
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, clusters may reach up to 10 cm wide and 6–8 cm tall
searchText.dimensions: Branches (Lobes) each branch is 0.5–3 cm wide and 2–6 cm tall
searchText.chemical-reactions: Spores brownish in KOH. KOH instantly black on all surfaces and flesh. Flesh unchanging when sliced.
searchText.microscopy: Spores vaguely ellipsoid to more or less subglobose—occasionally slightly lobed, 8–11 x 6–8 µm, spines 1 µm wide, 0.5–1 µm high, basidia 40–70 x 6–10 µm, clavate to widely cylindric; 4-sterigmate
searchText.overview: Coral-like fungus with densely packed, dark branches that emit a foul odor

searchText.hymenium: Irregular, lobed or flattened branches which are split at their ends, giving them a fringed appearance.
searchText.cap: Not clearly differentiated, as the fruiting body is more of a lobed or fringed mass rather than the typical mushroom cap.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: N/A for this species due to its unique fruit body structure.
searchText.stipe: Absent.
searchText.description: Brown.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found associated with coniferous trees, particularly pines.
searchText.edibility: Edibility: Inedible, with a tough and woody consistency.
searchText.fruit-body: The entire structure can range from 3-10 cm across and up to 5 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its terrestrial, fan-like, and fringed structures that often form dense mats on the ground.
searchText.microscopy: Microscopic features: Spores are ellipsoid, 9-12 x 6-7 µm.

searchText.cap: N/A
searchText.hymenium: N/A
searchText.stipe: Elongated, club-shaped structure (stroma) which is dark brown to black, emerging from the parasitized host fungus.
searchText.ecology: Parasitic on truffle-like fungi, especially species of Elaphomyces.
searchText.edibility: Not edible.
searchText.fruit-body: Up to 6 cm tall.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid and smooth, 3-4 µm x 1.5-2 µm.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its parasitic growth on underground fungi and its club-shaped, above-ground stroma.

searchText.hymenium: Smooth, resupinate, covering the surface of the substrate
searchText.cap: N/A (Forms a crust-like fruit body without a defined cap)
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate, fully attached and spreading flat across the substrate
searchText.stipe: N/A (Lacks a stipe as it is a crust fungus)
searchText.spore-print: Spore print pale brown to rusty-brown
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal, on decaying wood or forest litter in coniferous and deciduous forests, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, due to its tough, crust-like structure
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body thin, spreading crust on wood, covering large areas of substrate, up to 10–20 cm in patches
searchText.dimensions: Crust thickness less than 1 mm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, 7–10 x 5–6.5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Found as a spreading layer on decaying wood or forest litter

searchText.hymenium: Pores round to slightly angular, cream to pale ochre; ~3–4 per mm
searchText.cap: Semicircular to shell-shaped, often overlapping in tiers; concentrically zoned ochre, buff, orange-brown to grey-brown; alternating finely tomentose, velvety and smoother zones; margin thin and paler
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Pore surface covers the underside of the bracket
searchText.stipe: Absent; broadly attached and sessile
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot on dead hardwood, especially beech and oak; fallen trunks, branches, stumps and standing dead wood; overlapping clusters; annual but persistent, visible year-round
Inedible; tough, leathery and corky
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; often forming much larger overlapping masses
searchText.flesh: White to cream, tough-fibrous and corky, unchanging when cut
searchText.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to slightly curved/allantoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5.5–8 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent
searchText.overview: Ochre-zoned hardwood bracket with broad hairy bands and cream pores

searchText.hymenium: Pores, small and round (4–6 per mm), white to cream when young, becoming yellowish with age
searchText.cap: Shelflike, semicircular to fan-shaped, velvety to tomentose surface when young, often zoned, margin often wavy
searchText.stipe: Lacking, fruiting body is attached laterally to the substrate
searchText.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, grows on decaying hardwoods, often found on logs, stumps, or fallen branches, year-round
searchText.edibility: Inedible due to tough, woody texture
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, caps measure 5–15 cm wide and 1–3 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: Yellowish to reddish-brown KOH on cap surface
searchText.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to slightly curved, smooth, hyaline in KOH, 5–7 x 2–3 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate
searchText.overview: Medium-sized shelf fungus with a velvety cap surface and a poroid hymenium

searchText.hymenium: Gelatinous, irregularly lobed or brain-like in appearance, bright yellow to orange in color.
searchText.cap: Absent, as this species forms gelatinous fruiting bodies.
searchText.stipe: Absent, as this species forms gelatinous fruiting bodies.
searchText.description: Not applicable
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, commonly found on decaying wood, particularly on fallen branches and logs in forested habitats.
searchText.edibility: Generally considered edible and used in culinary dishes in some cultures.
searchText.fruit-body: Size varies, typically ranging from a few centimeters to several decimeters across.
searchText.microscopy: This species does not produce conventional spores.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its gelatinous, brain-like fruiting bodies that are bright yellow to orange in color. It is commonly found on decaying wood in forested areas, where it contributes to the decomposition process. In some cultures, it is valued as an edible fungus and used in various culinary dishes.

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are crowded and white, often with a slightly serrated edge.
searchText.cap: Convex to flattened with age, smooth, and pure white; sometimes with a slight umbo at the center.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, solid, and white; it can be somewhat swollen at the base.
searchText.description: White.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in association with deciduous and coniferous trees.
searchText.edibility: Edible but not particularly sought after due to its bland taste. Caution is advised as it can be confused with other toxic white mushrooms.
searchText.fruit-body: Cap diameter of 5-10 cm; stipe length of 6-12 cm.
searchText.overview: Characterized by its entirely white appearance, from cap to stipe to gills.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, 5-7 x 3-4.5 µm.

observations.location: Tallinn Botanical Garden, Kloostrimetsa, Harju County

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, emarginate to adnate, bright yellow, turning ochre with age
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, slightly depressed in the center, with a dry, fibrillose to scaly surface, color is typically yellow to greenish, with darker brownish scales concentrated in the center
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, slightly tapered at the base, bright yellow, with faint longitudinal fibrils
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pine trees, often found in sandy soils in coniferous forests, appears in late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Historically consumed, some populations are reported to rhabdomyolysis with repeated consumption
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 5–12 cm tall
searchText.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 7–9 x 4–5 µm, and inamyloid, basidia four-spored
searchText.overview: Distinctive mushroom with a convex to flat, yellow to greenish-yellow cap adorned with darker brownish scales

searchText.hymenium: Gills that are white to cream, adnate to emarginate, not particularly crowded.
searchText.cap: 4-8 cm in diameter. Convex becoming broadly convex to nearly flat in age, dry and slightly scaly, colors ranging from yellow-brown to reddish-brown.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, usually lighter at the top and darkening towards the base, often with white to off-white fibrils.
searchText.fruit-body: 5-12 cm tall.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, growing exclusively under birch in deciduous and mixed forests.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but not highly regarded. Some caution advised as it can be confused with toxic species.
searchText.microscopy: 5-8 x 3-5 µm, elliptical, hyaline.
searchText.overview: Recognized by its yellow-brown to reddish-brown cap and its presence in both deciduous and coniferous woodlands. The adnate to emarginate gill attachment and the white spore print are also indicators.

observations.location: Jaapani Aed, Kadriorg, Tallinn, Harju County

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, pale to light brown, sometimes with a slightly pinkish hue, not staining when bruised
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming flat or slightly depressed with age, with dark brown, fibrous scales, margin wavy, inrolled when young
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, brown to reddish-brown, with a fibrillose surface, base slightly swollen, basal mycelium white
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with coniferous trees (pines), growing alone, scattered, gregariously, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Reported edible, but has bitter taste and tough texture
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 3–8 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative or red on cap surface.
searchText.odour: Odour sweetish, slightly mealy, or not distinctive
searchText.taste: Taste not distinctive, or slightly bitter and farinaceous
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid or occasionally subglobose, smooth, 4–8 x 4–6 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium-sized mushroom with a fibrous, scaly brown cap and a bitter taste

searchText.hymenium: Gills, white to cream, becoming slightly yellowish with age
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, sometimes with a shallow depression in the center, smooth and dry, white to pale cream in color, sometimes with a yellowish tint at the center
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapering toward the base, white or pale cream in color, with a smooth to slightly fibrous surface
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in coniferous forests, associated with pines and other conifers, it grows solitary or in small groups among moss and needles
searchText.edibility: Inedible, unpleasant odor and taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body 5–10 cm
searchText.odour: Odour is unpleasant, reminiscent of coal gas or rotten rubber
searchText.microscopy: Spores smooth, elliptical, 8.1-13.0 × 5.5-8.2 µm, basidia typically 4-spored, 40-55 × 9-12 µm
searchText.overview: Small to medium-sized mushroom that is notorious for its unpleasant odor

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, white to pale cream, sometimes becoming grayish with age, edges slightly scalloped, not staining when bruised
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, flattening with age, surface smooth to finely fibrillose, adorned with fine scales, grayish-white with a slightly darker center, margin inrolled when young
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, white to pale gray, slightly fibrillose, may develop grayish discoloration at the base, no ring or veil
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broadleaf trees (e.g., beech, oak) and conifers, in sandy soils or grassy areas, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible, but considered of mediocre quality
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body Medium-sized, stipe 4–8 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, 5–7 × 3–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium-sized mushroom with a pale gray, scaly cap, crowded gills, and a farinaceous odor

searchText.hymenium: Gills, moderately crowded, whitish to pale gray, becoming stained darker with age
searchText.cap: Convex to flat, sometimes slightly depressed, covered with fine gray to dark gray fibrillose scales on a lighter gray background, margin inrolled when young, becoming wavy with age
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, whitish to pale gray, fibrillose, smooth to finely scaly, lighter than cap, without a ring, base slightly thickened
searchText.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with pines, in sandy or well-drained soils, growing in large groups or troops, late summer to late autumn
searchText.edibility: Traditionally considered edible but now discouraged (rhabdomyolysis in high consumption reported)
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4–8 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Not changing color when bruised
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH and FeSO₄ reactions negative on cap and stipe surfaces
searchText.microscopy: Ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, 5–7 × 3–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored, cystidia absent
searchText.overview: Medium-sized grey Tricholoma with a finely fibrous-scaly cap, adnate to notched gills, and a pale fibrillose stipe

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, pale cream to light brown, often becoming darker with age
searchText.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, reddish-brown to cinnamon-brown, covered in coarse, fibrous scales
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, somewhat fibrous, reddish-brown to pale brown, covered with fine fibrils, base slightly bulbous, lacking a ring
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with spruces (rarely with other conifers), in coniferous woodlands, alone, scattered, or gregariously, autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible, due to its bitter taste
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4–10 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH negative, gray, purplish, or reddish to brown on cap surface
searchText.odour: Odour mealy, sometimes fruity and sweet
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, smooth, 5–8 x 4–5.5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate
searchText.overview: A medium-sized, reddish-brown mushroom with a scaly cap and fibrous stipe

searchText.hymenium: Gills, close to crowded, yellow, gleaming when fresh
searchText.cap: Convex at first, becoming broadly convex, nearly flat or shallowly depressed with uplifted margin, golden yellow background with fine grey-brown to fibrils concentrated toward the center
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, pale yellow; smooth to faintly fibrillose, hollow in mature specimens, base with whitish basal mycelium, no ring
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood of conifers, alone, scattered, in groups, summer to fall
searchText.edibility: Inedible, poor quality and bitter
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 2-5 cm long, 3-10 mm thick
searchText.flesh: Flesh does not change much when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface yields a red to pink or orange reaction
searchText.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, hyaline in KOH, ~4-8×4-6 µm; inamyloid, cheilocystidia 50-62.5×10-15 µm, cylindric to subclavate
searchText.overview: Wood-decay mushroom with a golden-yellow cap adorned with fine brown scales, yellow gills

observations.location: Kloostrimetsa soo õpperada, Tallinn, Harjumaa, Eesti

searchText.hymenium: Gills, crowded, bright yellow, becoming darker with age, not staining when bruised
searchText.cap: Convex to broadly convex, flattening with age, covered in purplish scales on a yellow background, giving a fibrous appearance, margin sometimes slightly wavy
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, bright yellow with reddish to purplish fibrils, fibrous texture, often hollow or slightly swollen at the base, no ring or veil
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying conifer wood, in clusters or scattered groups, summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Conditionally edible mushroom of low quality, only at a young age, mature become bitter
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe 5–10 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH red on cap surface, flesh yellow to pale yellow
searchText.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, 3–5 x 2.5–5 µm, basidia 4-spored
searchText.overview: Medium to large mushroom with a striking yellow cap covered in purplish scales

searchText.hymenium: Short-gills frequent, pale brownish to brownish yellow at first, becoming darker brown, edges faintly whitish at maturity
searchText.cap: Convex at first, becoming broadly convex or nearly flat, brown to cinnamon brown, fading to nearly buff, mostly bald, when fresh with whitish partial veil remnants
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Broadly attached to the stem, close or nearly distant
searchText.stipe: Slightly fibrillose to fibrillose-scaly, whitish to brownish, poorly defined, ephemeral ring zone but without a true ring, basal mycelium white
searchText.spore-print: Spore print brownish yellow to cinnamon brown
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying wood, grass / leaf litter, soil in parks, woodlands and forest clearings, (mild late winter), early spring
searchText.edibility: Considered inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 2–5 cm long and 1–4 mm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface negative or grayish
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 6.5–9.5 x 4–5.5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 25–35 x 4–6 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate
searchText.overview: Small mushroom with a finely scaly, powdery cap and slender stipe

searchText.plasmodium-phase: The active, feeding phase appears as a moist, slimy, gelatinous mass, usually pale pink to reddish, slowly moving across decaying wood and consuming microorganisms
searchText.fruiting-bodies: Forms dense, crowded, cushion-shaped to cylindrical sporangia, initially bright pink to red, transitioning to orange, rust-red, or dark brown as they mature, with a dry, granular surface
searchText.description: Spore mass powdery and rusty-brown in mature fruiting bodies
searchText.ecology: Saprobic, found on decaying logs, stumps, and wood debris, late spring to autumn, favoring moist, shaded environments
searchText.edibility: Inedible
searchText.fruit-body: Fruiting body individual sporangia are 2–20 mm long and 1–2 mm wide, entire clusters may span several centimeters across
searchText.microscopy: Spores spherical, finely warted, 6–8 µm, interconnected by a capillitium network
searchText.overview: Strikingly vibrant slime mold that transitions from gelatinous pink plasmodium to dense, colorful fruiting masses

searchText.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, pinkish-brown to brown.
searchText.cap: Convex to flat as it matures, brown with a velvety or slightly rough texture.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, paler than the cap, often swollen or bulbous at the base, adorned with a fine white netting (reticulation) near the top.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, found under broadleaf trees and conifers.
searchText.edibility: Technically edible but not recommended due to its extremely bitter taste.
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 10-15 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Mycorrhizal fungus identifiable by its brown cap, pinkish-brown tubes, and the distinctive netted pattern on its stipe. Although it closely resembles some edible boletes, its notably bitter taste makes it unpalatable. This bitter quality serves as a crucial identification characteristic, distinguishing it from look-alikes.

searchText.hymenium: Pores, small and angular, yellow to olive-yellow when young, becoming olive-brown with age
searchText.cap: Convex, becoming flat with age, dry and velvety, cracked with a reddish flesh, color reddish-brown
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe
searchText.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often tapering at the base, yellowish with reddish streaks, surface smooth or slightly reticulate near the top, no ring or veil
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal with oaks, beeches, and pines, found on acidic soils, late summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Edible but of mediocre quality, has slimy texture
searchText.fruit-body: Medium, cap 3–8 cm in diameter, stipe 4–10 cm long, 0.5–2 cm thick
searchText.chemical-reactions: Ammonia negative to brownish on cap, negative on flesh, KOH negative to brownish on cap, orangish on flesh, iron salts olive on cap, negative on flesh
searchText.microscopy: Spores boletoid-fusiform, smooth, 10–14 x 3–4 µm, yellowish to golden in KOH, inamyloid
searchText.overview: Medium bolete, recognized by its cracked, velvety cap revealing reddish flesh

searchText.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, with fine, yellowish to olive-brown pores.
searchText.cap: 4-10 cm in diameter. Convex, becoming more flattened with age; yellow-brown, olive-brown, or sometimes reddish-brown, often with a slightly downy or felty surface.
searchText.hymenium-attachment: Adnate or slightly descending the stipe.
searchText.stipe: Cylindrical, often with a slightly swollen base; pale yellow or yellow-brown, sometimes with a net-like (reticulated) pattern near the top.
searchText.description: Olive-brown to brown.
searchText.ecology: Mycorrhizal, associating primarily with broadleaf trees and occasionally with conifers, in woods, parks, and forests.
searchText.edibility: Edible, but not highly regarded due to its somewhat bland taste.
searchText.fruit-body: Stipe up to 8 cm tall.
searchText.overview: Distinguished by its velvety cap and its yellow-brownish tones. Unlike some boletes, it doesn't undergo significant color changes when bruised.
searchText.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid and smooth, 11-14 x 4-5 µm.

searchText.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced, interveined; pale yellow to yellow-ochre, becoming slightly orange-ochre with age
searchText.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat with a shallow central depression or umbilicus; smooth, hygrophanous, slightly viscid when moist; yellow-ochre, orange-brown, usually darker centrally
searchText.stipe: Very slender, tough and wiry; yellow-ochre near apex, dark reddish-brown to chestnut below; finely tomentose, with ochre to tawny basal mycelium; ring absent
searchText.ecology: Saprobic on conifer needle litter, twigs and woody debris; coniferous and mixed forests; scattered to densely gregarious; summer to autumn
searchText.edibility: Inedible; bitter and insubstantial
searchText.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2.5–8 cm long and ~0.1–0.25 cm thick
searchText.flesh: Yellowish to orange-brown, very thin and pliant, unchanging when cut
searchText.odour: Distinctive and pleasant scent reminiscent of Moneses uniflora
searchText.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~5.5–8 × 3–4 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, fusoid to clavate; caulocystidia present; clamp connections present
searchText.overview: Tiny orange-brown conifer-litter omphalinoid with a wiry dark stipe

searchText.hymenium: Perithecia embedded in the black stromatic surface, appearing as minute pimple-like bumps with ostioles; white powdery conidia produced externally during the asexual stage
searchText.fruit-body:
Erect, slender, cylindrical to flattened, often forked or antler-like; black, finely hairy near base, with conspicuous white powdery tips when young; becoming entirely charcoal-black and minutely roughened at maturity
Fruit body small to medium; ~2–8 cm tall and ~2–8 mm thick
searchText.stipe: Short to elongated, black, tough and wiry, sometimes longitudinally grooved; base broadened and covered with dark brown to black tomentum
searchText.description: Spore mass white from asexual conidia, dark brown to black from mature ascospores
searchText.ecology:
Saprobic, causing soft rot on decaying hardwood; fallen branches, stumps, logs and buried woody debris; scattered to densely clustered; year-round
Inedible; tough, rubbery and insubstantial
searchText.flesh: White to cream internally, solid, tough and elastic, unchanging when cut
searchText.chemical-reactions: Amyloid apical ring turning blue in Melzer's reagent
searchText.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid to bean-shaped, inequilateral, smooth, brown, ~9.5–13.5 × 4.5–6 µm; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~140–220 µm long; conidia hyaline, smooth, narrowly fusiform-clavate, ~8.5–12 × 3.5–4 µm
searchText.overview: Black antler-like candlesnuff fungus with distinctive white powdery tips on decaying hardwood
